en: Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Having recently attained the six supernormal powers, Mahāmaudgalyāyana desired to deliver his parents and repay the kindness of their nursing him. He then used his divine eye to survey the world.
In the meantime, he saw his deceased mother reborn among the hungry ghosts; she was seen without food or drink, her skin and bones standing together.
Maudgalyāyana was filled with sorrow and immediately took a bowl of rice to go and feed his mother. When his mother received the bowl of rice, she used her left hand to shield the bowl.
As he held food in his right hand, before it had even entered his mouth, it transformed into glowing coals, so that he was unable to eat.

Maudgalyāyana cried out in great distress, wailing and weeping as he hurried back to report this to the Buddha in full detail. The Buddha said, "The roots of your mother's transgressions are deeply entrenched."

This is not something that can be remedied by your power alone. Although your filial piety moves heaven and earth, even the celestial deities, terrestrial spirits, malevolent demons, heretics, Daoist masters, and the gods of the Four Heavenly Kings cannot do anything about it.
You must rely on the majestic spiritual power of the Sangha of the ten directions to attain liberation. I shall now explain the method for deliverance so that all may be saved.
May all those in distress be freed from sorrow and suffering. The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

"On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when the Saṃgha observes the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, one should, for the sake of parents of seven generations past and parents living in the present who are beset by calamities, prepare food of a hundred flavors and five fruits, vessels for drawing and pouring water, fragrant oil, lamps and candles, couches, mats, bedding, and all the sweet delicacies of the world."
Place it in a basin and offer it to the assembly of virtuous monks of the ten directions. On this day, all the holy multitudes— some may be in mountain retreats practicing meditative concentration,

some may have attained the fruits of the four paths, some may be walking in meditation beneath trees, some may possess mastery of the six supernormal powers while teaching śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
and some may be great beings, bodhisattvas of the ten stages, manifesting as bhikṣus by skillful means— are present in the great [assembly].
Within this assembly, all share a single mind as they receive the *pātra-bhara* meal. Possessing pure precepts, the path of the noble Sangha is vast and profound in virtue.

Those who make offerings to such self-disciplined monks shall cause their present parents and six kinds of kinsmen to escape the suffering of the three miserable realms and attain liberation at that very moment;
their food and clothing will become spontaneous. If their parents are currently living...

Such a person shall enjoy happiness and merit for a hundred years. If their parents of seven generations are reborn in heaven, they will be born spontaneously with sovereign mastery within the radiant flowers of the celestial realm.
At that time, the Buddha commanded the assembly of monks from the ten directions: "First, perform a prayer of blessing on behalf of the donor's family.

May the parents of seven generations cultivate the mind of meditative concentration, and only then receive the food. When first receiving the food, one must first place it before the Buddha in the stupa or monastery.
Before the Buddha, after the monks had finished their prayers of blessing, he himself partook of the food.
At that time, the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana and the assembly of great bodhisattvas were all filled with great joy; Maudgalyāyana’s weeping and wailing ceased completely.
On that very day, Maudgalyāyana’s mother was immediately liberated from the suffering of a hungry ghost for one kalpa. Maudgalyāyana again addressed the Buddha, saying: "As for my disciple..."
"Because of the power of the merit of having taken refuge in the Triple Gem and the majestic spiritual power of the Sangha, your birth mother has been delivered.

If, in future ages, all disciples of the Buddha likewise offer the *bōron* (alms bowl) to rescue and deliver their present parents, and even their parents up to the seventh generation, would this not be appropriate?
The Buddha said, "Excellent! You have asked well. This is precisely what I wished to explain, and you have now [spoken it]."
He asked again: "Good son, if there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs, kings, crown princes, ministers, high officials,
the three dukes and hundred officers, or commoners of the myriad people who practice loving-kindness and filial piety,

they should all first perform it for their present parents and their parents of the past seven generations on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the Buddha’s Day of Joy, during the Saṃgha’s Pravāraṇā."

On this day, one should prepare food of a hundred flavors and place it within an *urṇāpātra* (alms bowl). This is offered to the monks of the ten directions who have completed their retreat (*pravāraṇā*). One should make this vow:
"May my present parents live for a hundred years, free from illness and all suffering and affliction.

May my ancestors up to the seventh generation be liberated from the suffering of the hungry ghosts (*preta*) and be reborn among humans and devas, where their merit and happiness shall be boundless. This is how a disciple of the Buddha cultivates filial piety.
As for those who follow [this path], they should constantly remember their parents in every thought-moment, even extending to their parents of seven generations.

On the fifteenth day of the seventh month each year, they should always, with filial piety and compassion, call to mind the parents who gave them birth, and prepare the *bowl-offering* (*urabon*) to bestow upon the Buddhas and the Sangha, thereby repaying the kindness and love of their parents in nurturing and raising them. All disciples of the Buddha should thus respectfully uphold this.
Uphold this Dharma. At that time, the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana and the disciples of the four assemblies rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
This concludes the *Ullambana Sūtra* spoken by the Buddha.

Regarding the mantra for repaying the kindness of one's parents: "In the world, there is no being who does not derive life from their parents. If one can recite this mantra and observe the rites of mourning and honor those long deceased, there is no kindness that will not be repaid."
[Response] Homage to Mṛtadāpāye Svāhā.
The Ritual for Recitation on the Fifteenth Day of the Seventh Month for the Ullambana Offering.
The pure regulations for those who have left the household life are fully recorded herein; worldly worthies and sages alike should follow this model.
In the first month, one must enter a stupa or monastery to perform a great assembly and make offerings.
All sons and daughters who are filial and wish to repay the kindness of their biological parents must begin on the first day of the seventh month, offering incense every morning as a daily service.

Dedicate yourself to single-minded focus. Recite the *Sūtra of the Contemplation of Amitābha* or perform prostrations before the Thirty-five Buddhas on behalf of deceased parents to repent for their transgressions.
This will ensure they most swiftly proceed to the Buddha-land of Immeasurable Light. Thus it is said: [Insert prayer here]
We share this same filial resolve: to cultivate the causes for the Pure Land, to repay the kindness of our two parents, and to repent and eliminate the sins of the three obstacles.

May those who remain obtain fortune and longevity; may those who have passed away attain transcendence. May all enemies and kin throughout the entire Dharma-realm together be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing.
Having finished reciting the *Ullambana Sūtra*, recite the name of Amitābha Buddha in his true golden color (*etc.*).

Recite the name of Amitābha Buddha one hundred times. Recite the names of Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of the Pure Sea each ten times. Having finished, perform the dedication as follows:
By means of these practices, may all roots of goodness repay the debt of gratitude for the labor and virtue of my parents: may those still living enjoy boundless merit, happiness, and longevity;

may those who have passed away leave suffering behind and be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nourishment (*Sukhāvatī*). May all sentient beings within the four debts of gratitude and the three realms of existence, and all beings suffering in the three miserable paths and eight difficult conditions, together receive the cleansing of their flaws through repentance, so that they may all emerge from saṃsāra and be born in the Pure Land.
When evening arrives, having completed the worship of the Thirty-five Buddhas, one says: "We, with a shared vow of filial piety... (and so forth).

When this is finished, one recites the *Amitābha Sūtra*. Upon finishing the recitation of the *Nian wangsheng zhou* (Mantra for Rebirth), one intones: "The True Golden Color of Amitābha Buddha... (and so forth).
Recite the name of Amitābha Buddha one hundred or one thousand times, together with the names of the Bodhisattvas and other holy ones,
and make this vow: "I pray that my parents— whether they currently exist or have already passed away—
wherever they may dwell and wherever they are born, may Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva shine their radiance upon them."

Candle. Sustained by the power of vows, the three obstructions are eliminated and the five faculties are perfected. One gives rise to the aspiration for Bodhicitta and cultivates the causes for the Pure Land.

Those who remain shall fulfill their allotted lifespan and ultimately return to the Jewel Land; those who pass away shall immediately cast off the various realms of existence and take rebirth within a lotus womb.

Beholding the wondrous form, they clarify the mind; hearing the profound discourse, they enter the stages. Receiving the prediction of enlightenment before one’s eyes, they manifest emanations throughout the dust-motes of lands. Broadly...

May all sentient beings be delivered and ascend together to the wondrous land. We humbly pray that our hearts of filial piety may penetrate deeply into the Dharma of the Ultimate Path, so that we shall not be excluded from the assembly of future Buddhas, but become their destined retinue.
May the two adornments be fully perfected and the three enlightenments simultaneously realized.
Though the nature of phenomena has its limits, may our vows be boundless; may we all enter the ocean of the Tathāgata’s vow-nature.
Turn around to face one another. Distribute food and perform the rites as usual.
If there is leisure in the afternoon, recite the *Ullambana Sūtra*, or upon finishing the recitation of the *Amitābha Sūtra*, recite the name of Amitābha Buddha one hundred or one thousand times;
likewise, recite the names of Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of the Pure Sea ten times each.
The dedication prayer says: "By these roots of goodness cultivated through practice... (and so forth).

Alternatively, one may further recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Amitābha Sūtra*, the "Universal Gate" chapter (*Samantamukha-parivarta*), the "Universal Worthy" chapter (*Samantabhadra-parivarta*), or various dharanis such as those from the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra*.
The Ritual for the Recitation of the *Ullambana* Feast (Concluded).
A Commentary on the *Buddha-bhāṣita-ullambana-sūtra*, with Preface; *Xiaoheng Chao*, Volume One.
Expounded by the Śramaṇa of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, Yu Rong; Transcribed.

[Commentary] How marvelous is the Holy Lord! His accumulated filial conduct is peerless; he has established a model for his disciples and perpetuated excellent regulations so that they do not fall into decline.
To understand the purport of the sutra, one must be proficient in the text of the commentary (*śāstra*). In explaining this commentary, there are three major divisions:

first, an explanation of the title of the commentary; second, the identification of the author of the commentary; and third, an explanation of the main body of the commentary. The title of the commentary is divided into two parts; first, the explanation [of the title].
The Main Title. This is followed by the commentary and the preface. The main title is divided into two parts: first, an analytical explanation; second, a collective explanation.

The analytical explanation is further divided into two: first, an analysis of the title of the sūtra being explained; second, an analysis of the characters of the commentary explaining it. Regarding the title of the sūtra:
in the language of India, it is *buddhāvatamsakanāmamahāvaipulyasūtra*; in the language of China, it is "The Awakened One" (*Jue-zhe*).
It is called the *Sūtra on Saving Those Hanged Upside-Down*.

Now, because it accords with local customs to generate goodness, its phrasing is smooth and compliant, and it contains manifold meanings, it combines both Chinese and Sanskrit terms while retaining certain phonetic corruptions and abbreviations; thus it is titled the *Buddha-spoken Ullambana Sūtra*.
"Buddha" (*buddha*) in Sanskrit is abbreviated as "Fo" (佛) in Chinese; this means "the Awakened One. Here, "one" (*zhe*, 者) signifies the agent, whose essence is—

It is untainted (*anāsrava*). The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are conventional designations. The essence of awakening is wisdom (*prajñā*). It discerns and severs hindrances; it illuminates both the ultimate and the conventional truths;

it awakens oneself and awakens others; and its practice of awakening is perfected. These three types of awakening correspond respectively to the exclusion of ordinary beings, the followers of the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas.
Only the Tathāgata alone has reached the other shore, presiding over the ten directions and grasping the five natures.
He is called the Teacher. Because his three types of awakening are perfectly luminous, he is named Buddha. In the Sanskrit language, this is *nirdeśa*, which translates here as "Expounding.

He vibrates the perfect sound to awaken the multitude and proclaims the wondrous meaning to accord with their capacities; he benefits beings and guides the deluded, and thus he is named the Expounder.
Regarding the term *yulanpen*: those who translate the scriptures in the Great Song today state that these are all corruptions and abbreviations of the Sanskrit language.
In its complete and correct form, it should be called *ulambana*. It carries the meanings of filial piety, offering, gratitude, and being suspended upside down.
The word *pen* is likewise a corruption; formerly it was called *pénzuǎnà*, now it is called *ménzuǒluó*, and it is also called *ménzuǒnǎ*. [In Chinese: Flower.

Regarding the term "vessel of salvation" (*jiùqì*): interpreting the phrasing according to its underlying meaning, it is called a "vessel for rescuing those in inverted suspension. One should prepare vessels of gold, silver, or other materials according to one's means;
within these vessels, one should place food, a hundred flavors, sweet delicacies, the five fruits, and other such exquisite items to make offerings to the Triple Gem.

This merit shall support one’s parents and benefit both the living and the deceased. The four meanings [of this practice] are intended to signify that by practicing filial piety, one... [the text continues].
One makes offerings to accumulate merit, thereby repaying the kindness of those who have nurtured one and rescuing others from the suffering of being "hanging upside down.

This primarily takes the sense of rescuing those hanging upside down as its core meaning, while other meanings are included as well. Since hungry ghosts and others have their hearts scorched by thirst-mirages and their bellies oppressed by the fire of hunger, their lives consist of nothing but gasping breaths;
their suffering is like being suspended upside down. By making offerings to accumulate merit, one rescues them from this suffering of being upside down; therefore, [it is so called].

This is for the sake of its name. However, the underlying meaning has both general and specific aspects. As for the specific aspect: Maudgalyāyana, having attained the Way, wished to repay the kindness of his parents.

He perceived through his vision that his deceased mother had fallen among the hungry ghosts; yet, as his supernatural powers were insufficient to save her, he addressed the World-Honored One, expressing his grief and earnest plea in full detail.
The Buddha immediately instructed him in the offering of the *Ullambana* bowl; by gathering merit to dedicate toward her rescue, she was immediately delivered.
To be free from suffering, the sutra below states: The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana, "On the fifteenth day of the seventh month,

when the Sangha of the ten directions performs the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, one should prepare food of a hundred flavors and five fruits, water jars and basins, fragrant oil, lamps and candles, couches, mats, and bedding— every kind of worldly delicacy—
and place them within the vessels to offer as alms to the assembly of virtuous monks of the ten directions."
It continues, saying: "At that time, Maudgalyāyana’s mother was immediately liberated from the suffering of an eon of hungry ghosts on that very day.
As for those who understand this—whether they be members of the Sangha, laypeople, kings, ministers, or commoners—all should establish this bowl-offering for their parents.
Baonan passed away. Therefore, the subsequent scripture states:

"If there are monks, nuns, kings, crown princes, or even commoners who practice compassion and filial piety, they should all, for the sake of their present parents and their deceased parents of the past seven generations," [perform offerings].
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, place food of a hundred flavors within the *bowl of liberation* (*urabon*) and offer it to the monks of the ten directions who have completed their retreat.
May our parents of the present life enjoy a lifespan of a hundred years, free from illness and all suffering and affliction.
May our parents of seven generations be released from the suffering of the hungry ghosts and be reborn among humans and devas, where their merit and joy shall be boundless. The Bowl.
The term "pan" (vessel) refers to the vessel capable of saving; "uraga" (or ulam) refers to the suffering to be saved from.
Thus, the "Uraga Pan" is called the "Uraga-bun" (Uraga-vessel), according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound) analysis. The Sanskrit term *sūtra* was formerly translated as *shudara*.
*Śūtra* (脩妒路) is a corruption; it is here translated as *Kṣānti-sūtra* (契經). This preserves the essence while abbreviating the function, simply calling it a *sūtra*.

Vasubandhu explains the term *sūtra* through four meanings: because it can "string together" (1) the basis (*āśraya*), (2) the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), (3) the phenomena (*dharma*), and (4) the meaning (*artha*).

That which is spoken of in a certain place, by means of something, for a certain purpose, is called the "basis. [The characteristics refer to] the characteristics of the ultimate and conventional truths, and the wholesome...

Regarding the dharmas such as skillful means and the meanings such as the underlying intent (*samdhāya*), the *Shangsheng shu* (Commentary by Shangsheng) states: "Sūtra" means to collect, to thread together, to be constant, and to be the Dharma.
Birth is gathered and sustained by the teaching, forever severing the cage of afflictions; principle relies upon the text to be threaded together, long remaining free from dispersal and extinction.

It is the eternal track for the hundred spirits and the excellent regulation for the myriad leaves [of the Buddha's teachings]. Because it benefits beings and elucidates the truth, it is designated as a "sūtra. Now, as for the essence of this sūtra:
It has as its nature the four factors of phonemes (*śabda*), names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*). This is because these four factors are able to express meaning.
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that a single phoneme and its meaning constitute the essence of a sūtra. When the single factor of phonemes is expanded, it includes names and phrases;
when contracted, it includes sound. Thus, in total, it takes five factors as its essence: sound, name, phrase, syllable, and the expressed meaning. For this reason...
Because it excels in encompassing and benefiting through five dharmas, this sūtra is named the *Ullambana Sūtra*.
Since its speaker is the Buddha, it is called "spoken by the Buddha" (*buddha-bhāṣita*). This *Ullambana Sūtra* spoken by the Buddha is therefore named the *Buddhabhāṣita-Ullambana-Sūtra*.

Furthermore, that which is spoken is precisely the *Ullambana Sūtra*. It should be understood that the *Ullambana Sūtra* spoken by the Buddha [is named] according to the principles of *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound) and *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound).
Second, to distinguish the meaning of the word "commentary" (*shu*): "Commentary" (*shu*) is synonymous with "record. It carries the sense of compilation and recording.
Because it compiles and records the corresponding texts and meanings of various teachings to explain the intent of this sūtra, it is called a "commentary" (*shu*). Moreover, as for "commentary":

A *shu* (pronounced with the level tone) means to distribute, to divide, and to decide. It is called a *shu* because it distributes and clarifies the meanings of the text, distinguishes its underlying purports, and decides upon the relative superiority or inferiority [of interpretations].
Its substance consists of five factors: the sounds, names, phrases, and sentences of the commentator (*shuzhu*), as well as the meanings they express.
However, since the compositions of former sages are invariably intentional, there are briefly three intentions for composing this commentary on the sutra.

First, it is to repay the requests of both the monastic and lay communities. Thus, the sub-commentary below states: "Now, having returned to my hometown, I have established [this teaching] according to the days.
Elders of both the clergy and laity, moved by a mixture of sorrow and joy, have followed its practice;

with one voice and in unison, they requested the composition of this new commentary, so as to satisfy their expectations and elucidate the essential Way. Second, it is because I wish to benefit my parents and others. As stated below: "I..."

That which is now praised and recounted is for the sake of those who are currently living and those who have passed away, both self and others, so that they may be free from suffering and always abide in peace and happiness.
Thirdly, it is because I wish to preserve these ritual protocols to show them to future generations. As stated below: "Zongmi has relied upon this for practice and veneration for many years;

furthermore, I have lectured on its teachings to reveal them to those who have not yet heard them. In order to establish a model for later students, I have composed this commentary. Emperor Gaozu of the Southern Qi dynasty constantly...
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, one sends the *ulambana* offerings to various monasteries to provide for the monks during the *pravāraṇā*.
Yan’s Family Instructions (*Yanjia jiaxun*) states: "Regarding the *ulambana* feast on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, I hope that you will practice it without ceasing.
That which has been esteemed by sages and worthies since antiquity has a long history. It was during the third reign of the Great Song, in the year of Dingyou."

In the third month of autumn, the Emperor succeeded to the throne. Reflecting upon the profound kindness of Heaven, in the third month of summer he issued an edict to the Monastic Registrars of the two precincts to inquire about the ritual procedures for the *Ullambana* (Alaṃbana) festival.

At that time, Daśi Dashi, the Great Master and Registrar of the Left Precinct, commanded the purple-robed śramaṇa Xingcai to compile the ritual procedures based on the sūtras and commentaries, which were then presented to the Emperor.
The Emperor, having received it, performed the rites according to the Dharma. Consequently, the lecturing and listening to this scripture flourished.
Now, in the fourth generation of the Emperor, in the year *wuxu* (642 CE), the month of *guimao*, he succeeded to the imperial throne.

By the beginning of autumn, he issued an edict for thirty-seven monks to establish a *dharmāśoka* at the Yanqing Hall for seven days and seven nights; during the day they were to lecture on this scripture, and at other times perform ritual recitations.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, another edict was issued for two hundred and fifty monastic officials from the two streets—

namely, the Tripiṭaka masters who translated scriptures and those who lectured on the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras— to assemble at the site of the ritual hall to pay homage to eighty-four thousand precious stūpas containing śarīra relics.
At Changchun Hall, a Ullambana feast was established to gather all manner of sublime benefits to support his father.
The King’s celestial carriage repays the vast grace of Heaven; such an extraordinary event of the Imperial Court surpasses antiquity and transcends the present—never before has there been its equal.
At that time, I was also among those present, and thus I have briefly recorded this, hoping that the wise and virtuous may take note.
It is simply a matter of "the superior acting and the inferior following. This can be understood from the topical outline (*shouke*). Regarding the subsequent *paribhāṣā* (explanatory analysis):

the original purpose of composing this commentary (*śāstra*) was to explain the meaning of the scriptural text and to manifest the intent of the sūtra; therefore, its name is designated according to the scripture it explains.
"Commentary on the *Buddhabhāṣita-Ullambana-sūtra*" is an example of the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound. This can be understood from the topical outline. Second, the *paribhāṣā*.

Regarding the "Preface and Sequence" (bing xu): "Preface" (xu) means to set forth. It sets forth the beginning and end of the filial path of this sutra, responding to the heart of the filial son, uprooting the suffering of his two parents, and repaying the kindness of their nurturing and raising;
it also records the circumstances by which these teachings spread to this land and the reasons for composing this commentary.
Furthermore, "preface" (*xu*) means "thread" (*xu*). Just as a cocoon gains its thread, once the thread is exhausted, one has the silk of the entire cocoon;

when a commentary (*shu*) gains its preface, once the preface is exhausted, one has the meaning of the entire scripture. "And" (*bing*) means "to include. It is not merely an exegesis of the scripture, but includes the composition of this preface as well.
Therefore, it is said "Together with the Preface. △ Second, identifying the author of the Commentary.
[Commentary] Composed by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Chongguo. [Sub-commentary] As for Chongguo:
it is the present Xichong County in Guozhou. In the past, during the Han dynasty, it was the county of Chongguo.
Now, the old name is cited, with the character for "county" (*xian*) omitted; thus it is called Chongguo.
However, the author of this commentary originally resided in Chang’an at Caotang Monastery, later entering Mount Zhongnan.

The reason for citing "Chongguo" here is intended to signify that he practiced the Way of Filial Piety in accordance with the sutras, as it was his parents’ home and the place of his birth—thereby demonstrating that his conduct was rooted in filial sincerity and an unforgetting devotion to his kin.

Because of [the term] *śramaṇa*. "Śramaṇa" is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term; in full it is *śramaṇa*, which means "one who has stilled evil. It is so called because one stills what is unwholesome.
It is also called "diligent stilling," because one diligently cultivates various virtues and stills what is unwholesome. The *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) states:
"The meaning of 'stilling' (*śama*) in *śramaṇa* is that by attaining the Dharma, one finds temporary tranquility; this is also the stilling of evil. The correct pronunciation is... [text truncated].
*Śramaṇa*. Also called *śramaṇaka*; this means "merit" (*guānláo*), referring to the fact that one has cultivated the wondrous Way and possesses merit.
Here, the Sanskrit term is abbreviated, hence it is called *shāmen*. As for Zongmi, this is the name of the author of the commentary.
The inscription is extremely extensive; its essentials are summarized as follows: Chan Master Guifeng was styled Zongmi; his surname was He; he was from Guozhou.

He was a native of Xichong County. He was born in the first year of the Jianzhong era and received full ordination in the second year of the Yuanhe era. Later, he visited Master Yuan of Suizhou to receive the transmission of the seal of the mind.

Furthermore, he traveled extensively to seek out renowned masters, greatly expanding his knowledge and insight. He lectured on the *Awakening of Faith*, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda Śāstra*, and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

Subsequently, he composed commentaries on the *Awakening of Faith*, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda Śāstra*, and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

His commentaries and sub-commentaries on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Ullambana Sūtra*, the *Dharmadhātudarśana*, and the *Pratibhāna-praṇidhāna Sūtra*, as well as his *Chan yuan quan* (Investigation into the Source of Chan), which compiled the Chan terminology of various schools, along with his letters, verses, and discourses, total more than ninety fascicles; all have been transmitted to the world.
In the second year of the Tahe era, on the Qingsheng Jie festival, Emperor Wenzong issued an edict for him to enter the inner palace to receive an audience.
Regarding the essentials of all dharmas, he was granted a purple robe and square-cut cassock. He soon requested permission to return to the mountains.
On the sixth day of the first month of the first year of the Huichang era, he passed away while seated in the Xingfu Pagoda Cloister.

On the twenty-second day of that same month, the clergy and laity enshrined his whole body at Mount Guifeng for cremation, from which dozens of *śarīra* relics were obtained. His secular age was sixty-two; his monastic seniority (*bhikṣu-vaṃśa*) was three [years].
14. This is the posthumous stūpa for the Chan Master Dinghui (Qinglian), erected later. As for the term "narrative" (*shu*): it means to recount, to describe, or to compose.
Internally, it records the teachings of the Tripiṭaka; externally, it gathers from various books. There are no words that do not pass through the classics, and no matters that are not ancient.

It compiles and recounts literary meanings, arranging them into chapters and sections; thus it is called a "narrative. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-vyākhyā* states: "To recount principles is called a narrative. First...

Because it comes from a cause, it is called "arising"; because it is produced through effort, it is called "conditioned"; and because it newly arises now, [it is so designated]. △ Third, the explanation of the main text of the commentary has two parts:

first, the commentator’s introduction; second, the commentator’s main exposition. Within the first part, there are four sections: first, a general clarification of filial piety as the origin and motivation for the arising of the sutra;
second, a formal manifestation of the purpose for which this sutra was preached by the Buddha; third, the transmission of the teaching to this land... [text continues]
The Master Tuzuisheng performed the ritual service. The four sections consist of verses extolling the virtues of the Buddha Śākyamuni and prayers for aspiration.

That these four sections follow this specific order is the established literary form: when one wishes to formally extol a particular matter, one first provides a general account of its origins and background.

The words reach far, yet the intent lies near. This general exposition of the Way of Filial Piety originally resides in the realm of cosmic resonance (*qi xiang*). It gradually permeates all living beings;
for both Śākyamuni and the Sage Confucius take filial piety as their fundamental principle when establishing teachings to transform the people.

Thus, there is the text of the first section. Having provided this general exposition, one may then inquire in detail: for what reason did the Buddha preach this sutra? Therefore, there is [the second section].

The second [section] clarifies the purpose for which the Buddha preached this sūtra. As for that purpose: it was for the sake of filial sons who wish to rescue their compassionate parents from suffering and intend to repay the kindness of their upbringing;
therefore, he preached this sūtra to demonstrate its sublime practice. This explains the circumstances in the Western Land (India).
Next, one should reveal the causes and conditions by which it spread and was transmitted here in this land (China); thus, there is the third [section].
The teachings have flowed into this land and are observed and practiced according to the ritual manuals.

Here, the sons of the Śākya, relying on these instructions, establish assemblies, lecture on the sutras to exhort the masses, and compose commentaries to explain the scriptures, thereby establishing a model for future students. Now, as he is about to compose a commentary, he seeks the protection of the Sage;

thus, he first articulates his intention for composing the commentary before setting pen to paper. Therefore, there is the fourth section: a hymn extolling the virtues of the Buddha Śākyamuni and a prayer for blessings.
Therefore, the four sections follow this sequence. In the first three [sections], the first clarifies the beginning and end of filiality;
the second [clarifies] its origin in the realm of qi and phenomena.
[Commentary]: It begins with the primordial chaos and pervades heaven and earth.
[Commentary]: The primal qi of purity, before the clear and the turbid had been differentiated, was shaped like a bird’s egg; this is called Chaos (*hundun*).

Once the clear and the turbid were already differentiated, they are called the Two Polarities (*er-yi*). It is said that the clear qi ascended; being vaulted and unobstructed, its circular covering is called Heaven (*tian*).

The turbid qi sinks downward; vast, solid, and thick, it is called Earth when it first bears [all things]. With humans dwelling in its midst, these three are collectively termed the Three Powers (Sancai).
The *Zhouyi Gouming jue* states: "Before the Great Earth was divided, it was named Taiyi (Great Ease); then there was Taichu (Great Beginning)."

There is the Great Beginning (Taishi), the Great Primal Essence (Taisu), and the Great Ultimate (Taiji); these are called the Five Transitions. When the phenomena and their appearances have not yet taken form, it is called the Great Change (Taiyi).
When the primal qi first begins to sprout, it is called the Great Commencement (Taichu). The initial stage of phenomena and appearances is called the Great Beginning.

When forms undergo transformation and possess substance, it is called the Great Primal Essence. When forms and substance are first fully constituted, it is called the Great Ultimate. These transform and circulate the five qi.

Therefore, they are called the Five Transmissions (*wuyun*). When the phenomena of qi, appearance, and substance are fully present yet not yet separated from one another, these are all names for the *Taiyi* (Great Ease), of which there are five types.
The *Lidiji* states: "When heaven and earth have not yet been divided, it is called *Taiyi*. When the signs of qi first begin to sprout, it is called *Taichu* (Great Beginning).
When heights and depths correspond to one another, it is called *Taishi* (Great Origin). Once substance and appearance are fully formed, it is called *Taisu* (Great Purity)."
Heaven is high and earth is low; this is called the Great Ultimate (*taiji*). The round is pure and the square is turbid; these are called the Two Polarities (*liangyi*).
Humans dwell between them, completing the Three Powers (*sancai*). The *Yiwei Tonggua* states: "The Great Ultimate gives birth to the Two Polarities.
This means that the light and pure qi rises above to become Heaven, while the heavy and turbid qi sinks below to become Earth. With humans added to these, they are named the Three Powers.
The *Xùguǐ* (Sequence of the Hexagrams) of the *Yì* says:

"Only after there are Heaven and Earth and the myriad things do the rites of ruler and subject, father and son, elder and younger, and husband and wife arise, along with the distinctions between the honorable and the humble, and the superior and the subordinate. Now, the manifestation of filial piety begins within the primordial *huànchùn* qi;
it permeates the five phases (*wùyùn*) and gradually follows the primordial qi as it fills and pervades Heaven and Earth throughout the three realms.
"Talent" (*cai*) means to penetrate all things. Thus, the *Xiaojing Yuanshenqi* says: "The primal qi is in a state of chaotic unity; filial piety is contained within it.
The *Liji*, in the "Jiyi" chapter, records that Zengzi said: "As for filial piety: set it down and it fills heaven and earth; spread it out and it spans the four seas;
apply it to future generations and there is no distinction between morning and evening; extend it and cast it forth to the east..."
It accords with the Eastern Sea; extending it, it accords with the Western Sea; the same applies to the Southern and Northern Seas. (The *Erya* states:
"The Eastern Yi, the Western Rong, the Southern Man, and the Northern Di—these four who are obscure and ignorant are called the Four Seas. To summarize its meaning:

from the Son of Heaven above down to the common people below, throughout all times—years, months, days, and nights—and in all places—the four directions, above and below—at [all these times and places],...

Regarding all things—whether noble or base, high or low—in every instance of advancing or retreating, moving or remaining still, speaking or remaining silent, and in matters of likes and dislikes, joy and sorrow, one should always act in accordance with the principles of the people and the myriad things;

this is what is called filial piety (*xiao*). As for those who increase or diminish their practice of filial piety, among all sentient beings, whether in the hidden realm or the manifest world, who possess parents, they should always be cautious in their conduct.
To be cautious in conduct is to respect one’s own person. To respect one’s own person...
This means not damaging one's physical integrity. Not damaging one's physical integrity means not causing one's parents anxiety;
therefore, it is called filial piety (*xiao*). The Master said: "To cut down a tree or kill an animal at a time that is not appropriate is not filial piety. Zengzi said:
The body is the physical legacy bestowed by one’s parents. How could one dare not to revere this legacy? To be undignified in one’s private conduct is a failure of filial piety;
to be disloyal toward one’s ruler is a failure of filial piety; to be disrespectful in office is a failure of filial piety; to be untrustworthy toward friends is a failure of filial piety;
and to lack courage on the battlefield is a failure of filial piety. If these five duties are not fulfilled, calamity will descend upon the family.
How could one dare not to revere one's kin? Now, to clarify the Way of Filial Piety: viewed from beginning to end, it encompasses the five phases;

viewed from top to bottom, it penetrates the three powers (the Heaven, Earth, and Human). Viewed across the four seas, it spans all things. Its ultimate virtue is profound and subtle, deep and yet vast;
thus it is said that it begins in the primordial chaos and fills the heavens and earth. II. It permeates all living beings.
*Liṅ* (Spirit).
[Commentary] It penetrates both humans and deities, and permeates both the noble and the humble.

[Sub-commentary] Filial piety penetrates both the hidden (*yōu*) and the manifest (*xiǎn*). Regarding the manifest, "humans" is cited to encompass others such as beasts; regarding the hidden, "deities" is cited to encompass others.
[This applies to] ghosts and so forth; thus, it encompasses both humans and spirits. From the Son of Heaven above down to the common people below, there are five classes of persons in total.
Among them, those such as slaves and servants are all termed "lowly," while the rest, regardless of age, are termed "noble.

Although noble and lowly differ, in practicing filial piety and serving one's parents, they are no different from one another; therefore, [filial piety] penetrates both the noble and the lowly. Thus, it is called the "five classes."
Regarding "humans," there are five categories: first, the Son of Heaven; second, the feudal lords; third, the high ministers and great officers; fourth, the scholars; and fifth, the common people.
Each has its own chapter, which are collectively termed the "Five Forms of Filial Piety," as explained in the *Classic of Filial Piety*. The preface to that scripture states:

"Although the applications of the five forms of filial piety differ, the source of the hundred practices is not distinct. Thus, the commentary says this. △ Second, Confucianism and Buddhism are equally observed.
[Commentary] Both Confucianism and Buddhism take this as their fundamental principle.

[Sub-commentary] The preceding section, based on Confucian teachings, has set forth the origins and details of filial piety. This passage points to both Confucianism and Buddhism as taking it as their fundamental principle.

The fact that the Buddhist teachings take this as their fundamental principle is omitted in the main commentary for brevity; I shall now provide it as an aid. It penetrates both the spiritual and the human realms, and spans both the noble and the humble, beginning with the ultimate truth.

It reaches the ultimate limits and fills the world; it encompasses both the holy and the ordinary, and extends throughout all realms of existence. Both Confucians and Buddhists take it as their fundamental principle.
Now, that which the Confucian school venerates consists of the Five Constant Virtues, of which benevolence (*ren*) is the foremost. Benevolence, in turn, takes filial piety (*xiao*) as its root.

Based upon these five virtues, one establishes oneself and spreads one’s fame, brings peace to the state, and achieves orderly transformation. They are the source of a hundredfold righteous deeds; for this reason, they are venerated. Therefore—

The *Classic of Filial Piety* states: "Filial piety is the root of virtue. Regarding the so-called Five Constant Virtues—benevolence (*ren*), righteousness (*yi*), propriety (*li*), wisdom (*zhi*), and trustworthiness (*xin*)—to cherish life and loathe killing is benevolence;
to recognize kindness and repay it is righteousness; to be respectful and diligent toward elders and juniors is propriety;
to be quick-witted and possessed of much knowledge is wisdom; and to establish conduct that may be relied upon is trustworthiness. It further states: "Not killing is benevolence; not stealing..."
Righteousness consists in being purposeful; propriety consists in not being disorderly; wisdom consists in not being licentious; and trustworthiness consists in being loyal and sincere.

Because these five originate from this [human nature], kings employ them to govern the state, and gentlemen employ them to establish their person. That they must never be neglected for even a moment is what defines them as the Five Constant Virtues.
That which is the primary tenet of the Śākya teaching consists of the Three Studies, of which the Precepts are foremost. Furthermore, the essence of the Precepts is filial piety.
Because of this filial piety, his fame is heard throughout immeasurable worlds;

he is able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, severing hindrances and realizing the principle to ultimately achieve Buddhahood. Since it is the source of the ten thousand virtues, it is held as the primary tenet. Thus, the Brahmā...

The *Jingang jing* (Diamond Sūtra) says: "Be filial toward one's parents, teachers, monks, and the Triple Gem; be filial toward the Dharma of the Ultimate Way. Filiality is called the precepts (*śīla*).
This is the fundamental source of all Buddhas, the root of practicing the Bodhisattva path, and the foundation for all the sons of the Buddha within the great assembly.
As for the 'Three Studies,' they are referred to as discipline (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). To prevent wrongdoing and give rise to goodness is called discipline."

Concentration (*samādhi*) is defined as the mind being one-pointed upon a single object; wisdom (*prajñā*) is defined as decisive discernment and selection. Furthermore, ethical discipline (*śīla*) and concentration constitute the gateway to merit (*puṇya*), while wisdom constitutes the gateway to knowledge (*jñāna*).
Through these two gateways of merit and knowledge, one benefits both oneself and others, transcends the suffering of birth and death, and enters the bliss of *nirvāṇa*.

One should constantly and uninterruptedly cultivate these three trainings—the sublime practices of merit and knowledge—to realize the three bodies: the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body.
The body is eternally abiding; it is, in sequence, immovable and characterized by uninterrupted continuity.
This is called the peerless threefold eternity that transcends the world, unlike the minor five kinds of eternity found in the mundane world. △ Third, pointing out and concluding with praise.
[Commentary] It is nothing other than the Way of Filial Piety (*xiàodào*).
[Sub-commentary] This identifies and sets forth the practice of filial piety while excluding other forms of goodness; hence it says, "it is nothing other than the Way of Filial Piety.

The gentleman makes this his essential task; when the foundation is established, the Way arises. The Bodhisattva binds himself by means of this as his precepts (*śīla*); when the precepts are established, the fruit is fulfilled. Filial piety...
"Filiality" (xiao) means the principle of being obedient, loving, and respectful, following one's parents' commands. "The Way" (dao) means the principle of taking correct reasoning as the foundation.

It is precisely through this practice—loving and respecting elders, obeying their commands without opposition, demonstrating principles, and benefiting others—that one can give rise to manifold virtues;

therefore, it is called "Filial Way" (xiàodào). Furthermore, the *Commentary on the Classic of Filial Piety* (*Xiàojīng shū*) states: "Filiality is the general term for serving one’s parents. It also implies 'to nourish' (chù), meaning to cherish..."
It is also *shùn* (accordance). It means to serve one’s parents well. This refers to the way of serving one’s kin:

constantly maintaining it in one's heart, exhausting oneself in providing physical care and nourishment, being joyful and affectionate in one's inner mind, and following their will without opposition; therefore, it is called *xiào* (filiality). *Dào* (the Way) means the sense of thorough penetration.
Filial conduct penetrates throughout the world, and the people thereby attain harmony and concord. *Yú* (it) is a particle used for emphasis. △ Second, the actual exposition.
This sutra clarifies two reasons for the Buddha’s teaching. First, his compassionate response to filial sincerity.
[Commentary]: He responds to the earnest sincerity of the filial son, rescues his parents from their suffering and calamity, and repays the boundless grace and virtue of Heaven.
[Commentary]: "Should" (應) means to respond or attend to. A filial son is called a "filial son" because he is obedient and respectful; it does not refer specifically to one who is observing mourning.

Maudgalyāyana’s earnest and sincere invitation to the Buddha contained both a general and a specific intent. The specific intent was for the sake of his deceased mother, who had fallen among the hungry ghosts.
Unable to save themselves, they entreated the Buddha to seek the Dharma so as to deliver them. Furthermore, those who have attained realization do so because all people possess parents;
seeing that these parents are in distress, they desire to rescue and liberate them in order to repay their kindness.

Thus, they entreated the Buddha to reveal the essential and sublime Dharma-gate. Therefore, the World-Honored One, in response to their sincere devotion, preached this Dharma-gate to manifest its essentials.
[One should] act to rescue one’s parents from suffering, hardship, and peril.

As for "parents," this refers to both one’s biological parents and parents up to the seventh generation (as the general and specific textual passages have already been cited previously). Regarding "Hao Tian" (the Vast Heaven): the *Erya* states, "In spring it is called Cang Tian;
in summer, Hao Tian; in autumn, Min Tian; and in winter, Shang Tian. "Hao" means "great. It refers to the sky during the height of summer, when the sunlight is scorching.
The vital energy (*qi*) fills the six realms of existence without end. It is by means of this that the various grains, crops, fragrant herbs, and groves of trees reach maturity.

Heaven bestows this grace, yet it never has a mind to complain of its toil and hardship. Parents are likewise so: they give birth to me and nourish me; their bellies were more patient toward me than my own.
They turned toward the dry and moved toward the damp for me, suckling and raising me; they swallowed the bitter while spitting out the sweet.

As they grew up under their compassionate instruction, [the parents'] heart of pity and concern never abandoned them for even a moment. Regarding such kindness and virtue, [the parents] never once felt weary of the toil and hardship involved.
Therefore, the debt of gratitude owed to one's parents surpasses that of the vast heavens. The *Enzhong jing* (Sutra on the Weight of Gratitude) states: The Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"When humans live in this world, their parents are their kin. Without a father, one is not born; without a mother, one is not nurtured."
For this reason, one is entrusted to the mother’s womb; for ten months the body is carried within. When the years are complete and the months fulfilled, both mother and child face peril.
Upon birth, one falls onto the grass. It continues, saying: "There is no father who is not affectionate, and no mother who does not nourish.

A compassionate mother nurtures her child, even going so far as to leave the carriage behind. From the ten fingernails, she consumes the impurities of her child. The child drinks the mother’s milk—eight *hu* and four *dou*."
When one calculates and deliberates upon the kindness of one's mother, it is as vast as the great heavens and has no limit. Alas, compassionate mother! How can her grace ever be repaid?

The Buddha revealed sublime practices so that such filial sons might recompense her kindness and repay her virtue; thus the commentary says this. △ Second, pointing out the details and concluding with praise.
[Commentary] It is none other than the teaching of the *Ullambana-piṭaka*.

[Sub-commentary] The concluding praise is as can be understood. △ Third, the transmission of the teaching to this land and its observance according to ritual: Part Two. First, seeking the Dharma and practicing it in accordance with the rites;
this further has two sections. First, mourning for and commemorating deceased relatives.

[Commentary] Zongmi’s transgressions: in his youth, he lost his parents; he has constantly experienced the sorrow of snow and frost, and harbors forever the resentment of wind-blown trees. [Sub-commentary] "Transgression" (*xìn*) refers to the omen of calamity.

"In his youth" refers to the years of childhood. Now, as a son... morning... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a Buddhist commentary, likely the *Zongjing lu* or related works by Zongmi. The translation reflects the specific terminology and structure of the original.)

In the evening, one serves their parents, providing respectful care and enduring labor; following their moods without offense, offering warm and cool water to bring them joy, and not grieving when they fall ill or pass away, one thus attains eternal blessings and longevity.
By serving them with delicious food, even when parents are ill, a child might say they were unskilled in nursing;
how much more so in the event of their death? This is surely my own transgression, whose calamity has reached my parents, leading to such a state for my child.
Regarding the loss of both parents at a tender age: concerning "snow and frost," the *Jiyi* (Meaning of Sacrifices) states:
"In autumn, when the frost and snow have fallen, the gentleman treads upon them and necessarily feels a heart of melancholy; this is not merely because of the cold.

In spring, when the rain and dew have moistened the ground, the gentleman treads upon them and necessarily feels a heart of trepidation, as if he were about to see them again. He is startled by their shadow.
It is a matter of transformation. Thus, during the seasonal transitions, they offer one another consolation, all expressing words of poignant feeling and longing remembrance.
Whenever the Master encounters scenes of snow, moonlight, frost, or dew, he reflects upon his parents and constantly harbors a sense of sorrowful grief.
In the "Meaning of Sacrifices" (*Jiyi*), Yue Zheng Zichun says: "When lifting a single foot, one dares not forget one's parents;
when uttering a single word, one dares not forget one's parents. Regarding the "Wind and Tree" (*Fengshu*), Gao Yu says in the *Han Shi Waizhuan*:
"The tree wishes to be still, yet the wind does not cease; the son wishes to provide for his parents, yet they do not wait. That which goes forth and does not return is age.
Furthermore, "that which cannot be seen again is one's parents" (from the *Kongzi Jiayu*; Master Qiwu also voiced this lament). Gao Yu traveled throughout the world for study from his youth;
later, upon returning, he lost his parents, and thus he uttered this lament. Its principle is like that of wind and trees: if the wind ceases, the trees will surely become calm and still.
If one has parents, one must certainly attend to them with service and nourishment, offering reverence and joy. [The Master] laments that he himself lacks such parents to serve and nourish;

thus he utters this sigh. The Master of the Commentary (*Sūshǔ*) was likewise: he perpetually harbored the grief of the "wind-blown tree" (the mourning for one's parents), grieving that he could not personally attend to and nourish his own parents.
Part Two: Reflecting on Repaying Their Hardships. This section has two parts. First: reflecting that the worldly path of filial piety does not benefit the deceased spirit.
Furthermore, there are two [points]. First, one’s thoughts reach the limit of filial sincerity.
[Commentary] "I venture to say" (qie yi): that is, to think privately.
It does not take the form of spoken words; one reflects on it in private thought. The *Hanjian* says: "Heaven..."

The mound for a son was three *ren* high, planted with pine trees. For the feudal lords (*zhūhóu*), it was half that height, planted with cypress trees. For the great officers (*dàfū*), it was eight feet, planted with *luán* trees.
For the scholar-officials (*shì*), it was four feet, planted with *huái* trees. For the common people (*shūrén*), there were no mounds; they planted willows and poplars.
According to the *Hòuhànshū*, pines and cypresses were planted universally. Today, when one speaks of "mounds" (*fēnlǒng*), it generally refers collectively to gravesites, burial mounds, and hills.
Furthermore, in ancient times, once the mourning period for one's parents had ended, the son would carry earth on his back to form their burial mounds and plant cypress trees in rows.

He would dwell in a hut by the grave for three years to exhaustively manifest his filial sincerity. The *Biographies of Filial Virtue* states: "Cai Shun of Runan, courtesy name Junzhong, was filially devoted to his parents.

After the funeral rites for his parents were completed, he remained in a mourning hut at the edge of the grave. Birds and beasts followed him there to roost and sleep; whenever he wailed, [they likewise responded]."
Zhubi yin (Assisting the Lament). A person from the Later Han period. *Leilin* states: Yanwu was a native of Dongyang in Kuaiji. He was filially pious;
after his father passed away, he carried earth on his back to build a tomb. He moved a flock of crows to assist him in carrying the soil.
Blood flowed from the mouths of the crows, and for this reason the place was named Shangwu County. It was later changed to Yiwu County. This refers to a person from the Former Han period.

"Throughout one's life" means for the duration of a single lifetime. "Zheng and Chang" are names of sacrificial rites. The *Ji tong* (Explanations of Sacrifices) in the *Liji* states: "In all sacrifices there are four seasons:
the spring sacrifice is called *yue*; the summer sacrifice is called *di*; the autumn sacrifice is called *chang*; and the winter sacrifice is called *zheng*.
For the sake of literary convenience, the text mentions only autumn and winter, which serves as a reflection for the spring and summer. I have reflected on this privately.
For the remainder of this one life, he dwells in a hut at the tomb and guards the mound, cherishing the memory of the deceased’s voice and countenance until the end of his days.

Throughout the four seasons, he performs the *yue*, *di*, *chang*, and *zheng* sacrifices, exhausting every filial act to repay the deceased’s kindness and virtue. Thus, the *Classic of Filial Piety* says:

"One provides a coffin and outer shell, a patterned shroud and inner coverlet, and then carries the body forth" (*zhou shi* refers to the inner coffin, which encloses the body; *zhou guan* refers to the outer shell, which encloses the inner coffin; *yi* refers to the clothes used for the dressing; *qin* refers to the... [inner coverlet]).

A single shroud is used to lift the corpse into the coffin and to cover it. The *fu* and *gui* vessels are displayed while one grieves and mourns them (the *fu* and *gui* are names for sacrificial vessels;

they hold one dou and two sheng, with feet one cun high and shaped like tortoises. The *fu* is square inside and round outside; the *gui* is round inside and square outside. Both have vermilion interiors and lacquered exteriors; the vessels themselves are plain and unadorned to manifest a heart of grief and sorrow).

One beats the breast and leaps, wailing and weeping, sending off the deceased with sorrow. (The "leaping" of men refers to jumping with the feet; the "beating" of women refers to exposing the chest and striking it). One divines the location of the burial site.

[One] establishes the *zhào* (the boundary markers). [The term] *zhái* refers to the burial pit; *zhào* refers to the precincts of the tomb. Because the rites of burial are of great importance, one divines to select and settle the location.

One constructs ancestral temples (*zōngmiào*) to offer sacrifices to them as spirits (*guǐ*). [The character] *zōng* means "venerable," and *miào* means "likeness" or "image. One establishes these venerable images to offer sacrifices according to the ritual for spirits, as if seeing one's parents again.

One performs sacrifices in spring and autumn, reflecting upon them according to the seasons. [This reflects the changes between winter and summer; as cold and heat shift, one’s feelings of resonance increase accordingly. By sacrificing during the four seasons, one manifests filial reflection. (The preceding notes are all commentaries; they are extensive and fully contained within that text. △
Second, the demonstration that [such practices] are useless through concession and refutation.
[Commentary (Shu): Although one may extend filial thought, it does not assist the Way of the Spirits.
[Sub-commentary (Chao): Question: Maintaining the graves for a lifetime and offering sacrifices at the four seasons are sufficient to express the earnest sincerity of a filial son.
To repay the profound virtue of their labor, why not act accordingly? Why merely contemplate it? This is explained as follows:
the first phrase is concessive, while the second phrase is restrictive. "Although" (*sui*) is a term used for concession and restriction. "Contemplate" (*si*) refers to emotion.
Although one may freely exercise the sentiment of filial piety and earnestly maintain the ancestral mound for a lifetime and offer sacrifices throughout one's life, nevertheless, one cannot...

It may provide some benefit to the spiritual consciousness on the path of the netherworld. Furthermore, the former phrase speaks of advancing, while the latter speaks of retreating; reflect upon this advancement and retreat, and you will see that in the end it is entirely without benefit.
While there may still be some slight benefit in honoring and supporting them while they are alive, once they have passed away, the offering of ancestral sacrifices provides no assistance at all.

If even when offering *ping* and *fan* herbs during the *yue* and *di* sacrifices, one does not fail in their duty toward their parents, yet if one were to take life for the *zheng* and *chang* offerings, the resulting calamity would instead fall upon one’s parents.
This would merely serve to spread empty fame and provide no benefit to the Way of the Spirits.

Furthermore, if one’s parents reside in the realm of ghosts, they might be able to partake of the sacrifice; but if they are born in other realms, how could they possibly receive the offerings? Moreover, among the ghosts...

Those who possess wealth and are free from obstacles can provide for the ancestral sacrifices; conversely, those who lack wealth and are reduced to begging at others' doors turn their offerings into poison.
Therefore, I have reflected upon this and refrained from doing so. △ Second, the profound depth of the Buddha-dharma can support one's parents. Third.
First, seeking the Dharma and succeeding; second, having sought it, attaining the Dharma-gate.
[Commentary]: He thoroughly searched through the teachings of the sages and worthies, reverently seeking a method for the posthumous offerings.
To have attained this Dharma-gate is truly a sublime practice.

[Commentary]: “Thereupon” (*sui*) means to follow from what precedes and initiate what follows. Because the worldly filial piety described previously does not assist the Way of the Spirits, he thereupon searched for the teachings of the sages and worthies (*shengxian*) to seek the methods for the posthumous dedication of his parents.
Those prior to the realization of the Path in the Three Vehicles are called “worthies” (*xian*); this is because they cultivate merit and wisdom and possess virtuous qualities.
Those from the realization of the Path onward are called “sages” (*sheng*). “Sage” (*sheng*) means “correct” (*zheng*), as they are endowed with the untainted (*anāsrava*) [wisdom].
Because it is wise, correct, and reasonable, this teaching spoken and studied by the noble ones reveals the gateway to immeasurable mundane and supramundane benefits.
Within this teaching, one reverently aspires to seek out methods for providing support and for the elevation of the deceased;
having thus fulfilled one’s wishes, one finds this Dharma-gate within the Tripitaka, which is truly called a sublime practice. Dharma.

[Commentary] This means that from the Son of Heaven down to the scholar-officials (*shìrén*), families and states have transmitted this practice through generations, all establishing ancestral temples (*zōngmiào*). [Sub-commentary] Regarding "families and states":
