The Lord’s temple (the father). The temple of the great-great-grandfather is even more honored; therefore, he is given the title "Great Lord" (*dajun*). The temple of the manifest grandfather (*xiankao*) (the great-great-grandfather; "manifest" clarifies that the great-great-grandfather occupies the highest position among the four ancestral temples). The temple of the grandfather (*zukao*).

(Ancestral refers to the beginning. This temple marks the beginning of the royal house; therefore, they are called the "Patriarchs and Ancestors. All of these receive monthly sacrifices. The distant temples are designated as *tiāo*, and there are two such *tiāo*.

(2) The Two *Tiāo* Ancestors. These are the temples of Wén and Wǔ. Since both Wén and Wǔ were subject to the rule of eventual removal, they are termed "distant" (*yuǎn*). Yet, because they were specially retained for their meritorious services, they are called *tiāo*. The term *tiāo* signifies "transcendence," meaning that they have transcended and ascended above [the regular line].

"Sacrifices and seasonal offerings cease. (The phrase "sacrifices and seasonal offerings" refers to the four seasonal sacrifices. Because Wén and Wǔ were specially retained, they do not receive monthly sacrifices. "Beyond the *tiāo* is the altar (*tán*). (This refers to the father of the Gāozǔ.

The *zhāo* lineages are deposited in the Wǔ *tiāo*, and the *mù* lineages are deposited in the Wén *tiāo*. They are not sacrificed to during the four seasons; however, if there is a prayer or petition, they are brought out to the altar to receive sacrifice. "Beyond the altar is the cleared ground (*shàn*). (This refers to the grandfather of the Gāozǔ.)

One must not remain on the altar. If there is a prayer or supplication, one goes out to the *shàn* (sacrificial mound) to receive the sacrifice. When there is a prayer at the altar or the *shàn*, one sacrifices; when there is no prayer, one ceases. Once removed from the *shàn*, one becomes a *guǐ* (spirit).

(If there is another who has been moved from the altar to the *shàn*, then the former occupant of the *shàn* is moved into the stone casket to become a *guǐ*; this is not for the purpose of prayer. Only during the *dì* and *xiá* sacrifices is such a spirit brought forth.

A feudal lord establishes five ancestral temples, one altar (*tán*), and one mound (*shàn*). These are called the temple of the father (*kǎo miào*), the temple of the grandfather (*wáng kǎo miào*), and the temple of the great-grandfather (*huáng kǎo miào*). The monthly [sacrifices]...

All these were sacrificed to. Sacrifices were offered at the temple of the recently deceased father (xiǎnkǎo) and the temple of the grandfather (zǔkǎo), but only for the seasonal offerings of *xiǎng* and *cháng*.

Beyond the grandfather, one established an altar (*tán*); beyond the altar, one established a cleared space (*shàn*). Sacrifices were offered at these altars and cleared spaces only when there was a specific prayer; otherwise, they ceased. Beyond the cleared space, they became "spirits" (*guǐ*).

A Great Officer established three temples and two altars, namely the temple of the father (*kǎo*), the temple of the grandfather (*wǎngkǎo*), and the temple of the great-grandfather (*huángkǎo*); sacrifices were offered only for the seasonal *xiǎng* and *cháng*. As for the recently deceased father... [text fragment ends].

For the *kǎo* (grandfather) and *zǔkǎo* (great-grandfather), there were no ancestral temples; when there was a need for prayer, an altar was erected to sacrifice to them, and once removed from the altar, they were regarded as *guǐ* (spirits).

For an *shì* (lower-ranking officer) who had inherited the position, there were two temples and one altar—namely, the temple of the *kǎo* and the temple of the *wángkǎo* (paternal great-grandfather)—where sacrifices of *xiǎng* and *cháng* were performed, but only then. For the *huángkǎo* (paternal great-great-grandfather), there was no temple;

when there was a need for prayer, an altar was erected to sacrifice to him, and once removed from the altar, he was regarded as a *guǐ*. For an *guānshī* (official head of a department), there was one temple—namely, the temple of the *kǎo*. For the *wángkǎo*, there was none.

They establish shrines to sacrifice to them; once they have passed away from being the "recently deceased" (*wangkao*), they become "spirits" (*gui*). Common officers and commoners have no shrines; when they die, they are called spirits. (The *shishi* are the upper officers;

the *guanshi* are the middle and lower officers; the *shushi* belong to the class of clerks and recorders. The royal ministers who practice filial piety establish these ancestral shrines (*zong*). "Ancestral" (*zong*) means "venerable"; "shrine" (*miao*) means "likeness.
They establish the physical likeness so that the ancestor is revered as if present, and they perform solemn sacrifices to him. This is based on the *Shangshu*.
In this, the Duke of Zhou speaks: "Since antiquity, when the former kings established ancestral temples to sacrifice to their kin, they did not designate specific dynasties. (Part Two:
Granting and Restricting to Reveal that Filial Piety Can Generate All Virtues.)
[Commentary]: Although the applications of the five types of filial piety differ, the source of the hundredfold conduct does not vary.

[Sub-commentary]: As for the "five types of filial piety," they are: first, the filial piety of the Son of Heaven; second, the filial piety of the feudal lords; third, the filial piety of high ministers and great officers; fourth, the filial piety of scholars; and fifth, the filial piety of commoners.
While these five persons differ from one another, as for their path of filial piety, are they one or are they different? Therefore, this...
Thus it is said. Although the five types of filial piety differ in their specific applications, the source of all hundred practices—the Way of Filial Piety—is no different.

Water is called a "source" (*yuan*); though water divides into a thousand branches, they all flow from that source. Humans have a hundred practices, which all arise from filial piety; therefore, filial piety is like a source. II.
Quoting Texts to Explain and Establish [the Meaning] (in three parts): 1. Filial Piety as the Foundation of Morality and Virtue.
The essence of these two filialities constitutes the foundation for establishing the teachings. These two categories are unified.
[Commentary] Therefore, in the "Chapter on Opening the School and Clarifying the Meaning," it is designated as the essential path of supreme virtue.
Virtue and the Way take this as their substance, and the methods of instruction arise from this (Filial Piety).
[Commentary] Regarding the "Chapter Opening the School and Clarifying the Meaning": Among the eighteen chapters of the *Classic of Filial Piety*, this is the first chapter.

The sub-commentary states: "Opening" (*kai*) means to unfold; "school" (*shū*) means the fundamental source. Within this chapter, the fundamental source of the Way of Filial Piety is unfolded, and the essential meaning of the Way of Filial Piety is clarified.
The Sutra says: "The former kings possessed the ultimate virtue and the essential Way, whereby they brought harmony to the world and its people."
"By employing this, harmony is achieved; those above and below harbor no resentment. The Commentary states: "Ultimate" (*zhì*) refers to the culmination of the investigation of principle.
Virtue (*dé*) is the foundation of all practices; therefore, it is called "Ultimate Virtue. "Essential" (*yào*) means that by means of one, many are subsumed.

The Way (*dào*) is the essence of all principles; therefore, it is called the "Essential Way. Filial piety is the essence of the Way and the foundation of virtue. The sage-kings of former generations employed this.
The ultimate virtue and essential way serve to accord with the hearts of the people throughout the world. The people rely upon them and naturally live in harmony with one another;
among those of high and low station, there are none who harbor resentment toward each other. Furthermore, there is another principle: the ultimate virtue is singular—filial piety.

Second is fraternal respect (*ti*), and third is ministerial service (*chen*). These practices of fraternal respect and ministerial service arise from filial piety (*xiao*). The "Chapter on Extending Virtue" states:

"Teaching by means of filial piety is for the purpose of showing reverence to all those in the world who are fathers; teaching by means of fraternal respect is for the purpose of showing reverence to all those in the world who are elder brothers.

(If one takes filial piety and fraternal respect as the basis of instruction, then among all those in the world who are children and younger brothers, there will be none who do not revere their own fathers and elder brothers.)"

This teaches how a minister should show reverence toward those who are rulers of the world. (By taking the way of the minister as the teaching, there will be no one among the ministers of the world who does not revere their ruler.
That which possesses this virtue is the embodiment and the root; it serves as the fundamental essence of extensive reverence.
It serves as the fundamental source for universal guidance. "Ultimate" (*zhì*) means the head and the pinnacle;

it is the foremost leader of all virtues and the wondrous apex that penetrates the minds of all beings, and is therefore called "Ultimate Virtue" (*zhìdé*). As for what are called the essential paths, they are: first, filial piety; second, fraternal respect; and third, joy.

The four rites and the five reverences—filiality (*xiao*) and fraternal respect (*ti*)—all arise from filiality. The "Chapter on the Essential Way" states: "In teaching the people affection and love, nothing is better than filiality;

in teaching the people ritual propriety and compliance, nothing is better than fraternal respect. (This means that in teaching the people to love their parents and to be ritually compliant toward their elders, nothing surpasses filiality and fraternal respect.

*Ti* means friendship. "In transforming customs and changing social mores, nothing is better than music" (when customs are shifted and changed, they first enter through the sounds of music, and the transformation follows).

The human mind is rectified precisely through the virtue of the ruler. The arising and transformation of this rectification are manifested through music. When the sounds of music are sorrowful and resentful, one knows the state is perishing and in disorder; when the sounds of music are harmonious and beautiful, one knows the state possesses good governance. Thus, [music] brings peace to the sovereign and order to the people.

Nothing is more excellent than ritual (*li*). (Ritual is that by which the distinctions between ruler and subject and father and son are rectified, and the differences between male and female and elder and younger are clarified;

thus it can bring peace to those above and transform those below. Ritual is simply reverence. (Reverence is the root of ritual. Ritual takes solemnity, frugality, and dignified reverence as its primary principles. Without reverence, ritual cannot be practiced; therefore, reverence is taken as its root. To follow this Way is principle. It is the root.
To manifest this principle to the sovereign and the people is the foundation, arising from the multitude.
"Virtue" (*de*) means essential, concise, and sublime. To briefly set forth filial conduct is to subtly accord with the human heart.

Those above are benevolent and harmonious; those below are sincere and concordant. Therefore, it is called the "Essential Way. This ultimate virtue universally clarifies the conduct of filial piety, fraternal respect, and loyalty of a minister.

Its intent lies in reverence; for filial piety can give rise to reverence. The Essential Way comprehensively elucidates filial piety, fraternal respect, joy, ritual propriety, and reverence. It is complete.

He enumerates the various practices; those preceding are narrow while these are broad. All take filial piety as the correct and fundamental, while other practices are regarded as secondary and derivative.
Therefore, this commentary states that it "designates [filial piety] as the supreme virtue and essential way," and explains that "virtue and the Way take this as their substance."
The dual exegesis of the essential path to supreme virtue takes filial piety as its fundamental substance. Furthermore, the ancient sages established the five teachings:
the father’s righteousness, the mother’s kindness, the elder brother’s friendship, the younger brother’s respect, and the son’s filial piety. These five teachings arise from filial piety;
if the text does not concern filial piety, it is not a teaching. Thus, the *Classic of Filial Piety* states: "Filial piety is the root of virtue."
This is the source from which the teachings arise. △ Third, filial piety is the source of the Way of life.
[Commentary] How could there be a gentleman who does not strive for the root (filial piety and fraternal respect)?
[Commentary] *Wu* (diligence) means to be urgent and single-mindedly devoted. *Ben* (the root) refers to filial piety and fraternal duty. This commentary is an exegesis by way of contrast;

its intent is to clarify that the gentleman is one who is urgently and single-mindedly devoted to the practice of filiality and the conduct of brotherly affection. Furthermore, *ti* (fraternal duty) means "to change.

It means changing from negligence to reverence, and changing from contrariness to compliance. When such filial piety and fraternal duty are established, the five constant virtues and the Way and Virtue follow accordingly.
From this, [filial piety] arises. This explains that filial piety is the source of all hundredfold deeds. Thus, the *Lunyu* says: "The gentleman applies himself to the root.
When the root is established, the Way arises. Is not filial piety and fraternal respect indeed the root of being human? (In the *Xiaojing*, "di" is written as "ti.")
△ Second, specifically revealing the three-year period to manifest the Sage’s intention. Part one: The meaning of the three-year mourning for parents.
[Commentary]: Since this is the eternal law of heaven and the fundamental righteousness of earth, it must be made possible for others to aspire to and follow.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "it is the eternal law of heaven and the principle of earth," the *Xiaojing* states:

"Filial piety is the eternal law of heaven, the principle of earth, and the conduct of the people. The sub-commentary (*shu*) explains: "Eternal" (*jing*) means constant; "principle" (*yi*) means benefit.
Heaven possesses the sun, moon, and stars which illuminate all below; this constitutes the constant way of heaven. Earth produces the hundred grains, grasses, and trees to provide for humanity.
This is the principle and benefit of the earth. When human beings are born between heaven and earth, they receive the vital breath of heaven and earth to form their bodies.
Therefore, they should emulate the constant brightness of heaven and the constant benefit of earth, while constantly practicing filial piety to serve their parents above.
Furthermore, a scripture states: "Emulate the brightness of heaven and rely on the benefits of earth to bring harmony to the world. For this reason—

Their teachings were perfected without solemnity; their government was orderly without severity. (By establishing teachings based on filial piety, they modeled themselves after the constant brightness of Heaven and the constant benefits of Earth.

Because they acted in accordance with the hearts of the people of the world, their instructions and commands were effective without waiting for sincere solemnity, being perfected spontaneously; without employing harshness, order was maintained spontaneously. The former kings saw that teachings could transform the people;
therefore, they led them with universal love, and the people did not neglect their parents. (Universal means broad. The ruler loved his...)
The ruler uses this to transform the people; the people are transformed by the virtue of their sovereign, and there are none who neglect or abandon their parents.

When he sets forth virtue and righteousness, the people are inspired to practice them (to expound the excellence of virtue and righteousness so that they are admired by the multitude, the people then conceive the thought to emulate and practice them). When he leads by means of reverence and yielding, the people do not contend (reverence consists of being solemn, upright, and centered;

yielding consists of deferring merit and honoring the good; transforming the people through such transformation, the people do not compete or quarrel). When he guides them with ritual and music, the people become harmonious and friendly (through ritual...).
Examine their traces; delight them so as to rectify their hearts, and they will be harmonious. Show them what is good and what is evil, and the people will know the prohibitions.

(Showing them what is good to lead them forward, and showing them what is evil to stop them, the people will understand the prohibitions and dare not violate them. Regarding the requirement that they must strive to reach [the ideal] or bow in compliance:

when there is the mourning for parents, no grain broth enters the mouth for three days, and the period of filial mourning lasts for three years. When those who are unworthy raise their hearts toward these practices, it is called "striving" (*qi*).
Furthermore, when the worthy and accomplished bow their heads to follow [the deceased], it is called "bending down to comply" (fǔcóng).

The ancient sages established this time limit with the intention that those practicing filial piety should either ascend to meet [the deceased] or descend to meet them; thus it is said, "one must cause them to reach up or bend down.
The *Liji*, *Tangong* chapter, states: "Zengzi said to Zisi, 'Ji, when I was observing the mourning rites for my parents, not even water or gruel entered my mouth.'"

Section Seven: Zisi (the son of Boyu and grandson of Confucius) said, "The former kings established the rites such that those who went beyond them would stoop to reach them, and those who had not yet reached them would stand on tiptoe to attain them.
(To stand on tiptoe is called *qi*; to bow the head is called *fu*. Therefore, when a gentleman observes the mourning for his parents, he does not take water or grain into his mouth for three days;
he uses a staff before he can rise. (In the mourning for a parent, one does not eat nor drink thin gruel for three days.)

If [the mourning period] were too short, it would suppress the worthy and accomplished; if it were too long, it would neglect the unworthy. Balancing these two extremes for three days may be called "attaining the mean. The three-year mourning period is likewise intended to cause both the wise and the foolish to look up with reverence and aspire toward it.

The *Classic of Filial Piety* states: "Mourning does not exceed three years; this shows the people that there is an end. The commentary says: This explains the duration for maintaining filial mourning.
Although a son suffers lifelong grief once his parents have passed away, he observes the mourning rites for three years.
This is because people vary in their degree of virtue and folly; thus, the periods of mourning could not be fixed at a single number.
Therefore, a three-year period was established. The reason for this is stated in the *Analects*: "A human being, after three years, is finally released from the embrace of his parents.
Consequently, the mourning for one's parents is limited to a maximum of three years. It is hoped that those who are virtuous will be able to sever their grief and bring it to an end.
It is out of compassion that one stoops to accommodate them. As for those who are unworthy, one causes them to exert effort and strive toward reaching that standard.
To observe the three-year mourning period is for a filial son to bring the way of his parents to completion;
therefore, from the Son of Heaven down to the common people, the three-year mourning period is the universal rite of all under heaven. △ Second, the reprimand and admonition of the non-virtuous.
[He is] like Xiao Zhi and his peers. [Commentary:
Although he discusses the collapse of ritual and music, he ultimately censures those who wear brocade and eat fine rice. [Sub-commentary:

The *Lunyu* records that Zai Wo asked about the three-year mourning period, saying, "One year is already long. (His surname was Zai, his name Yu, and his courtesy name Ziwo. He was a disciple of Confucius.)

"Zi was a disciple; 'one year' refers to the completion of a full year. For a gentleman not to practice the rites for three years, the rites will surely fall into ruin; for him not to practice music for three years, the music will surely collapse.
When the old grain has perished (meaning it is exhausted) and the new grain has risen (meaning it is ripe), and when fire is drilled from different woods, then one year may suffice.

(Ma said: "In spring, one takes fire from the elm and willow; in summer, from the jujube and apricot; in autumn, from the oak and hornbeam; in winter, from the locust and sandalwood. Within a single year, the wood used for drilling fire differs; hence it is called 'changing the fire' [guǐ huǒ].")

The Master said, "If you were eating fine rice and wearing patterned silk, would you feel at ease? Zai Wo replied, "I would. (He did not grasp the Master's meaning. The Master said, "If you feel at ease, then do it.
When a gentleman dwells in mourning, he eats delicacies but finds them tasteless; hearing music brings him no joy; his dwelling is uneasy.
Therefore, he does not do these things. Now, since you feel at ease, you may do them. Zai Wo withdrew, (realizing his own error). As for the three-year [mourning period]...
A year of mourning is the universal mourning practice for the world (Kong says: beginning from the Son of Heaven down to the common people).
Do I, too, possess this three-year affection for my parents? (Kong says: This refers to a son’s desire to repay his parents; their kindness is as vast as heaven and has no limit.
Does Zai Yu, however, possess this three-year affection for his parents? △ Third, the concluding eulogy.
[Commentary] How profound! How great is filial piety! As for the virtue of the sages, how could there be anything that surpasses filial piety?
[Sub-commentary] When Zengzi had heard of the five grades of filial piety, he marveled and sighed, saying, "How profound! How great is filial piety! He further said, "Zengzi asked:
'May I venture to ask whether the virtue of the sages has nothing that surpasses filial piety? (Is it not the case that they possess no other sage-like virtue?)"

"Is there anything that surpasses filial piety? The Master said: "Among the natures bestowed by Heaven and Earth, humanity is the most noble. (Nature refers to birth; among the myriad things born by Heaven, humans are the most intelligent and precious.

Among human practices, none is greater than filial piety. (It is the source of all conduct. In filial piety, none is greater than honoring one's father. (Honor means to respect. In honoring one's father, none is greater than associating him with Heaven.

In this regard, Duke Zhou was such a person. (Heaven produces the myriad things, and the father gives birth to the son. To respect one's father is the greatest thing; therefore, he is associated with Heaven.)

They were sacrificed to together. This began with the Duke of Zhou, who used his father as a correlate to Heaven; hence it is said, "As for the person," referring to the Duke of Zhou. His surname was Ji and his name was Dan. During the reign of King Cheng of Zhou, he served as Grand Preceptor (*taishi*), being the foremost among the Three Dukes (*sanguo*);

thus he is called the Duke of Zhou. In ancient times, the Duke of Zhou performed the suburban sacrifice to Houji to correlate him with Heaven. (Houji was the founding ancestor of Zhou. The "suburbs" refers to the suburban altar, also known as the Round Mound (*yuanqiu*), the place where Heaven is sacrificed to.

When the Duke of Zhou acted as regent, he performed the suburban sacrifice to Heaven and thereby honored his founding ancestor, Houji, so that he might sit alongside [the Supreme Deity] and partake of the food at the Round Mound above, in correlation with the Great Sovereign of the Azure Heaven.)
The fundamental principle was: "He sacrificed to King Wen in the Mingtang to pair him with the Supreme Deity" (The Mingtang is the palace for promulgating government policies.

It is located within seven *li* to the south of the city. Because it occupies a place of Yang-ming, it is called the Mingtang. Duke Zhou honored his father, King Wen, by having him join the sacrifice and partake of the food alongside the Five Sovereign Deities of the five directions atop the Mingtang).

Consequently, those within the four seas each came to sacrifice according to their respective duties. (When the ruler performed the rite of solemn pairing, it was seen that his virtue and instruction extended throughout the four seas; thus, the feudal lords within the seas each cultivated their offices.)

[They] were presented to assist in the sacrifice. Now, how could the virtue of the Sage exceed that of filial piety? (This concludes the response to Zengzi. Even the Sage governs by relying upon filial piety.
△ Second, explaining that the teaching takes filial piety as its foundation, in two parts. First, the heading.
[Commentary] Next, the explanation that the teaching takes filial piety as its foundation.

[Sub-commentary] Among the various sūtras and śāstras, the Seven Buddhas are mentioned because they may be analogized to the establishment of ancestral patriarchs in the secular world, similar to the system of the seven ancestral temples.
Furthermore, it is because the disciples are taught to be filial and obedient toward their parents for seven generations. It is also said: "The sentient beings of the six realms..."
Because all [beings] are one's parents, filial piety is established as the fundamental source of the teachings. As for the "Seven Buddhas," they are Vipaśyin and the others.
△ Second, the actual exposition has two parts. First, a general clarification of the Buddha’s teachings, which further divides into two.
First, distinguishing the provisional and the real according to the Buddha’s fixed teachings.

[Commentary]: All Buddhas possess both the true body (*dharmakāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Śākyamuni, as the transformation body, expounds the provisional teachings adapted to the capacities of sentient beings;
Vairocana, as the true body, expounds the ultimate, real teaching.

[Commentary]: The Buddha has three bodies, namely: the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Furthermore, the Reward-body is twofold: the self-enjoyment [body] and the other-enjoyment [body].

Regarding the provisional and ultimate nature of these four Buddhas, there are two interpretations. First, the Dharma-body is called "ultimate," while the Reward and Transformation bodies are "provisional."
The "real" refers to the true essence of all phenomena (*dharmas*). The "expedient" refers to the provisional traces of phenomenal characteristics. The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"The manifested transformation body is not the true Buddha, nor is it the one who preaches the Dharma. "Manifested" (*ying*) signifies retribution; it carries the meaning of responding to causes, referring to the self-enjoyment [body].
"Corresponding" (*ying*) means manifesting in accordance with [the needs of beings]. It manifests in accordance with the ten stages; this is the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhoga-kāya*).
These two—the Body of Correspondence and the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*)—are neither the true Buddha nor the true teacher of the Dharma.

This is intended to reveal that the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*) alone is the true Buddha and the true teacher of the Dharma, such that the wisdom of the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) merges in silent union with the true nature; in meaning, this is equivalent to verbal teaching. Second:
The Dharma-body and the Body of Self-Enjoyment can be known only by Buddhas among Buddhas; as these are the basis of these bodies, they are called "real.
If it concerns the Body of Enjoyment for Others and the Transformation Body, all classes of ordinary beings and sages alike are able to see them;
as these are the derivative aspects of these bodies, they are called "provisional. The merits of self-benefit belonging to the real bodies of the Dharma and Retribution do not [correspond to]...
Regarding "teaching according to capacity" (*jishō*): because the provisional body manifests for the benefit of others, the Buddha teaches the Dharma in accordance with their capacities.

This is extensively demonstrated in such scriptures as the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* and treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. As for the other-enjoyment body (*parasaṃbhoga-kāya*), it manifests ten grades of bodies for bodhisattvas of the ten stages and teaches the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) and so forth;
these are all termed the "True Teaching" (*shikyō*). The subtle principle expounded therein accords with the capacities of the bodhisattvas and is not provisional.

Furthermore, as for its transformation body (nirmāṇakāya): when it preaches the Dharma of the Three Vehicles to ordinary beings of the three vehicles and to the noble ones of the two vehicles, it is called the "Teaching of Reality" (samyak-yāna) when addressing those with the capacity of the Mahāyāna, and the "Teaching of Expedient Means" (upāya-yāna) when addressing those with the capacity of the two vehicles. This is as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The sheep, deer, and ox carts are metaphors for the Three Vehicles; this is because the provisional and the real differ.

Nevertheless, the essence of the Dharma is like a rain of a single flavor that moistens the three types of grass. While the grasses differ, the rain is one; while the capacities of the Three Vehicles differ, the Dharma is of a single flavor.

Because the understanding and realization of these capacities vary individually, the teachings are categorized according to those capacities; thus, there are the sudden, the gradual, the provisional, and the real.

The reality and so forth are distinct. The reason for this is that it is because the Buddha, having cultivated loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity throughout vast eons in the past, accorded with the varying depths of sentient beings' wisdom and understanding, establishing transformations suited to their capacities to benefit them.
Once his cultivation was perfected and he reached the stage of fruition, he no longer applied deliberate effort; rather, his mind arose spontaneously, mobilizing great compassion.
Responding to all capacities and expounding all dharmas, through the power of spontaneity, a single utterance conveys manifold meanings.
According to the varying depths of sentient beings' faith and understanding, they each receive it differently.
For those of small capacity, this very same word manifests the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle, causing them to awaken and enter it; for those of great capacity, this very same word manifests...

The Mahāyāna Dharma causes them to awaken and enter it. When addressed to those with the capacity for sudden awakening, it is called the Sudden Teaching; when addressed to those with the capacity for gradual awakening, it is called the Gradual Teaching.

This is explained at length: according to what is being addressed—whether it be the treatment of greed or hatred, their depth or shallowness, or the provisional or the real—the teachings differ according to the capacities of beings, resulting in immeasurable distinctions. Thus, Vimalakīrti said: "The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice..."

He preaches the Dharma, and sentient beings each attain understanding according to their respective types. The *Avataṃsaka* also says: "The Tathāgata, within a single utterance, expounds an ocean of boundless sūtras.
Yet, the current commentary states: "Śākyamuni’s transformation body preaches expedient teachings adapted to capacities.
This is far too restrictive. The Tripiṭaka Master Ci'en said: "In the Sanskrit language, it is Vairocana; here [in Chinese], it is translated as..."
"Universal Quiescence" (*pianji*) refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), as it denotes pervasive stillness. In Sanskrit, this is *Vairocana*, which means "Universal Radiance.

In this commentary, when Vairocana, the True Buddha, preaches the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, he is called "True" (zhen) because his own name signifies the true essence (*tattva*). As the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Good son, since I truly attained Buddhahood, it has been immeasurable, incalculable, and inconceivable."

this is the true Buddha (*dharmakāya*). Now, the response body is the function (*vyavahāra*), while the true body is the essence (*svabhāva*).

Since the function does not depart from the essence, it is called the "true [body] that is identical with the response. This is because the true Buddha is spoken of precisely upon the basis of the response body. Therefore...
The eyes of Vairocana are for his own enjoyment; this is called the True Buddha preaching the Dharma in response to sentient beings.

If one speaks of the "True" in contrast to the "Responsive," it refers to a True Buddha distinct from and outside the Responsive Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), because the essential nature and the modes of application of its activity are distinct.
As it is said, the individual faculties, marks, and signs of the True Buddha as the self-recompense are each and every one infinite. If [one considers] the other-transformation...
Buddhas each have their own [distinctions of] great and small, as they manifest according to the capacities of sentient beings.
Since he now preaches the Dharma in accordance with such capacities, this Vairocana refers to the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), which is termed the Responsive Buddha (*nirmāṇabuddha*).

If one reverses the above explanation—that is, the Responsive arising from the True—this means that the Responsive Buddha is spoken of upon the basis of the True Buddha; for the true essence and its functional application are inseparable, as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

It is said: "The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm, universally appearing before all sentient beings. The upper phrase refers to the True Buddha (*dharmakāya*), and the lower phrase refers to the Responsive Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*).
This is called the Responsive Buddha who is identical with the True [Buddha], universally benefiting all sentient beings.

If one were to speak of a Responsive Buddha distinct from the True [Buddha], this would mean explaining the Responsive Buddha as something separate from the True Buddha; it would be a case where the true essence and its responsive function are practiced as different things.
Because their characteristics are distinct: as it is said, the true Buddha (*dharmakāya*) manifests his own retribution and is seen only by Buddhas, for he does not face sentient beings.

The *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) faces sentient beings to preach the Dharma. Thus, whether the true Buddha and the response-body Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*) are identical or different, they are sovereign and unimpeded;
this is called the inconceivability of all Buddhas. This commentary follows the first category, and thus takes Śākyamuni as the true Buddha.
The teaching of the ultimate truth (real teaching) relies on the third category. Śākyamuni, the transformation Buddha, teaches the provisional teaching.
Master Ci’en relies on the fourth category; therefore, it is only Vairocana who preaches the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.

[Commentary] Regarding differences in observing mourning: initially, upon death, the mourning practices of Confucianism and Buddhism are largely the same; it is after the burial that they differ. The *Xiaojing* states: "The Master said:
When a filial son mourns for his parents, he does not wail with drawn-out sobs; his deportment lacks ritual grace; his speech is unadorned; and he wears..."
One finds beauty distasteful, music joyless, and fine food insipid; this is the expression of sorrowful grief. The Commentary states:
"Weeping without sobbing" means that the sound of weeping is not drawn out or winding. When the intensity of pain reaches its peak, the voice flows in a single breath, departing without returning;

There is no longer the deportment of stately pacing; sorrow and grief reside in the heart, and one’s speech is not embellished with refinement.

When a filial son loses his parent, his heart feels as if it has been severed. The wise and accomplished feel this pain for the rest of their lives, while the unworthy feel no such grief until the day ends.

When a filial son beholds them, he is moved to think of his parents; their reality truly crushes his heart.
Therefore, though fine clothing is upon his body, his mind finds no peace. Hearing songs and music, his heart finds no joy. "Zhi" (旨) means "exquisite" or "beautiful. [This is] sorrow.
Grief resides in the heart; even when eating delicacies, one finds no sweetness. One subsists on coarse vegetables and thin gruel merely to fill the stomach.

This sentiment of sorrow and grief is comprised of the six preceding matters. Nevertheless, when the ancient sages established the laws, there were distinctions between the *qí* and *zhǎn* mourning periods for parents.

For a father, one wears the *zhanshuai* (unhemmed sackcloth) mourning for three years. While the father is still living, one wears the *qishuai* (hemmed sackcloth) mourning for the mother; this is removed after one year, though one observes "mourning of the heart" (*xinsang*) for three years.
From the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month of the first year of the Shangyuan era of Emperor Gaozong of the Tang dynasty, Empress Wu submitted a memorial.

[Commentary] To "explain" means to provide offerings and lecture on the sutras to support their karmic retribution.

Form and emptiness enter into one another; the large and the small contain one another. They function with sovereign mastery, such that all things are without obstruction.

how then could it be stretched? If it were by contracting the ocean, since the great ocean is deep and vast, its original state remains as it was.
"How is it contracted? "A mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru. The question is likewise so. Please show the mode of operation (*ākāra*).
One should instruct him, saying: "If there were such a mode of operation for expansion and contraction as you describe, it would be something conceivable (*cintya*).
However, because the mode of operation for expansion and contraction is inconceivable (*acintya*), its unfolding and rolling up cannot be discussed."

For this reason, it is called "inconceivable. [Commentary] The commentary explains that there are three occasions for the rite of releasing living beings (*fangsheng*): (1) at the end of the year; (2) when the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is completed; and (3) on memorial days (*jichén*). On each of these, one must release life for the sake of one’s parents according to one’s capacity. This applies for periods of seven days, up to seven times seven days;

it likewise applies to the initial seven-day period, all subsequent seven-day intervals, the day of concluding the wailing (*zuku*), and the day of the *xiang* anniversary. This differs from current secular custom, which merely fulfills the requirement of three years. [It also includes] the "Bowl Assembly for Bestowing Precepts" (*shijie penhui*), as described in this sutra... [and so forth].

I exhort all sentient beings to light lamps, create banners, release living beings, and cultivate merit, so that they may cross over suffering and calamity and not encounter various hardships.

what Your Majesty dreamed must surely be this. Emperor Ming believed this to be true and immediately dispatched eighteen men, including Cai Yin, Qin Jing, and Wang Zun—the latter serving as a Doctor of the National University—to travel westward in search of the Buddha-dharma.

A portrait of Śākyamuni was painted upon white felt, and one scroll of the *Sutra of Forty-two Sections* was brought forth; this was the very beginning of the Buddha-dharma in this land.
Calculated according to the sixty-year sexagenary cycle, it has been fifty-two years since the accession of King Mu of the Zhou dynasty.
In the year of Ren-shen, on the fifteenth day of the second month, Śākyamuni entered parinirvāṇa.
From that time until the first year of Qianxing in the fourth reign of the Great Song, the year of Ren-xu, a total of one thousand nine hundred and seventy-one years have elapsed.
"Zhou and Kong" refers to the two sages, Duke of Zhou and Confucius. The *Commentary on the Classic of Filial Piety* (*Xiaojing Shu*) states:

"The Master’s surname was Kong, his given name was Qiu, and his courtesy name was Zhongni. He was a native of Queli in Pingchang County, Zou City, within the state of Lu. The *Basic Annals of Yin* (*Yin Benji*) says:
Confucius’s father was Shuliang He; his mother was of the Yan clan, named Zheng.
He was born in the twenty-first year of Duke Xiang of Lu and passed away in the fourth month of the summer in the sixteenth year of Duke Ai. He was seventy-three years old.
The *Guochen Ji* states that the Master lived during the twenty-sixth year of King Ling, the twenty-third sovereign of the Zhou dynasty, which was the gengxu year.
He was born on the fourth day of the eleventh month in the year [of the reign of] Emperor Shuai.
He passed away on the eighth day of the fourth month in the *renxu* year, the forty-third year of the reign of King Jing, the twenty-sixth sovereign of the Zhou dynasty. As the *Liezi* says:
The Grand Minister of Shang went to see Confucius and asked, "Is Qiu a sage? Confucius replied, "As for being a sage, how would I dare to claim such a thing?

Rather, I am merely one who has studied extensively and possesses much knowledge. The Grand Minister of Shang said, "Were the Three Kings sages? (The Three Kings are those of Xia, Yin, and Zhou. Yu of Xia served as the Minister of Works under Shun;

The nineteenth generation. As for Yin: it originally was the Shang dynasty, which later changed its name to Yin. During the Yin period, King Tang was a minister of Jie of Xia; seeing that his ruler was unrighteous, he subsequently attacked him. He transformed all under heaven through his virtue. This lineage of father and son lasted for thirty generations.

King Wen of Zhou first became the Western Chief (*xībó*). Residing in Qizhou, more than eight hundred thousand households of the people of Zhou surrendered to the Chief; he provided them with food and clothing. His son, King Wu, succeeded to the throne and attacked the unrighteous Zhou.

His virtuous transformation extended throughout the world. Thus, from father to son, there were thirty-seven generations. Confucius said: "The Three Kings were skilled at employing the wise and the brave. As for their sagehood, I, Qiu, do not know it. He further said: "Were the Five Emperors sages?
(The Five Emperors are Shaohao, Zhuanxu, Gaosin, Tang Yao, and Yu Shun. They established education to transform the people; these teachings are called the Five Canons. — Confucius.
[The Master] said: "As for the Five Emperors being skilled at employing benevolence and righteousness—regarding their sagehood, I, Qiu, do not know it.

He further said: "Were the Three Sovereigns sages? (The Three Sovereigns are Fuxi, Shennong, and Huangdi; they established teachings to instruct the people, which are named the *Sanfen*. Confucius said: "As for the Three Sovereigns being skilled at acting in accordance with the times—regarding their sagehood, I, Qiu, do not know it.
The Grand Chancellor of Shang was greatly startled and asked: "If that is so, then who is a sage? Confucius—
The Master’s countenance shifted slightly, and he said: "In the West, there was a sage who did not govern yet was not in disorder;
who did not speak yet was trusted; who did not transform others yet they acted spontaneously. Vast and expansive! The people were unable to name him.
The *Kongji jing* (Sūtra on Emptiness and Stillness) states that the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī is named Kong Qiu. Thus, we know that the Duke of Zhou and Confucius were sages. It is known.

People have not yet attained an understanding of the principle of cause and effect; therefore, [the Master] remains silent and does not speak of it, instead causing them to focus their mindfulness on the profound kindness of their parents and to perform sacrifices at the ancestral temple.

Regarding the commentary on "loving the ritual while preserving the sheep": the feudal lords of the various states all performed sacrifices at the ancestral temple early every month at the beginning of the lunar cycle.
However, during the seven generations from Duke Wen to Duke Ai of the state of Lu, they did not carry out these administrative rituals.

The officials continued to provide the sacrificial sheep. The *Lunyu* states: "Zi Gong wished to abolish the sheep presented for the *gao-shuo* (the announcement of the new moon). (Zheng says: 'Raw meat is called *xì*;

according to ritual, the ruler makes the announcement of the new moon at the temple every month and performs a sacrifice, which is called the *zhāo xiǎng*. Since the time of Duke Wen of Lu, this practice had ceased; seeing that the rite was being neglected, Zi Gong wished to remove the sheep.

The Master said: 'Ci! You cherish the sheep, but I cherish the rite. (Bao says: 'If the sheep remains, the rite can still be known through it; if the sheep is gone, the rite will surely fall into disuse.')**

[This is] also [the case]. [It means] to cherish and protect. A man of discerning wisdom and virtue now understands that the principles of Buddhist causality and retribution have a definitive destination;

thus, one is fit to rely upon them to honor and elevate the spirits of the deceased. One should not continue to cling to the provisional teachings of the Confucian school by slaughtering living beings to sacrifice at the ancestral temples.
△ Second, the explanation of the reason for the exhortation has three parts. First, the merit of releasing living beings.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, among the greatest of merits, none is greater than the gift of life. This is the fundamental cause for becoming Śakra or Brahmā, analogous to the great virtue of Heaven and Earth (as stated in the *I Ching*).
[Commentary] The ten wholesome and ten unwholesome actions are established as opposites. Among the ten unwholesome karmas, none is a greater transgression than taking life;
among the ten wholesome karmas, none brings greater merit than giving life. Giving life in its inferior grade is the cause for rebirth in the human realm;
in its middling grade, it is the cause for rebirth in the heavens of the desire realm; and in its superior grade, it is the cause for rebirth in the heavens of the form and formless realms. Now...

Among these, one category of the causes for becoming Śakra is briefly cited for the middling grade; for the superior grade, the causes for becoming a Brahmā King in the four dhyānas of the form realm are cited in general.
Therefore, giving is the fundamental cause for birth as Śakra or Brahmā. This is analogous to what the *Yi* (Book of Changes) says:
"The great virtue of Heaven and Earth is called life-giving; the great treasure of the sage is called his station. Now, since [one] has killed...
It is said that among the world’s perversions of virtue, none is more harmful than [the sacrifice of life]. △ Second, killing living beings is not benevolence.
[Commentary]: Now, to kill those [beasts] to sacrifice for these [ancestors], how can this be close to a benevolent heart? If such a thing could be tolerated, what would not be tolerable?
[Commentary] To love life and loathe killing is called benevolence (*ren*). "This" (*shi*) means "this very thing. "Patience" (*nin*) means "tolerance. "Who" (*shoku*) means "whom.

To kill those oxen and other animals to sacrifice them to these ancestral spirits (*kō*) and so forth—in doing so, one does not draw near to the heart of benevolence; on the contrary, one harms the nature of life.

it brings calamity upon the divine way (hence there are two classes among travelers: those who sing and those who wail).

at dusk, the *Xunü* mansion is at its zenith, and the Dipper points to the center of the *Shu* position. (After the *Frosts Descend*, the sun is in the *Di* lunar mansion; at the time of dusk, the *Xunü* mansion is centered, and the Dipper points to the *Shu* position.

Furthermore, during this month, he orders the relevant officials to gather and stack fodder to nourish the sacrificial animals. (In the ninth month, one collects and stacks wood and grasses for fodder. "Sacrificial animals" refers to those of pure color.)

[They slaughter] oxen, sheep, and pigs to provide for the August Heaven and the Supreme Deity, for the famous mountains and great rivers, for the ghosts and spirits of the four quarters, and to sacrifice to the spirits of the ancestral temple and the altars of soil and grain.
They do this to seek blessings for humanity; yet, though they claim to be seeking blessings, because they take life, they are in fact establishing enmity and resentment.
"Leun" means to advertise. It is simply that the son advertises his own empty fame, while conversely bringing calamity upon his father.
The Mother Goddesses (Mātṛs) are deities of the Way. The *Piyu jing* (Sūtra of Similes) states: "Five hundred hungry ghosts proceed while singing and dancing;
five hundred virtuous people proceed while weeping. The Tathāgata said: "In the households of hungry ghosts, descendants perform meritorious deeds and shall attain liberation;
this is why they sing and dance. In the households of virtuous people, descendants engage only in killing and will soon undergo great [suffering]."
It is suffering; therefore, they weep. Question: Since Confucius was a sage, why did he cause people to kill living beings to sacrifice in the ancestral temple?
If calamity reaches one’s parents, and the descendants take life, is there not fault in that? What is the purpose of this? Answer:

He established the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of those to be taught, with the sole aim of benefiting all beings. The matter is superficial while the intent is profound; he did not adhere to minor details. As the World-Honored One said:
No living being may be intentionally killed, for the purpose is to lead the enlightened to practice compassion.

Nevertheless, it is permitted for Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*) to kill those with evil views and wicked people, so that all may give rise to right view and refrain from committing unwholesome karma.
When Confucius established the laws for sacrificing to the ancestral temple, he intended for all people to practice filial piety.

One does not commit the crimes of immediate retribution. Filial piety is the source of a hundred virtues; it increases what is beneficial and diminishes what is harmful. By attending to the immediate, one’s intent reaches the distant;

this is merely a matter of gradual transformation. I hope that the worthy and accomplished among you will, regarding both Confucianism and Buddhism—within Buddhism, distinguishing between the provisional and the ultimate—observe the capacities of beings, whether sharp or dull.

Thus we know that King Wen’s sacrifice of vegetables and fruits surpassed Zhou’s lord’s sacrifice of the three great cattle. By analogy with that, the fragrance of filial virtue is pure and refined through fasting.

those who are in the three evil realms, such as that of hungry ghosts, shall be reborn in the human or celestial realms, and those already in the human or celestial realms shall further increase their merit, longevity, and the fortune of seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma. △ Second, because [the spirits] cannot accept offerings.

Filial toward sentient beings: when [the Buddha] emerged from the golden coffin, he joined his palms and inquired after Māyā. It should be answered thus:

Therefore, both those in the household and those who have left it should all practice filial piety and show loving respect toward their parents. II. Nurturing.
"Thus they bring about their joy.

[Commentary] Regarding "the two types of support bring about their joy": the Confucian brings forth a pleasant voice and a humble demeanor, performing such acts as providing warm water and cold water, and regular inquiries after one's well-being;
thus there are traditions such as fanning the bed and warming the mat. The Buddhist, however, apportions and reduces his robes and alms-bowl according to the degree of faith or slander he encounters.
Thus, there are those such as Prince Sutasoma who cut their own flesh to satisfy their hunger.
[Commentary] "To provide for them with joy" means to serve and attend to them in accordance with their wishes, thereby bringing happiness to one's parents.

When they err, one should respond with a cheerful countenance, kind words, a gentle expression, and a humble demeanor, offering subtle admonitions. In winter, one provides warm bedding; in summer, one provides coolness.
Fan the bed. At night, arrange the covers and pillows; in the morning, inspect [the parents] during their period of settled rest. Thus, the *Quli* states:

"If the parents have faults, one should admonish them with lowered breath, a gentle voice, and a pleasant countenance. If they do not follow the admonition, then rise up and show reverence. It further states:
"The ritual for one who is a son is to provide warmth in winter and coolness in summer; to settle the bedding at dusk and inspect them at dawn. (*Dongguan Hanji*)
It is said: Huang Xiang, courtesy name Wenqiang, was a man of integrity and filial piety. His household had no servants, so he personally attended to his parents' needs.
In summer, he would fan their bed and pillow; in winter, he would warm their bedding and mats with his own body. Regarding filial piety in the Buddhist tradition, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
If one's parents do not believe in the Triple Gem, one should provide them with little, fearing that doing so would diminish their merit.
If they do believe in the Triple Gem, one should provide for all their needs and encourage them to resolve upon the Bodhi-mind.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that by respectfully making offerings to one's parents and to Dharma masters, one obtains immeasurable merit. The *Sūtra on Great Requital of Kindness* relates that in the past, Śākyamuni...
He was the crown prince named Sujāti. At that time, his father, the king, was usurped by the minister Rāhu and sought to have him killed.
The king, along with the queen and the prince, fled to another country. Having traveled a long distance by mistake, their provisions were exhausted and they were weary.
Every day, the prince cut three jin of his own flesh; one jin he offered to his father, and one jin he offered to his mother.
He ate one *jin* himself. Only when the Prince’s flesh was exhausted did he reach that country and escape his suffering and hardship.

His heart was devoid of joy; he ceased his indignation and abstained from fine food.
