When King Wen ate once, King Wu ate once; when King Wen ate twice, King Wu ate twice. After twelve days, he recovered.
Regarding the use of meat as medicine, the *Bao'en jing* states that the six non-Buddhist teachers... [text fragment ends].
[The king] slandered the Buddha, claiming he was unfilial. The Tathāgata then told him that in the past, he had once been the Prince Kṣāntivādin.
At that time, his father the king fell gravely ill. The ministers sought to find someone who did not harbor anger, intending to take his eyes and marrow to prepare a miraculous medicine.
The prince replied, "I am such a person. He then summoned a caṇḍāla, who cut through his bones to extract his marrow.
He gouged out both his eyes, compounded them into medicine, and his father-king took it and was immediately cured of his illness.
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) states: Dharma Master Liliang’s mother was elderly and ill;

carrying both his mother and the commentaries on the sutras and treatises, each on one end of a shoulder-pole, he would not bear to carry them on his back, so he carried them crosswise. Wherever he went, he propagated the Dharma and benefited others.
He attended to his parents' needs without fail; people of the time called him "Lang of Horizontal Travel. Daoji, Jingtuo, Dandanmu, and others were not alone in this practice.
IV. Regarding mourning, one should express the utmost grief.

[Commentary]: Regarding the fourth point, "manifesting one's grief at a funeral": among the Confucians, there was King Wu Ding who did not speak for three days, and Zi Gao whose tears flowed as blood;

among the Buddhists, there was Maudgalyāyana who cried out loudly. Although the methods of the "Tamer of Men" (the Buddha) and those of the Confucian rites differ, in both cases, their grief was excessive.

[Commentary] "To manifest one's grief in mourning" means that when parents pass away, a son exhausts his filial heart, reaching the utmost limit of sorrowful sincerity through wailing, leaping, and weeping.
The *Analects* records: Zizhang said, "The *Book of Documents* states: 'Gaozong remained in seclusion for three years and did not speak. What does this mean? (Confucius said:
"Gaozong was the king who restored the prosperity of the Yin dynasty; his name was Wuding. 'Liang' means sincerity; 'yin' means silence. He remained silent for three years. Zizi—

He said: "Why must it necessarily be Gaozong? All ancients were like this. When the ruler passed away, the various officials took charge of their respective duties and waited for three years before taking over the administration themselves.

(Kong Yingda says: "Zhongzhai" refers to the Minister of Heaven, the high minister who assists the King in governance. Only after the three-year mourning period is completed does the King personally resume the administration.

The commentary on the *Shu* says: "When the various officials had business, they did not consult the ruler; each took charge of his own affairs, binding himself and his official duties, and listened to the Zhongzhai, the highest minister. 'Listen' means to follow. 'Zhong' means great. Ziga was [the son of] Gao...

The character "chai" (柴) is also used in this sense. The *Tangong* states: "When Gao Zigao was observing the mourning rites for his parents, he wept blood for three years—weeping so silently that it was as if blood were flowing—and he never showed his teeth, meaning he neither spoke nor smiled.
Regarding "the Controller who carries the coffin": "Controller" refers to Śākyamuni; "carrying the coffin" refers to carrying the coffins of one's parents.
The *Sūtra on King Śuddhodana’s Nirvāṇa* says: "At that time, King Śuddhodana was gravely ill and near death. He wept..."
Tears fell as he thought of Siddhārtha and the others. He addressed the multitude, saying, "My life is about to end.

It is my regret that I do not see Nanda, Ānanda, and Rāhula; this is what I lament. Even if I were to see them, though they would not be saved, since they have not yet escaped birth and death, how could it not be a source of suffering?
When the people heard this, there was none among them who did not weep. The Buddha was at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
They were fifty yojanas apart. Knowing the king’s intention from afar, [the Buddha] immediately told Ānanda, "We should go there to fulfill the king's wish.
Nanda said to the Buddha, "The king is my father; his deeds have been extraordinary and have benefited the world.
We should now go to him to repay the kindness of his upbringing. Ānanda spoke again, "He is my uncle; please allow me [to go]."
"He has gone forth as a disciple of the Buddha; I also wish to go. Rāhula spoke again, "He is my grandfather.
My father abandoned his kingdom to seek the Way, and it was through my grandfather's upbringing that I was able to go forth. Now I too wish to pay him my respects. The Buddha said:
"Welcome. He then used his supernormal powers to leap into the air and arrive at the city of Kapilavastu, emitting a great radiance.
All the people of the kingdom could not help but weep. The Buddha addressed the assembly, saying, "You should all reflect that birth and death are suffering;
only the Way is true. As the Buddha emitted light, it relieved the King's ailment and brought him peace. The King, knowing the Buddha had returned, focused his mind with single-minded devotion.

Overwhelmed with joy, he rose from his seat without realizing it. In a moment, the Buddha entered. The King raised both hands to receive the Buddha’s feet and said, "I only pray that the Tathāgata will let his hand touch my body;
this is now the last time I shall see the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
The Buddha placed his hand upon the King’s forehead and said, "The King is a person of pure conduct; the defilements of his mind have already been removed. Regarding the King—
While lying on his side, he raised his face, joined his palms, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying, "I gaze upon the Tathāgata, my eyes never turning away;
my vows are now fulfilled. He then passed away. The Śākya sons wailed and lamented; they prepared a shrouded coffin and enshrined him within it, adorned with the seven treasures.
The Buddha and Nanda stood before the bier, standing with solemn reverence; Ānanda and Rāhula stood behind the bier.
Nanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "Sire, my father the King raised me; I pray that you grant me leave to carry the coffin. Ānanda and Rāhula made the same request.
The Buddha contemplated the violent sentient beings of the future who would fail to repay the profound kindness of their parents; therefore, he personally carried the coffin himself.
The great trichiliocosm shook six times, and all the mountains surged and submerged like boats upon the water.
The devas, Śakra, Brahmā, yakṣas, pretas, and others all came to the funeral, offering to carry the coffin on behalf of the Buddha. The Buddha granted their request. The Four Kings...

They each took their turn to carry it, having reduced its size. The Buddha held an incense burner and walked before the coffin. An Arhat from Vulture Peak Mountain ascended into the air to follow the Buddha.
The Buddha commanded that the sandalwood be used to cremate the King, his father; the great assembly wailed and wept. The Buddha addressed them, saying:
"Impermanence, suffering, and emptiness possess no solidity. Like an illusion, a transformation, or the moon reflected in water, life does not endure for long."
The assembly merely perceived this fire as hot; yet their desires were even hotter. After the fire had been extinguished, they collected the *śarīra* relics and erected a stūpa to make offerings.
The assembly requested that the World-Honored One explain the rebirth destination of the king. The Buddha said, "The king has been reborn in the palace of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven.
Upon hearing this, the assembly rejoiced, prostrated before the Buddha, and withdrew. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: At that time, Mahāprajāpatī and...
The five hundred bhikṣuṇīs all attained the state of *aśaikṣa*. Upon hearing that the Buddha would enter parinirvāṇa three months after the passing of Kāśyapa, they thought to themselves:
"We cannot bear to witness the Buddha entering parinirvāṇa; it is fitting that we first attain extinction.
They immediately went to where the Buddha was and related the matter in detail. The Buddha silently granted his permission. Ānandā spoke again: "I now—"
"I shall no longer behold the Tathāgata’s countenance; today I am separated from the holy form and shall never see it again.
Having spoken these words, Ānanda circumambulated the Buddha seven times, as did the assembly of bhikṣus, before withdrawing to their respective monasteries.
He gathered the community of bhikṣuṇīs and took his leave to enter parinirvāṇa. Upon hearing this, five hundred bhikṣuṇīs all took their leave to enter parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha granted her request in full. Mahāprajāpatī then struck the *gandī* bell, spread out her sitting mat, and rose into the air, manifesting the eighteen transformations.
She returned to her original seat, entered the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments, and subsequently passed into parinirvāṇa.
The earth shook in six ways, and the devas wept with grief; the same occurred for the other five hundred bhikṣuṇīs.
The Buddha commanded the great general Yaśodharā to prepare five hundred couches, five hundred carriages for carrying ghee and oil, and five hundred wagons for flowers, incense, and firewood.
To offer worship to the remains of Mahāprajāpatī, the Buddha went to the nunnery and addressed Ānanda, Nanda, and Rāhula, saying:
"You all lift up the body of Mahāprajāpatī; I shall personally perform the offering. Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings came forward and said to the Buddha:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One will not trouble himself with this; we ourselves shall perform the offering. The Buddha said: "Stop, stop! The Tathāgata..."
What I am doing is not within the reach of you gods, nāgas, and others. Why is this? Parents provide their children with many benefits;
the kindness of their nurturing is profound, as they nourish them with milk, carry them in their arms, and embrace them. I shall now repay the kindness of my maternal aunt, Āmrapālī;
therefore, I personally make this offering. The parents of all Buddhas of the past and future have all entered parinirvāṇa first. All...
She offered herself as an oblation. Then Vaiśravaṇa commanded five hundred kings to go to Mount Candana and fetch fragrant firewood to cremate the bhikṣuṇī.
At that time, the World-Honored One himself lifted one leg of his couch, while Nanda, Rāhula, and Ānanda each lifted one leg;
they flew into the air and went to the cemetery. The remaining fourfold assembly then lifted the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs.
They took fragrant firewood and placed it upon the body of Āṣāḍhā. The Buddha spoke this verse: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
those who are born must die. To be neither born nor to die—this nirvāṇa is the supreme bliss.

After the fire was extinguished, the Buddha commanded Mahānāman to collect the relics of the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs and to erect a stūpa for them, so that they might receive merit throughout the long night.

[The merit is] immeasurable. Question: Maudgalyāyana cried out loudly, and the Tamer (Śākyamuni) carried the coffin on a litter. This is not mentioned in the Confucian Classics; the rites differ from worldly customs.
Why does the commentary state that it "manifests their sameness"? Therefore, I shall annotate this:

seeing that his mother had already died and was among the spirits, his grief reached its utmost limit, which is why he cried out so loudly. Śākyamuni, the Tamer, [performed] various offerings to his parents.
He left behind his physical remains; he personally carried the coffin and performed a *candana* cremation.

He erected a stupa for offerings that surpassed conventional rites, his grief being so extreme that it is said his sorrow was "excessive. △ Fifth, regarding the solemnity observed in sacrifices, there are two parts.
First, the accounts of the two schools.
[Commentary: Regarding the five sacrifices, one must exercise the utmost solemnity. Among Confucians, there are those who present bamboo shoots; among Buddhists, there are those who offer meals.
(Although the specific forms differ, the underlying intent of the sacrifice is largely the same.)

[Commentary]: “Yan” (嚴) means to be reverent; it denotes the height of respect. Once the burial has been completed, one reflects upon the deceased with affection and performs sacrifices at the four seasons, treating the dead as if they were alive.
At every time of sacrifice, one observes the fasts and purifies oneself through bathing; one awakens at dawn and remains sleepless. Therefore, this is called “yan.
The end of the *Xiaojing* (Classic of Filial Piety) states: “In life, serve them with love and respect; in death, serve them with grief and sorrow. This is the root of the people’s livelihood.”

It is finished. The principles of life and death are complete; the duties of a filial son toward his parents have reached their end. The *Book of Jin* states: Meng Zong, courtesy name Gongwu, was a native of Anlu in Jiangxia.
He served his mother with supreme filial piety. His mother was also virtuous by nature and was able to instruct him well.
Once, his mother had a craving for bamboo shoots, but as it was winter, no shoots were available. Meng Zong entered the bamboo grove and wailed piteously.

He sought them out, and bamboo shoots immediately appeared. He took them and presented them to his mother. People of the time all said this was brought about by the resonance of the filial son’s virtue.
He was a man of the Jin dynasty; his story of filial piety is passed down in tradition. Meng Zong held the office of Zonglang. His mother had a particular fondness for bamboo shoots.
Zong made offerings to them regularly. After his mother passed away, he wished to offer bamboo shoots for the winter solstice sacrifice;

he entered the bamboo grove and prayed with grief to Heaven and Earth, whereupon he obtained bamboo shoots to present as an offering. Later, he served as the Governor of Yuzhang and eventually rose to the rank of Minister (Situ).

His distribution of rice can be understood from this. Question: He offered bamboo shoots to his mother and distributed rice to the ghosts; since these two acts are distinct, why do you say they are the same?

Therefore, I have provided these annotations. When hungry ghosts long for rice, one offers them rice; when the deceased mother was fond of bamboo shoots, nothing but bamboo shoots were presented as an offering.

Each follows according to their own preferences, yet the intent of the sacrifice remains the same. Part Two: Repeatedly Manifesting the Confucian Tradition. Section One: Establishing the Reason for Sacrifices.

[Commentary: However, because the ultimate teachings have not yet appeared, it is difficult to propagate [the doctrine of] retribution; therefore, for the time being, the laws of sacrifice are established first, so that people may reverently serve the spiritual beings.
[Commentary]: The unsurpassed Buddha-dharma is the ultimate, true teaching; thus it is called the "Ultimate Teaching" (*zhìjiào*).

What this Ultimate Teaching elucidates is that good causes yield good retributions and evil causes yield evil retributions; the correspondence between cause and effect is termed "retribution and response" (*bàoyìng*).

When the Ultimate Teaching first arose in the Western Land (India), it had not yet reached this region (China). Because the faculties of people were not yet mature, it was difficult to propagate the principles of cause, effect, and retribution.

This is the underlying principle. Therefore, the Sage Confucius established teachings according to the capacities of his followers, instructing people in filial piety to repay the kindness of their parents:
by showing reverence and seeking joy for those currently living, and by offering sincere mourning and sacrifice for those who have passed away.

This causes them to serve the spirits of their parents with respect, intending to lead them to seek out where these spirits reside; only when the ultimate teaching arrives will its workings of cause and effect be revealed.
This is where one should take birth. △ Second, the evaluation and discussion that [the ancestors] cannot be two.
First, the ancestral parents eternally exist. 【Commentary】The spiritual essence is the cognitive nature of the parents; this sufficiently demonstrates the eternal existence of the ancestral parents.
△ Second, reproaching what has been lost.
[Commentary]: Since the physical form perishes while the spirit does not perish, how can one value the form while disparaging the spirit? The rest is as previously explained.
[Commentary]: Since the physical body perishes while the spiritual essence does not perish, yet one constantly sacrifices to it, how can one be said to value the form and slight the spirit?

To say that one brings forth reverence when [the parents] reside [at home], provides them with pleasure when they are nourished, and brings forth sorrow when they are ill—this is precisely to value and cherish their physical forms.
To take the grace of the Great Heaven and offer sacrifices to them according to the rites for spirits is precisely to treat one's parents as base and insignificant.

The spirits are likewise [responsive]. Inferring from this, one should abandon the ritual sacrifices provisionally established by Confucianism and instead rely upon the true principle of retribution according to the Buddhist teachings to accumulate merit for one’s ancestors.
The rest is as previously distinguished in the section on the similarities and differences between filial conduct [in Buddhism and Confucianism].
This sutra is now spoken in order to demonstrate these matters concerning filial conduct toward both the living and the deceased. △ Second, the conclusion.
[Commentary] The preceding section has concluded the discussion on the commonality of life and death.
△ Second, clarifying the commonality of sin and merit. First, revealing the commonality of sin.

[Commentary] Next, the commonality of sin and merit is distinguished. Regarding "sin": in the Confucian system, those who transgress the five penal codes shall be punished according to the five types of mutilation. However—

They are not eligible for amnesty. If they are released from prison, their names are listed among the seven heinous crimes (*saptānantarya*); if they receive the precepts, they are excluded by the seven prohibitions (*sapta-āvaraṇa*). Thus, they are certain to enter the Avīci Hell.

[Commentary] According to the *Shangshu*, the five punishments originated in the era of Shun; these are tattooing (*mò*), cutting the nose (*yì*), cutting the feet (*fèi*), castration (*gōng*), and capital punishment (*dàpì*).
Master Zheng’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "Tattooing" means carving the forehead and staining it with ink. This is not a matter that arose... [text ends].
[The punishment] is applied to those who enter [the capital] without following the principles of the Way and engage in litigation. *Ni* (劓) means to cut off one's nose.

*Geyu fu* (革輿服) refers to those who alter the established systems of vehicles and clothing; [the punishment] is applied to them. *Fei* (剕) means to amputate one's feet. Furthermore, it is applied to those who break through passes and bridges.
For those who breach city walls or palaces, this [punishment] is added. "Palace" refers to castrating males and confining females in dark chambers.
For men and women who engage in sexual intercourse without the rites and righteousness, this [punishment] is added. As for "great execution," it is the current death penalty.
For those who commit robbery, plunder, and the like, this [punishment] is added. From the successive reigns of the two dynasties of Xia and Yin, down to the Zhou...

In the time of Duke Shun, there were five hundred punishments for each category, totaling two thousand five hundred articles. By the time of King Mu of Zhou, Lü Hou was summoned to serve as Minister of Justice;
he increased the lighter penalties and reduced the heavier ones, setting one thousand for branding and mutilation of the nose, and five hundred for amputation of the kneecap.

There were three hundred offenses for the palace punishments and two hundred for capital offenses, totaling three thousand articles. Among these three thousand articles, none was greater than filial impiety;

hence it is said that "the articles exceed the five punishments. Regarding the "five dismemberments," this refers to binding the five limbs with five carts and tearing them apart both lengthwise and crosswise.
According to the *San shi guo chun qiu*, Chi Yang acted upon the words of his wife.
He killed his mother in the mountains. When the King of Qin heard this, he ordered her to be torn apart by five chariots.
Reversing the previous five phrases, such as "not showing reverence while living with her" and "not providing joy while supporting her," these are all the offenses of unfiliality.

The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "The seven heinous offenses (*saptānantarya*) are: shedding the blood of a Buddha; killing one's father; killing one's mother; killing one's preceptor (*upādhyāya*); killing one's teacher (*ācārya*);
disrupting the *saṃgha* that performs the *karmavācanā* and turns the wheel of the Dharma; and killing an arhat. If one commits even one among these seven, one is barred from receiving the precepts.

These are also called the 'seven obstructions' (*sapta-āvaraṇa*), because they obstruct and hinder the precepts. In the Sanskrit language, this is called *anantarya*; here it is translated as 'uninterrupted' (*mūrdhava*)."
Because the succession of suffering is continuous and without interval. △ Second, revealing the equality of merit. [Commentary] Regarding the equality of merit:
in the Confucian tradition, one is honored at the village gate; this is the retribution from Heaven above. In the Buddhist tradition, one’s precepts and virtue are polished and bright;

this is the cause for the Pure Land (as stated in the *Contemplation Sūtra*, one should cultivate the three types of merit. First, filially supporting one's parents... these three kinds of karma are the direct causes for the Pure Land of all Buddhas of the three periods).
[Commentary]: "To signal at the gate and village" means to honor and display [one's virtue] at the family door and in the local neighborhood.
As the *Hanshu* states: Guo Ju, courtesy name Wenju, was a native of Henei. His family was poor, yet he supported his mother.
He had once fathered a son who was then three years old. Ju said to his wife: "Our hunger and poverty are such that my mother’s age is already advanced; as for providing for her..."
My mother obtained delicious food and would instead give it to my son, thereby causing herself to go hungry. A son is easy to obtain, but a mother is difficult to find again.
Now, I shall kill her for the sake of my wife so that I may preserve my mother’s life. His wife followed his words;
he had his wife carry the son toward the back garden, where they dug a pit and buried him. Upon digging, they found a cauldron of gold. Above—
There is a record stating: "The filial son Guo Ju killed his son to save his mother. Heaven bestowed upon him one cauldron of gold; neither the officials could seize it nor others could take it.
Ju took the gold to the authorities, and the official issued an edict saying: 'Return the gold to him and honor his gate with an inscription.
There are many such former sages as Dong An and others. Those who comment on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* say that those who wish to be born [therein]..."

To attain rebirth in the Pure Land of the West, one should cultivate the three kinds of merit: first, being filial toward one’s parents, serving one’s teachers and elders, maintaining a compassionate heart and refraining from killing, and practicing the ten virtuous actions;
second, receiving and upholding the Three Refuges, fully observing the various precepts, and not violating the rules of dignified conduct.
Third, there are three types of practices for generating the bodhicitta: having deep faith in cause and effect, reading and reciting Mahāyāna sutras, and exhorting others to practice.

These three kinds of karma are the direct causes for the pure lands of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. Through filial piety one is born in a pure land; through lack of filial piety one enters hell.
Now, in order to demonstrate these offenses and blessings, this sutra is preached. △ Third, the conclusion.
[Commentary] The preceding section has concluded the general exposition of the way of filial piety.
△ Fourth, showing the superior field [of merit], which is threefold. First, the heading of the chapter is presented.
[Commentary] Fourth, showing the superior field:

△ Second, the extensive presentation of the modes of practice has two parts. First, a general explanation of the field of merit, which further has two parts. First, the actual manifestation of the field of merit, which further has three parts.
First, the three things used as metaphors.

[Commentary: It is like people in the world who, wishing to have the five grains abundant in their granaries and lacking nothing year after year, must take seeds of rice and wheat, plow the fields with oxen, and sow them;
for if they do not sow, [the supply] will be exhausted.
[Commentary] The five grains are *liáng*, rice, beans (*shù*), hemp, and wheat. Furthermore, Yang Quan’s *Wùlǐ Lùn* states:
"*Liáng* is the general name for *shǔ* and *jì*; *dào* is the general name for non-glutinous and glutinous rice; *shù* is the general name for all varieties of beans."

Each of the three [categories] has twenty varieties; the fruits of vegetables and trees assist the grains, each with twenty varieties. Taken together, these constitute the five grains (*pañca-dhānya*);
taken individually, they constitute the hundred grains (*śata-dhānya*). △ Second, using the Dharma to illustrate the metaphor.
[Commentary] It is the same within the Dharma. Taking compassion, reverence, and filial piety as the seed; taking food, clothing, wealth, and even one’s own life as the ox and the plow;
and taking the poor, the sick, the Triple Gem, and one’s parents as the field.
[Commentary]: Regarding the field of suffering consisting of the poor and the sick, one should give rise to a heart of compassion and provide them with food and clothing.

Regarding the field of merit consisting of the Three Jewels, one should give rise to a heart of reverence and offer them wealth and silks. Regarding the field of gratitude consisting of parents, one should give rise to a heart of filial piety and serve them with one’s body and life.
Among these three fields, the poor and the sick constitute the field of compassion; they should be regarded with pity. The Three Jewels and parents together constitute the field of reverence.

Fields [of merit] should be venerated. These three types are collectively termed "fields of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*). Furthermore, among the three mental states, filial piety is the general principle, while compassion and reverence are the specific ones.
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "All sentient beings of the six realms are one's parents; one should be filially obedient toward them.
They possess kindness and virtue, and thus one should revere and honor them. They suffer from poverty and illness, and thus one should compassionately relieve them. Regarding poverty and illness:
The Three Jewels, parents, and the three fields are fixed; the seeds of compassion, reverence, and filial piety are universal, for they can arise in all three fields.
Clothing, food, wealth, property, one’s own body and life, oxen, and plows are also universal, for they may be employed in all three fields.
△ Third, the correlation of the characteristics of practice.
[Commentary]: There are disciples of the Buddha who wish to attain the hundredfold adornments within the *ālayavijñāna* that are inexhaustible from lifetime to lifetime.

They must exercise compassion, reverence, and filial piety, providing clothing, food, wealth, and even their own lives to relieve the poor and the sick, and to honor and support the Triple Gem and their parents;
this is called "planting merit. If one does not plant [merit], one will remain impoverished and lacking in merit and wisdom, entering into rebirth.
The perilous path of death. That which is called the field of merit (puṇyakṣetra) is so named because it is like a field for sowing grain, which is called a grain-field.
[Commentary] Regarding "adorned with a hundred merits": there are a hundred instances of the karmic causes of meritorious conduct, which bring about the fruit of adornment.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 53, states: "Because there are ten aspects for each of the ten virtuous actions. That is to say, regarding non-killing: [doing so] partially, extensively, or completely;
for a short time, for a long time, or for as long as one lives; doing it oneself, encouraging others to do so, praising it, and rejoicing in it—these are called the ten kinds.
Ten times ten makes one hundred. 2. Second, further clarifying the distinctions between superior and inferior.

[Commentary: Furthermore, seeds may be potent, fresh, dry, or scorched; fields may be fertile, rich, hard, or barren. Likewise, there are degrees of earnestness or laxity in the mind of compassion, reverence, or filial piety;
poverty has its depths; illness has its severity; Buddhas have both true and emanated forms; emanations may remain in the world or enter nirvana; the Dharma has its Great and Small vehicles;
the teachings have their provisional and ultimate aspects; and the Sangha has those who uphold and those who violate [the precepts]. This applies even to parents.
There are seven types of fields for the present life; each one corresponds to whether the field is fertile or barren, which is clearly visible.
[Commentary]: When fresh and excellent seeds are sown in a field, every grain sprouts and bears fruit.

This is like the three minds being earnest and sublime, and pouring one's devotion into the three fields; merit is produced in each instance, benefiting both oneself and others. A barren [field], however, is not so.
If parched seeds are sown in a field, they may or may not sprout, and those that do bear fruit are few.
Likewise, when one performs tasks for the three fields with a mind that is lax and lacking in excellence, the resulting merit and benefit may exist or not; those who obtain the fruit are few.
Therefore, by means of this cultivation of merit, one should give rise to a sincere and earnest heart, providing relief with utmost devotion and serving with reverence.
Third, the fields. Although fields may be superior or inferior, the seed must be excellent; one should diligently practice and study this. The rest of the text can be understood accordingly.
△ Second, the actual exposition of this sutra.
[Commentary: Now, this *Ullambana* assembly possesses three kinds of "fertile fields," and is therefore called "superior. That is to say:

making offerings on the day of the Buddha’s Joy (*buddhānanda-dina*) to those of great virtue who have observed the *pravāraṇā* and maintain pure precepts—this is the superiority of the "Field of Reverence" (*guru-kṣetra*). Repaying the kindness of one's parents—this is the superiority of the "Field of Kindness" (*upakāri-kṣetra*).
When one's parents are in the midst of calamity and distress—this is the superiority of the "Field of Compassion" (*karuṇā-kṣetra*).
△ The third section: The intent behind the arising of the *Saṃyuktāgama*.
[Commentary] This sutra was taught in order to demonstrate this field of supreme merit.
△ Second: What is subsumed within the Piṭakas and Vehicles. Part one: Stating the headings of the chapters.
[Commentary] Second, regarding that which is subsumed within the *piṭakas* and *yānas*.
△ Second, the actual explanation of the inclusion, in two parts. First, the general indication.
[Commentary] "Piṭaka" refers to the Three Piṭakas; "yāna" refers to the Five Yānas.

△ Second, the detailed presentation of the two [divisions] has two parts. First, the inclusion within the Three Piṭakas also has two parts. First, the explanation of the meaning of the Three Piṭakas also has two parts.
First, the formal explanation of the Three Piṭakas is further divided into three. First, the Sūtra Piṭaka.

[Commentary: Regarding the "Three Piṭakas": first is the Sūtra, which is here translated as "Scripture in Accordance with Truth" (Qijing). "In accordance with truth" (qie) means to accord with principle and accord with the capacities of sentient beings.

"Scripture" (jing) is defined in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* as having the meaning of "pervading and encompassing. That is to say, it pierces through the meanings that ought to be known and encompasses those beings who are to be converted.
Among the three trainings, this teaching elucidates the training in concentration (samādhi).

[Commentary]: *Sūtra* is also called *sūtru*; both are corruptions. The correct term is *sūtrānta*, which means "Scripture that Accords" (*qìjīng*). "Scripture" (*jīng*) encompasses both doctrine and principle.
Because the doctrine accords with the principle, and the principle accords with the faculties [of sentient beings], it is called "Scripture that Accords.

When the essence is retained while the function is abbreviated, it is simply called "Scripture" (*jīng*). As for "Pitaka" (*zàng*), it has the meaning of "gathering and upholding. Because the teaching can gather and uphold the principle, it is called "Scripture that Accords."
The Pitaka. △ Second, the Vinaya-piṭaka. [Commentary]:
Second is the Vinaya, which here is translated as "Discipline" (tiao-fu). "Discipline" (tiao) refers to refining the three karmas; "subduing" (fu) refers to suppressing transgressions and faults.
This teaching elucidates the training in ethical discipline (śīla-śikṣā).
[Commentary]: *Vinaya*. Formerly translated as *bini* or *binie*, both of which are corruptions. This means "subduing" (*zhàofú*).
It is called "subduing" because it both disciplines and subdues; it pertains to both the teaching and its practice, for it was spoken by the Buddha and is upheld by both ordinary beings and sages.
△ Third, the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
[Commentary: Third is the Abhidharma, which here is translated as "Dharma-in-Relation" (Duìfǎ). "Dharma" refers to nirvāṇa and the Four Noble Truths;
"in Relation" means to face toward and to contemplate. That which performs this relating is sublime wisdom (*prajñā*). This teaching elucidates the training in wisdom.

[Commentary] *Abhidharma*. Formerly translated as *Abhidharma*, which is an error. This means "Dharma-Counterpart" (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*). That which can counter is wisdom (*prajñā*), encompassing both the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*).
That which is countered is the Dharma, comprising both the mundane (*laukika*) and the supramundane (*lokottara*).

This wisdom is directed toward the realization of the Dharma of Nirvāṇa, and furthermore, it is able to counter-observe and comprehend the Dharmas of the Four Truths. Because it is the counterpart of the Dharma, it is called *Abhidharma*. Dharma.
Yuan says: The Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma are three distinct categories, each established as a separate Piṭaka. Alternatively, there may be no distinction between them;

for instance, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* and others primarily elucidate the study of concentration (samādhi) and are thus called the Sūtra Piṭaka. The *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* and others primarily elucidate the study of ethical discipline (śīla) and are termed the Vinaya Piṭaka.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and others primarily elucidate the study of wisdom (prajñā) and are termed the Abhidharma Piṭaka. Accordingly...
There are many things to be explained, which are categorized into the Three Piṭakas. △ Second, the distinction between the transformative (vinaya) and the regulatory (śāsana).

[Commentary]: Now, the Sūtras constitute the transformative teaching (*huàjiào*), for they open, entice, transform, and guide. The Vinayas constitute the regulatory teaching (*zhìjiào*), for they restrict and govern conduct and practice.
The Śāstras, meanwhile, involve critical investigation to explain the meaning of the Sūtras and Vinayas.

[Commentary] The Sūtras demonstrate the characteristics of the causes and effects of good and evil, universally transforming those with the capacity of laypeople; this is called the "Transformative Teaching" (Hua-jiao).

The Vinaya section is primarily for the establishment of precepts (śikṣāpada): it enjoins the practice of good and the cessation of evil, demonstrating the characteristics of observance and violation;

it governs those who have left the household life, and is thus called the "Regulatory Teaching" (Zhi-jiao). The Śāstras primarily reveal wisdom, investigating and explaining the Sūtras and Vinayas, thereby manifesting what they signify.
The subtle principle permeates both the teachings of transformation (*huàjiào*) and the teachings of discipline (*zhìjiào*). **2.
Subsuming this Sūtra:** [Commentary: Now, regarding this *Ullambana* [Sūtra], according to its title, it is subsumed under the teachings of transformation and belongs to the Sūtra Piṭaka.

However, according to its underlying meaning and intent, it is also subsumed under the teachings of discipline and belongs to the Vinaya Piṭaka (for it prescribes that bhikṣus and others must perform this rite annually on the day of the *pravāraṇā*).

[Commentary] This clarifies the inclusion [of this scripture]. It relies on the primary [teaching] and not the auxiliary; it is a teaching of transformation (*vaipulya*) and is included within the *Sūtra Piṭaka*.
△ Second, the inclusion within the Five Vehicles, which has two parts. First, the explanation of the meaning of the Five Vehicles, which further has two parts. First, the general explanation.

[Commentary]: Regarding the "five vehicles" (*pañca-yāna*): a "vehicle" is so named because it functions as a means of transport. The five refer to humans, devas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas;
these five possess varying degrees of power, and their transportations vary in distance.

[Commentary] Regarding the five vehicles: the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states that they are called "humans" (*pudgala*) because of their extensive deliberation; the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states that they are called "humans" because their mental faculties are tranquil;
and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that those with luminous purity and sovereign spiritual efficacy are called "devas. As for "Śrāvaka" (Voice-hearer):

"voice" refers to the sounds of the Buddha’s teachings, and "hearing" refers to the arising of consciousness through the faculty of the ear to listen to and receive the Buddha’s voice; thus, they are named Śrāvakas. Regarding "Pratyekabuddha" (Solitary Realizer)... [text continues]

An *abhisambuddha* (Awakened One) is so named because they have awakened to and fully understood the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) through wisdom; thus they are called a *Pratyekabuddha* (Solitary Realizer).

They are also called a *Viviktacārī* (Solitary One) because, having attained the body of an Arya, they realize the state of *aśaikṣa* (one beyond training) through their own self-realization, independent of receiving the ultimate teachings from others.

A *Bodhisattva*—the full term being *Bodhisattva*—is composed of two parts: *bodhi*, meaning awakening, and *sattva*, meaning a sentient being. Their practice, in brief, is as follows: [text continues].
There are two gates: first, self-benefit, which takes great wisdom as its priority; second, benefiting others, which takes great compassion as its primary focus.

Because one seeks supreme enlightenment through these two benefits and delivers sentient beings (*sattva*) below, one is called a *bodhisattva*. Furthermore, *sattva* refers to the practitioner’s own person;
since this practitioner seeks great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), they are called a *bodhisattva*. As for "vehicle" (*yāna*), it means that which carries and transports.

The meaning of this [term "vehicle"] encompasses the essence of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit. That is to say: one understands the principle by relying on the teaching; one initiates practice by relying on the principle; and one attains the fruit by relying on practice.

In this process, practice and fruit constitute the primary movement, while teaching and principle assist that movement. All four are called "vehicles" (*yāna*). Among these, the vehicle of humans and devas is called the "human-deva vehicle.
Because the two destinies of humans and devas both consist of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) and share identical faculties and seeds, they are combined as one.

First: up to and including the Bodhisattva Vehicle, which is called the Bodhisattvayāna. In scriptures such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, these four vehicles are followed by the teaching of the indeterminate-nature vehicle (*aniyata-gotra-yāna*).
This refers to a certain class of practitioners who possess the potential for both [the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha] vehicles, or the three vehicles;
they may generate the aspiration [for awakening] earlier or later and practice the three vehicles through both sudden and gradual approaches, as explained in the commentary.
The opening and closing [of the sections] differ, yet they are not contradictory. △ Second, the detailed explanation of the five [vehicles]. First, the Human Vehicle.
【Commentary】 The Human Vehicle refers to the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts. It carries sentient beings across the three miserable realms (trāya) and brings them to birth in the human path.
It is like a small boat that has just barely crossed a mountain stream.
△ Second, the Vehicle of the Gods (devayāna).
[Commentary]: The second, the Vehicle of the Gods, refers to the superior grade of the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) as well as the four dhyānas and eight samādhis.
It carries sentient beings beyond the four continents and reaches the higher realms, just as a small boat crosses over small rivers and streams.
[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the human realm, one cultivates the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*). Inferior-grade ten wholesome actions lead to birth in the human realm.

Middle-grade ten wholesome actions, which are not necessarily associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), lead to birth among the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Superior-grade ten wholesome actions, when associated with the four dhyānas, lead to birth among the gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
when associated with the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), they lead to birth among the gods of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). [The four dhyānas...]

The four emptinesses together constitute the eight meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). Because their conceptual categories differ, they are presented as both sets of four and eight. △ Third, the Śrāvakas; fourth, the Pratyekabuddhas.
These two sections are combined into one. First, the names are listed and the dharmas indicated.
[Commentary] 3. The Śrāvaka Vehicle refers to the Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths. 4. The Pratyekabuddha Vehicle refers to the Dharma-gate of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
△ Second, the simultaneous manifestation of their characteristics.

[Commentary]: All are able to transport sentient beings across the three realms, reaching the *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder) and *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder) nirvāṇas, and becoming *arhats* as well as *pratyekabuddhas*.
They are all like great ships that cross over vast rivers and streams.
[Commentary] *Arhat*. This is translated as "Worthy" (*ying*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "Because they have already eternally destroyed the thieves of affliction;
because they will no longer undergo the body of segmented birth (*paricchinna-deha*); and because they are worthy of receiving the sublime offerings of the world.
The Sanskrit term is *Pratyekabuddha*; *Pratyeka* is an abbreviation for *Pratyekabuddha*. This is translated as "Solitary Realizer" (*Dujue*), also known as "Conditioned Realizer" (*Yuanjue*). △
The Five Bodhisattvas.
[Commentary] The five bodhisattva vehicles refer to the dharma-gates of compassion, wisdom, and the six pāramitās.

They transport sentient beings, enabling them to transcend altogether the realms of the three worlds and the three vehicles, reaching the further shore of unsurpassed bodhi and great parinirvāṇa, just as one would by means of a vehicle.
The ship has crossed the sea.
△ Second, the inclusion of this sutra.
[Commentary]: This present sutra is comprised within the vehicle of humans and devas; it belongs among the Śrāvaka Piṭaka.

[Commentary]: Maudgalyāyana’s mother merely spoke of being freed from suffering; she did not mention her place of rebirth. Her parents for seven generations were freed from the suffering of hungry ghosts and were reborn among humans and devas.

Therefore, this sutra is subsumed under the vehicle of humans and devas. Now, examining the Dharma, it is neither exclusively Mahāyāna nor Hīnayāna, but is determined according to the capacities of those who encounter it.
Depending on the specific capacity addressed, there is that which is auxiliary and that which is primary; thus, it is judged to enter the five vehicles based on what is primary.
It is not based on both [vehicles]. The Buddha preached this sutra for the sake of Maudgalyāyana, yet it also transforms others;

those with the disposition of the Śrāvaka vehicle are precisely the primary audience. It does not apply to Pratyekabuddhas, as there is no such assembly in the sutra. Among the five vehicles, it is subsumed under the Śrāvaka vehicle;
within the Great and Small Vehicles, it is subsumed under the Small Vehicle and is not the Bodhisattva vehicle. The emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is not explicitly revealed in this sutra.
This is because of its underlying meaning. However, the subsequent text states that when the Buddha preached this sutra, the assembly of great bodhisattvas all rejoiced;
this was because they heard the signs of the benefits of the *Ullambana* [Bowl] offering, which assists and praises those of lesser capacity, and thus gave rise to joy.
△ Third, the determination of the fundamental tenet, in two parts. First, the heading of the chapter.
[Commentary] Third, the determination of the fundamental tenet.

△ Second, the explicit revelation of the fundamental tenet, which has two parts. First, clarifying the fundamental tenet, which further has two parts. First, the explicit clarification of the fundamental tenet.
[Commentary] This sutra takes filial piety, the offering of alms, the eradication of suffering, and the repayment of kindness as its central theme.

[Sub-commentary] Regarding the "central theme" (zongzhì): the *Fayuan* states that "theme" (zōng) refers to the principle of veneration and honor, while "purport" (zhì) refers to the intent and underlying purpose.
This sutra takes filial piety and the extraction of suffering as its central theme (*zong*). A theme is precisely the essential purport (*zhi*).

Filial piety and the extraction of suffering constitute the ultimate intent that this sutra venerates, honors, and prioritizes. It also encompasses the requital of kindness and the offering of assemblies;

it is only through filial piety that one can establish these assemblies to requite kindness and extract suffering. Therefore, filial piety and the extraction of suffering are established as the central theme.
This is the essential meaning. △ Second, establishing the explanation through its meaning, which has two parts.
First, listing the two gates. [Commentary]: Now, they are distinguished by means of two gates: first, explaining the characteristics of the practice; second, correlating the number of phrases.

△ Second, the explanation according to the enumeration has two parts. First, the explanation of the characteristics of the first four meanings has two sub-sections. First, the formal explanation. [Commentary]:
"First" refers to Maudgalyāyana, who originally practiced with filial sincerity because his own strength was insufficient to repay the kindness of his parents;

therefore, he first entered the monastic life. Thus, as soon as he attained the six supernatural powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), he surveyed the three realms (*tridhātu*) and beheld his deceased mother reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).

Among the ghosts (those who have attained the Way are not necessarily all [reborn as] parents—as evidenced by the case of Maudgalyāyana, who left the home life precisely to repay their kindness)—though they were offered fragrant rice, it instantly turned into fierce flames.

Wailing in grief, he sought refuge with the Buddha; the Buddha then instructed him to establish a vessel-offering (*pén-gòng*) to rescue them from their bodies in the dark paths and liberate them from the suffering of one *kalpa*.
Thus, he did not fail his parents in nurturing them, but greatly repaid their labors.
[Commentary] Maudgalyāyana arrives at Kula. The first eight lines, the next four lines, the next two lines, and the final two lines explain the four meanings respectively. △ Second, the conclusion.
[Commentary] Examine the purport of the sūtra in detail; it is fully endowed with these four meanings.
△ Second, the correlation with the four sets of four phrases. 1. First, the general heading indicating the number.
[Commentary] Regarding the second, the correlation of the number of phrases: there are four sets of four phrases.
△ Second, the detailed exposition according to the headings has four parts. First, the four propositions regarding "filial piety" (xiao) and "obedience" (shun).

[Commentary]: Regarding the two characters "filial piety," there are four propositions of their own. First: filial but not obedient. This refers, for example, to the nourishment provided by the three sacrificial animals and the like.

[Commentary] The *Classic of Filial Piety* states: "One who serves their parents, when in a position of authority, does not act with arrogance; when in a subordinate position, does not act in disorder;

and when among the masses, does not engage in strife (‘masses’ refers to the multitude; ‘strife’ refers to competition). To be arrogant while in authority leads to ruin; to be disorderly while in subordination leads to punishment; to engage in strife among the masses leads to war.
If these three failings are not eliminated, then even if one daily provides the three sacrificial animals (ox, sheep, and pig) for nourishment, it is still considered unfilial."

[Commentary]: Second, there are cases where one complies with [the parent's wishes] but this is not filial piety. For example, if a parent who is ill requests food that is forbidden by medical precepts and one immediately provides it;
or if they wish to engage in improper conduct and one fails to offer counsel against it, and so forth.
[Commentary] The *Classic of Filial Piety* states: "When a father has a son who remonstrates with him, his person shall not fall into unrighteousness.

Therefore, when confronted with unrighteousness, a son must not fail to remonstrate with his father" (the character for "remonstrate," *zhēng*, is pronounced in the departing tone; it is a term for the most earnest admonition. When parents have faults, the son ought to offer the most earnest admonition).

[Commentary: The third [type] is both filial and compliant. This means that while there may be things concealed, there is no transgression; one follows [the parent's will] after three admonitions, observes their countenance to discern their intent, and does not alter anything for three years.
[Commentary]: When there is a fault, one conceals it and does not let it be heard outside. Without offending their countenance, one offers gentle words of admonition.

One follows and complies with their expression to observe their will and integrity. The *Liji*, "Tangong," says: "In serving one's parents, there is concealment but no offense" (*yǐn* means not proclaiming their faults;

*wúfàn* means not admonishing them by offending their countenance). "Attending to them on the left and right for their nourishment is without fixed method" ("left and right" refers to the constant manner of supporting them). [The son...]

Toward one's parents, one serves them with diligence until death and observes the three-year mourning period. (Diligence refers to laborious and humble tasks; "reaching" [the period] means that the expression of grief accords with the prescribed dress.

This is regulated by affection. In serving the ruler, one may commit offenses but must not conceal anything. Once one has offered remonstrance, if someone asks about the state's administration, one may speak of its merits and defects.

Those who attend to the ruler’s needs have their proper methods; they must not encroach upon the duties of others. They serve with diligence until death and observe the three-year mourning period for the deceased. (The mourning for the deceased is modeled after the service rendered to the father. All of these are based on righteousness.)

To establish the rule: serving one's teacher involves no transgression and no concealment. One attends to his needs on all sides with no fixed method, serving him diligently until death and observing a period of mourning for three years in spirit (*xinsāng*).

[This "mourning in spirit" means assuming a mournful countenance as if for a father, yet without wearing the ritual garments; this rule is established based on the intersection of affection and righteousness. The *Qūlǐ* states: "In the way a son serves his parents..."
If, after three admonitions, they do not listen, one should follow them while weeping aloud. The *Analects* states: "Zi Xia asked about filial piety. The Master said:

'It is difficult to maintain the proper countenance. (This means that it is indeed difficult to comply with and follow the expressions on one's parents' faces. It further says: 'While the father is alive, observe his intentions; when the father has passed away, observe his conduct.
If for three years there is no alteration of the father’s way, one may be called filial.'"
[Commentary] Fourth, those who are neither filial nor obedient. This includes cases such as burying one’s father in a body of water.
[Sub-commentary] According to a worldly tradition, Kunzi resented his father for not holding office; he subsequently buried his father in the Kunming Lake. Further textual verification is required.
△ Second, the four lines concerning the offering of provisions by the filial and obedient.
[Commentary]: Second, regarding the correlation between filial piety and the offering of sustenance, there are again four propositions. First:
filial piety without the offering of sustenance, such as that of Dong An and Wang Xiang.
[Commentary] The *Hanshu* states: Dong An, courtesy name Xiaozhi, was a native of Gouchang in Kuaiji. He lost his father at a young age and served his mother with the utmost filial piety.
Although his family was impoverished, his mother was always plump and cheerful. Wang Ji, a neighbor whose family was wealthy, had a mother who was thin;
Ji’s mother said to An’s mother, "Your family is poor and you are advanced in years. What offerings do you have that you remain so plump and cheerful?"
The mother of An said, "My son is filial and obedient; he does nothing unlawful. Because his heart is free from sorrow, he is plump and well-nourished.

She asked the foster mother, "Your family is wealthy with an abundance of fine delicacies; why do you say he is emaciated? The foster mother replied, "My son is unfilial and constantly commits unlawful acts.
This causes me constant grief and anxiety, and for this reason he is thin. When Ji heard this, he waited for an opportunity...
An was not present. [The assailant] then seized An’s mother by the hand, striking her with his fist and kicking her with his feet; he departed after inflicting this bitter humiliation upon her.
When An returned and saw that his mother was displeased, he questioned her. His mother recounted the incident in detail. An said, "This old woman spoke too much and could not restrain herself.

I feared my mother would be grieved, so I remained silent and did not speak. After his mother passed away and her burial was completed, An cut off the head of the man who had harbored the grudge and offered it as a sacrifice at his mother’s tomb, then bound himself.

He went to the local authorities; encountering a general amnesty, he was spared. He was a man of the Later Han period. The *Biographies of Filial Virtue* (*Xiaode zhuan*) states that Dong An later served as a Court Gentleman (*zhonglang*).
The *History of Wei* (*Weizhi*) states that Wang Xiang, whose courtesy name was Xiuzheng, was a native of Langya. The rest is as commonly recounted.
[Commentary] Second, making offerings that are not filial: performing rites such as fasting for the sake of seeking merit for oneself. Third, both [filial and meritorious]:
namely, the Ullambana Assembly. Fourth, neither: meaning to act perversely and be stingy.
△ Three: Filial Piety and Obedience versus Eradicating Suffering, in Four Propositions.

[Commentary]: The third section contrasts filial piety and obedience with the eradication of suffering, also forming four propositions. First: filial piety and obedience that do not constitute the eradication of suffering;
this refers to cases such as those of Dong Yong and others.
[Commentary] The *Hanshu* states: Dong Yong was a native of Yucheng County in Qingzhou. He lost his mother at a young age and raised his father alone.
After his father passed away, he lacked the means to provide for the burial. He borrowed ten thousand coins from another person, telling the lender:
"If I am unable to repay the money, I will offer myself as a slave. Once Yong had completed the burial of his father, he set out to become a slave. On the road, he encountered a...
The woman sought to become his wife forever. Yong said, "I am currently poor and lowly; I ought to be a slave myself. How could I dare to humble you by making you my wife?
The woman replied, "I feel no shame in poverty or low status. Yong then went with her to the home of the money-lender.
The master asked, "What is your wife capable of? The wife replied, "She weaves. The master said, "Weave a thousand bolts of silk for me, and I shall release you and your husband.
Thereupon she began to weave; after ten months, she had completed the thousand bolts. The master was greatly pleased and released them.
As they were walking back to the place where they had first met, the wife said, "I am a Weaver Girl from Heaven. Seeing your supreme filial piety, the heavenly deities sent me to assist you."
"Then you shall repay your debt. Having finished speaking, he flew into the air and departed. He was a person from the Former Han period.
[Commentary] Second, relieving suffering that is not filial piety: this refers to rescuing others from their suffering. Third, both are [filial]: this refers to the *Lanpen* (Ullambana) Assembly.
Fourth, neither is [filial]: this refers to those who commit minor transgressions.
△ Four Verses on Filial Piety and Repaying Kindness.
[Commentary]: The fourth section pairs filial piety with repaying kindness, also forming four propositions. First: filial piety that is not repaying kindness.
This includes such acts as protecting one’s hair and skin, avoiding arrogance and peril, and refraining from speaking what is contrary to the Dharma.

[Commentary] The *Classic of Filial Piety* states: "I do not dare to speak words that are not the laws of the former kings; I do not dare to perform deeds that are not the virtues of the former kings.
[Sub-commentary] Second, acts of gratitude that are not filial piety: such as supporting a wheel to repay a single meal, or practicing cultivation to repay a donor, and so forth. Third.
Both are [correct]. This is the Ullambana Assembly. Four are neither; these refer to those who betray their benefactors and rebel against them.
[Commentary] Regarding "supporting the wheels": the *Leilin* says that Ling Che was a man of Qi. When Zhao Dun, a high official of Jin, went out on a journey...

Beneath a mulberry tree, he saw a starving man. He poured out his pitcher to feed him. The man asked, "Who are you? The starving man replied, "I am a man of Qi; my surname is Ling and my given name is Que.

Zhongshen subsequently provided food for him. Later, when Zhongshen served Duke Ling as a gatekeeper, he offered forthright remonstrance to the Duke.
The Duke wished to kill him, so Zhongshen rose up; he called for the mastiff, which bit Zhongshen. Zhongshen fled and climbed onto a carriage, but one wheel had already fallen off.

II. The Dharma Taught has two parts. First, the explanation of the three characters that represent the expressed meaning (the *vācya*), which further divides into two. First, the individual clarification of the three [characters].
[Commentary]:
*Ullambana* is a term from the Western Regions; here it means "hanging upside down. *Ben* (basin) is a word from the Eastern Land (China), referring to a vessel used for rescue.
Following local custom, it should be called the "Rescue Basin for the Upside-Down Hanging."
[Commentary]: "Bōn" (盆) is a term from the Eastern Xia (China). As the translators of the Great Song dynasty now say, it was formerly called *pātra* (盆佐那), abbreviated as "bōn.
The new [translation] calls it *māṇava* (門佐羅) or *maṇava* (門佐曩); in the language of the Flower [Land], it means "a vessel for salvation."
This has already been explained above. If one says that *kaṇṭaka* translates as "basin," this is not the original intent of the sutra.

[Commentary]: This is because the soul of the Venerable One’s relative has sunk into the dark path; burdened by hunger and thirst, his life is like being suspended upside down.
Even with the majestic spiritual power of the Holy Son, there would be no way to rescue them from their state of being mired in mud and engulfed in fire.

[Commentary] Although the term "dark paths" (*āndha-mārga*) generally refers to the three miserable realms (*tri-durgati*), here it specifically clarifies the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*). The characters *zài* (則) and *qiě* (且) are both particles used for emphasis or conjunction.
As for "mud and fire" (*tú-tàn*), this refers to the perilous suffering of the hungry ghost realm, which is like being trapped in mud or falling into fire, without any means of salvation.
[Commentary]:

The Buddha commanded that a hundred flavors be prepared in basins as an offering to the Triple Gem. By looking up to the grace and radiance of the Great Assembly, he sought to rescue those in the dire urgency of being "suspended upside down.
It is from this meaning that the title of the sutra is established.
△ Second, the explanation of the word "sūtra" (*sūtra*) which expresses [the meaning]. This has two parts. First, the word-by-word explanation of the text.

[Commentary]: Regarding "sūtra": it primarily clarifies that it serves as a thread. The meaning is called "Kie-king" (*Sūtra*). A thread can string together flowers; a sūtra can hold the warp threads.
That which is expressed—the meaning—is like the warp and like the flowers; that which can sustain it—the text—can sustain and can string them together.
Now, following the conventions of the classical scriptures of this region, it is designated as "jīng" (sūtra). Borrowing the meaning to assist the name, the character "qiè" (seal) is further added.

[Commentary] Regarding the term *sūtra*: The *Fayuan* (Garden of the Dharma) states that in the Western Regions, the terms for "thread," "sewing-line," "weaving-thread for mats," and "holy teaching" are all called *sūtra* (Sanskrit:

*sūtrānta*). This term carries six meanings. Within the scriptural collections (*piṭaka*), it subsumes three: namely, thread, weaving-thread, and holy teaching. As for "holy teaching," this refers to the Vinaya and the Śāstras;
because they represent a portion of the meaning contained within the *sūtras*, they are all termed *sūtra*. [This was stated by] Vasubandhu and Maitreya...

The fourfold interpretation of "grace" (*en*) has already been recorded above. Regarding the two meanings in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* and the five meanings in the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, because these contain many such meanings, it is simply called a "sūtra" (*jing*) and not a "thread" (*xian*) or the like.
Your commentary discards the general application to sūtras while adopting the restricted sense of a "thread," which is a grave error that contradicts the treatises you yourself cited.

Within the initial introductory section, most sūtras possess two types of prefaces. The first is the "Preface of Certification of Faith," which states: "Thus have I heard this Dharma from the Buddha.
This clearly records the time and place of the teaching, establishing that the great assembly heard it together and that there is no error.

For this reason, a testimony of faith must necessarily appear at the beginning of a sutra. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The time, place, and persons are mentioned in order to engender faith."

[Commentary] When the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* was being preached, five hundred elders, including Ratnākara, each offered a parasol. After the Buddha had accepted them, he merged them into a single parasol.
Briefly stated, there are four meanings for this: first, by the Buddha’s supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), many were merged into one.

First, it is because he wishes to cause the donor to give rise to inconceivable thoughts. Second, by manifesting lands through the convergence of two [factors], he inspires in the donor the supreme resolve to cultivate the practice of purifying buddha-lands.
Third, it is to clarify that all phenomena lack fixed nature: many may become one, and many are not necessarily many;
one may become many, and one is not necessarily one. To those who awaken to the true mark (*dharmatā*), there has never been "one" or "many."

The four representatives of the elders are so called because they are currently awakening together to non-arising and will together attain Buddhahood in the future, as explained extensively in that commentary (*shu*).
When the Buddha preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he emitted light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows. Regarding "eyebrows" (*mei*), the commentary states:
The beauty of its countenance represents the superior charm of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) doctrine. "Between" refers to the two middles; it signifies that the teaching expounds the Middle Way.
White is the source of all colors, signifying that this Dharma is the origin of the Three Vehicles. It emits light to shatter the darkness.

[Commentary] The sub-commentary states: This refers to the words spoken by the Buddha when he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, at which time Ānanda requested instruction on four matters, and the Buddha commanded that these words be set aside.
[Sub-commentary] The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (or *Dacheng jing*) says: After the Buddha had accepted the invitation of Pāpīyas and was about to enter nirvāṇa, Ānanda wept with a choked voice.

that is, he was to ask about four matters (and so forth). △ Second, the specific narration of the four matters.

[Commentary]: Regarding the four matters asked, the Buddha answered each one individually: first, relying upon the four foundations of mindfulness (namely, contemplating the body as impure, contemplating feelings as suffering, contemplating the mind as impermanent, and contemplating phenomena as non-self);
second, taking the precepts as one's teacher; third, silencing and banishing monks of malicious character.
[Commentary] Regarding "taking the precepts as one's teacher": a teacher is defined as an instructor, craftsman, or model. There are two kinds of teachers: persons and the Dharma.
While the Tathāgata was in the world, the Buddha was the teacher; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Dharma is the teacher.
This is because rules and models depend upon the dharma of the precepts. Therefore, the Prātimokṣa precepts are your teachers. [This concerns] the evil-natured bhikṣu and the Brahma-pariṣad.
To "treat" means to purify; "brahman" (梵) means purity, and "maṇḍala" (壇) means the Dharma. One treats them through silent exclusion by means of the pure Dharma, performing a single *karmavācanā*.
Because the seven assemblies of disciples are not permitted to converse with them, it is said that they are treated through the "Brahman-maṇḍala."

[Commentary]: Fourth, at the beginning of all sutras, it is invariably stated: "Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was at a certain place, together with a certain assembly of such-and-such number of people."

[Commentary: Most sūtras possess six kinds of accomplishments. Although the text may be abbreviated or incomplete, the meaning must necessarily be complete.
These are: first, faith; second, hearing; third, time; fourth, the teacher; fifth, the location; and sixth, the assembly. If these six conditions are not complete, the teaching will not arise.
It must possess six [factors]; therefore, it is said to be "accomplished" (*siddha*).

[The *Chao*] states that according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, there are generally five: first, "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) constitutes the accomplishment of faith, as it generally manifests what has been heard to inspire confidence;
second, the phrase "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) constitutes the accomplishment of time; third, the Buddha...
1. The Teacher’s accomplishment. 2. The place of residence, such as Śrāvastī, is the accomplishment of the location. 3.
Being together with a certain number of people from a particular assembly is the accomplishment of the retinue. This is the fifth [element] in brief; in full, it should be stated:
"The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with Mahāmaudgalyāyana and the fourfold assembly of disciples."

[The preceding] is similar. However, the current commentator (Sūtra-master), relying on the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra*, establishes six types of proof; thus he says, "In this way," which refers to the accomplishment of faith (*śraddhā-sampatti*).

Since the text is concise and the meaning is obscure, the specific characteristics (*ākāra*) are difficult to discern. To what teaching should one point out [the correspondence] so that faith may arise?
Since the systems followed differ, one may instead follow the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*. 2. Pointing out the omissions in this sūtra.

△ Second, explaining the reason for this in three parts. First, the four characters "other sūtras" (*anyeṣu sūtreṣu*) are inverted.
[Commentary]: That is to say, some say, "I have heard such a Dharma from the Buddha," while others say, "I have heard such a Dharma from the presence of the Buddha.
Both are terms used to point to the Dharma.
[Commentary]: Some say, "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*); others say, "I heard thus. The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"One should know that the statement 'thus have I heard' is intended to avoid the faults of addition, subtraction, and deviation.

That is to say, by stating 'I have heard this Dharma from the Buddha,' one remains free from all faults of addition, subtraction, and deviation," and so on, until it says: "Therefore, the listener should..."
Having heard this correctly, one should contemplate it according to principle and diligently practice it.

The Tripiṭaka Master Zhen Di, relying on the *Vinaya-sūkṣma*, clarifies that when Ānanda ascended the seat to compile the Dharma-piṭaka, his body was like that of the true Buddha, endowed with all the marks and signs;

when he descended from the seat, he returned to his original form. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-saṃgraha* also states that sentient beings have three doubts, the first of which is doubt regarding the Buddha.

The Great Compassionate One arises from nirvāṇa to further proclaim the sublime Dharma. There are two doubts: first, that another Buddha has come from another direction to dwell here and preach the Dharma;
second, that Ānanda has transformed his body to become a Buddha and is preaching the Dharma for the assembly.
To eliminate these doubts, he points to this Dharma, saying, "Thus have I heard," because he previously attended upon the Buddha and personally heard it.
△ 2. This sutra does not mention "self. [Commentary]:
It does not mention "self" because it intends to demonstrate that all sages have realized the principle of non-self (*anātman*).
△ 3. The intention behind other sutras mentioning "self."
[Commentary]: As for those instances found in other sutras, they refer to Ānanda himself pointing to the provisional entity of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*);
this is not the same as the "self" (*ātman*) postulated by ordinary people, and thus there is no fault.

△ Second, the correct interpretation according to the text, in five parts. First, the interpretation of "Thus have I heard" (evam mayā śrutam), which has two sub-sections. First, the interpretation of the character "heard" (śruta).
[Commentary]: "Heard" refers to the auditory faculty (*śrotrendriya*) giving rise to consciousness (*vijñāna*) to listen to external sounds.
[Commentary] The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Hearing" refers to the ear-faculty giving rise to consciousness.

When one listens to and receives the sounds of the Buddha’s teachings, if it were merely the hearing of sound, it would reside solely in the ear; however, if one takes names and phrases as objects, it occurs within the mind.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* also states: "Hearing" refers to inference (*anumāna*). Setting aside the distinction between the ear and the mind, it is collectively termed "hearing. △ Second, the explanation of "thus" (*evam*).

[Commentary: The subsequent phrase, "Thus it is," refers to the fulfillment of faith. Generally speaking, one who has faith says, "This matter is thus," while one who lacks faith says, "This matter is not thus.
Therefore, Master Zhao said: "Faith is a term for accordant compliance."

[Commentary] The *Fahua shu* states: "In this way" refers to the inception of resonance and response (*ganying*). "In this way" (*ru shi*) receives its name because it accords with the capacities [of beings].

Thus, there is nothing that does not establish a designation. Sentient beings take "nothing that is not [in accord]" as their resonance; the Tathāgata takes "accordance with capacities" as his response.
The Sage who transmits the Dharma, wishing to demonstrate that the named teachings arise from the principle of resonance and response (*ganying*), therefore speaks as follows.

II. Manifesting the meaning of "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*). This has two parts. First, the direct explanation of "at one time," which further has two parts. The first part consists of the direct explanation through two meanings.

[Commentary] "At one time" (*ekasmin samaye*): This refers to the total designation for the completion of the teaching and listening when teacher and disciple are assembled together; it serves to distinguish this from other times.
[Sub-commentary] Regarding "at one time," the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* explains it through two meanings: first, the moment (*kṣaṇa*) of both the speaker and the listener.
The continuity [of the discourse] is completed through both speaking and listening. When the affairs of the Dharma assembly have concluded, it is collectively termed "one time.

Second, because the speaker and the listener meet together, with neither preceding nor following the other, speaking and listening occur simultaneously; therefore, it is called "one time. According to the *Pèishū*, it should be stated:
"When speaking and listening are completed, it is collectively termed 'one time. The harmonious gathering of teacher and disciple is what is meant by 'one time. (Part Two)
This is established through an explanation based on meaning.

[Commentary: This means that when the Tathāgata preached the sūtras, there were immeasurable occasions; they cannot be cited individually, and thus a single word suffices to encompass them all, which is why it simply says "once" (*eka*).
Furthermore, because the duration of time varies across different regions—being either extended or brief—it is collectively referred to as "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*).
[Commentary] This refers to what the *Śāstra* says: "The time—spring, autumn, and so forth—is immeasurable. If each specific instance were cited individually, it would become overly complex;
yet if one were to fix it to a single specific time, it could not universally respond to the capacities of ordinary and noble beings across all directions, whether sharp or dull.
Because the intent is to respond universally to all capacities, it is stated simply as "at one time" (*eka-samaya*), which signifies the simultaneous occurrence of both teaching and listening.

When an activity is completed, it is called "one time" (*ekakāla*). This term inherently contains meanings such as long and short durations. For those of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*), the duration is short because their realization and understanding are swift.

For those of dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*), the duration is long because their realization and understanding are slow. If one were to cite periods such as years or months, it would not apply to those of sharp faculties;
if one were to cite moments such as *muhūrta*, it would not apply to those of dull faculties. If one were to cite the four seasons or the twelve periods of the day, [it would not apply to either].
Because it accords with the capacities of the devas of the four continents, it is for this reason that it is stated simply as "at one time.

Regarding the phrase "in all directions" and below, this explains and establishes the meaning of the aforementioned "immeasurable time. The intent is to state that the temporal divisions in the various directions of the four continents are not fixed;

that is, the duration for ordinary beings and sages, and for those of sharp or dull faculties, is indeterminate. △ Second, resolving the examples by addressing objections. Part one: citing the previous example to raise an objection.
[Commentary] However, among the various sūtras, some do not specify the time, while others specify the location.
△ Second, the interpretation of the meaning of the text has two parts. First, pointing to the explanation of Cien (Ci'en).
[Commentary] Some interpretations are not adopted because they invite difficulties.

[Sub-commentary] There are interpretations that invite difficulties. As the *Xuanzan shu* states: Question: Regarding the place, there are distinctions between pure and impure; the place is definitively explained according to the capacities of beings.
