[Commentary]: The outline of the commentary has two parts. First, the direct explanation of this passage, which is divided into two sections. First, the general explanation of the meaning of the sutra, which is further divided into three parts.
The first [section] concerns the determination of the fruits of karma, which is further divided into two parts. The first provides a general explanation of cause and effect.

[Commentary: It is stated that objects transform according to the mind, and fruits are accomplished through karma. If the causes of hunger have not been eliminated, how can the conditions for satiety be brought about?
△ Second, the explanation by means of dharma and analogy.
[Commentary]: The hungry ghost has a mouth of flames; when food approaches the mouth, it blazes up. Water becomes hard ice; when ice approaches hot water, it solidifies.
△ Second, the minor sages are difficult to move.
[Commentary]: This shows that supernatural power cannot restrain the force of karma. To eliminate hunger, one must first eliminate stinginess;
thus, although the six supernormal powers were used to bring food, it brought disaster, and although a basin of a hundred flavors was provided, it resulted in suffering.

[Commentary] "Jin" (prohibit/restrain) is pronounced in the level tone. "Pen" (basin) refers to a vessel. A hundred flavors of food and drink were arrayed within the vessels to be offered to his mother;
as the food turned into fire, it is said that he brought her suffering. △ Third, the expression of alarm and admiration, exhorting reflection.
[Commentary]: How great is the ripening of karma! This is truly something worth reflecting upon.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the scriptural text. [Commentary]:
Now, with his left hand he shields the bowl, fearing that others might encroach upon it; with his right hand he pats the food, craving only for his own sustenance. This is stinginess.
Their greed was so fierce that it manifested in this way; how could they be sustained by inferior food? Therefore, it transformed into fire, and they were unable to eat.
△ Second, the conclusion returning to the introductory section.

[Commentary: The preceding section on the introduction is concluded. From here below is the second part, the main body of the teaching (*samyak-siddhānta-bhāga*). This text is divided into two sections:
first, Maudgalyāyana sorrowfully recounts the sufferings and calamities; second, the Tathāgata extensively reveals the causes and conditions.

[Commentary] Now, examining the three divisions in detail: first, the Introductory Division (*nidāna*). This section sets forth the origins and causes for the initial emergence of the discourse on the sutra;

as it serves as the gradual beginning of the Main Body (*samyukta*), it is called the Introductory Division. Second, from this point downward until the "Grace of Compassionate Love," constitutes the Main Body Division.
This is precisely the World-Honored One’s preaching of the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of his audience, adapting it to lead them toward cultivation, study, and progress.
The essential purport: because it establishes the principle of that which is revered and honored as supreme, it is called the "Section on the True Teaching" (Zhengzongfen).

The final five phrases at the end of the third [section] constitute the "Section on Circulation" (Liutongfen). Having finished explaining the benefits, the teaching is entrusted to the appropriate time and place, and the great assembly is charged with its protection and maintenance so that it may circulate without falling into decline;
thus it is named the Section on Circulation. The Section on the True Teaching has two parts. First, a specific demonstration of Maudgalyāyana’s expedient means for rescuing his mother.

Later, there is a general demonstration to the great assembly of the essential gate for supporting one's parents; this refers to the text of the final sequence. The initial section is divided into two parts:
first, Maudgalyāyana sorrowfully describes their suffering and distress; second, the Tathāgata extensively demonstrates the causes and conditions.
[Commentary] First:
Maudgalyāyana cried out in great lamentation, weeping with tears as he rushed back to inform the Buddha, recounting everything exactly as it had occurred.
[Sub-commentary] The commentary divides this section into three parts; first is the intent behind his report to the Buddha.

[Commentary] The author states: When a son is in urgent distress, he tells his father; when a minister is in urgent distress, he tells his sovereign. Since one’s own strength is insufficient, it is only right to take refuge in the Buddha.
△ Second, an account of what has been attained by oneself.

[Commentary: The disciple has diligently contemplated the Four Noble Truths and already realized the Threefold Knowledge (*trividyā*). He is capable of overturning mountains and rivers, and turning back the sun and moon. [Sub-commentary:

As for the "Threefold Knowledge": it consists of the realization of the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā-vidyā*), the realization of the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapāda-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā-vidyā*), and the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā-vidyā*).

These are three of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). They are established as the "three types of clear knowledge" (*tisro vidyāḥ*) in order to destroy ignorance regarding the three time periods.
As they are able to know the objects of the three periods—past, future, and present—clearly, directly, and without error, their wisdom is itself the realization;
thus they are called "wisdom-realization. In relation to the objects of the three periods, this should be understood as a *tatpuruṣa* compound. △ Third, the actual extension [of the teaching].
[The child] was filled with grief and supplication. [Commentary: Who would have thought that his mother was entangled in such extreme suffering, her life as precarious as being hung upside down?

He exhausted his filial sincerity and displayed every spiritual transformation, yet in the end he could not cause her evil retribution to be removed, nor provide even a moment’s relief for her starving belly. Therefore, he cried out in lamentation and rushed back home, fully...
I offer this earnest plea for compassion. [Commentary]:
Hereafter, the Tathāgata extensively demonstrates the causes and conditions. For now, based on the Tripiṭaka, the text is divided into eight major sections.

First, it reveals the profound gravity of the mother’s transgression; second, it clarifies the inferiority of the son’s virtue; third, it censures the powerlessness of heterodox paths; fourth, it manifests the correctness [of the orthodox].
The fifth [section] has the capacity to provide a means of rescue; the sixth demonstrates the True Dharma; the seventh shows the filial son attaining realization;
and the eighth shows the compassionate mother obtaining benefit.
[Commentary] The commentary is divided into eight sections; here they are condensed into two. The first six show the Tathāgata extensively demonstrating the methods for saving his mother.
The latter two show the signs of joy and benefit experienced by the assembly upon hearing [the teaching]. Students should follow the text and explain it by highlighting its essential points.
[Commentary] First:
The Buddha said, "The roots of your mother's transgressions are deeply entrenched.
[Sub-commentary] The commentary divides this into two sections; the first is a general explanation based on the scripture.
[Commentary] The sub-commentary states: A sutra says that during the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, Maudgalyāyana was named Rabu, and his mother’s name was Qingti.
When Rabu was about to depart on a journey, he instructed his mother, saying, "If any guests should arrive, you must prepare a meal.
After he had left, guests did arrive, yet the mother failed to provide for them; instead, she falsely feigned the preparation of a banquet. When her son returned, he asked: "Yesterday..."
When a guest arrived, [the son] asked, "How shall we prepare for him? His mother said, "Have you not seen the place where food is set out?
From that time until now, through five hundred lifetimes, your stinginess has continued in succession; therefore it is said that the roots of your transgressions are deeply entangled."

[Commentary] The *Shangsheng shu* (Commentary on the Birth Above) states: "The Buddha Dīpaṃkara is none other than the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. △ Second, the explanation of the meaning of this own sūtra has two parts.
First, the sequential explanation of the sūtra text, which further has two parts. First, the direct explanation of the scriptural text.
[Commentary]: "Sin" refers to the karma of body and speech; "root" refers to the mind of stinginess and greed. When these arise repeatedly and continue in succession, they become "deep";

when they become intertwined and firm, difficult to untie, they are called "knots. All that arises from stinginess constitutes sinful karma, not merely at that specific time, but even for a single instance of false speech.

[Commentary] Regarding "sin" (*āpatti*), which refers to the actions of body and speech: the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other texts state that volition capable of moving the body is called bodily action (*kāyakarman*);

volition capable of producing speech is called vocal action (*vākkarman*); and because the two types of volition—deliberative and decisive—are associated with the mind and cause the mind to act, they are called mental action (*manaskarman*).
Taking unwholesome volition, which is fearsome and loathsome, and designating it as "sin. Furthermore...
"Sin" (*pāpa*) means to destroy; it is so called because it destroys wholesome dharmas. "Roots" refers to the mind of stinginess and greed.

To be attached to wealth and dharmas already obtained, being unable to give them away and instead hoarding them, is called "stinginess" (*mātsarya*). To have a longing desire for things not yet obtained, as well as for their causes and conditions, is called "greed" (*lobha*).
Because of this stinginess and greed, various evils are drawn forth; thus, stinginess and greed are called "roots. As for "root," it means that which gives birth.
Because of this meaning, and because this stinginess and greed are close to the mind, they are called the "stingy and greedy mind.

Since the offenses of body, speech, and mind, as well as the roots of stinginess and greed, are all profound and deep, and are all fetters and bonds, they are called "deeply rooted and firmly bound offenses.
△ Second, the explanation that establishes the three matters.
[Commentary: This means that stinginess and greed are the roots of suffering; what one does constitutes the karma of suffering; and hungry ghosts constitute the fruit of suffering.
These are the three matters.
△ Second, a further explanation of the meaning of "roots."

[Commentary]: According to the ten grave precepts, stinginess (*mātsarya*) is also an action (*karman*), for it arises from greed (*lobha*) as its root, thereby giving rise to sinful karma. [Sub-commentary]:
Stinginess and parsimony are the foundation of one’s own distress and the cause of abandoning life; the absence of stinginess is the source of one’s own wealth.

The foremost principle for sustaining life, it instructs Bodhisattvas in gathering and transforming sentient beings. By establishing precepts that restrain stinginess, it is called the "precept against stinginess.
Once stinginess is restrained, karma has no basis to arise; instead, through non-attachment, one initiates acts of giving to gather and transform sentient beings.

According to the *Vijñaptimātra-yoga*, karma is volition (*cetanā*), which is among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*). Since stinginess is established based on attachment, it follows [the nature of its cause].

Regarding the enumeration of afflictions (*kleśa*): the essence of karma is volition (*cetanā*). Since volition permeates all three natures, there are consequently karmas that are wholesome or unwholesome.
The essence of stinginess (*mātsarya*), however, is not like this; because there is no such thing as "wholesome stinginess," to assert that stinginess is karma contradicts both reason and scripture.
III. Question and Answer to Resolve Objections (2). First, the objection regarding the realms of rebirth for those born many times (2). First, the question.
[Commentary] "The same. For five hundred lifetimes he was stingy; he became a human and then a ghost.
△ Second, the answer. [Commentary] Answer:
Humans and ghosts alternate, their creation and reception mutually supporting one another. If it were only a human body, it would not be called an evil retribution. If...

Only those with a ghost body should not create karma; however, it would not contradict reason for them to also become animals. It is simply that when the habit of stinginess is not eliminated, it is termed "continuity" (*saṃtati*). [Commentary]:
On the basis of a human body, one creates general karma for the ghost realm and shall receive the retribution of a ghost; on the basis of a ghost body, one creates specific...
Virtuous karma assists the karma created in a previous life within the body of a hungry ghost that induces birth in the human realm; thus, one immediately receives the fruit of the human state.
Therefore, it is said that "the creation and the reception mutually assist one another. The commentary explains this by way of contrast:

if there were only a human body, it would not be called an "evil retribution" because it was summoned by virtuous karma and was not induced by the karma of stinginess. If there were only a ghostly body, it would not be possible for it to have created the collective retributive karma of an evil realm.

Regarding the retribution for the human realm: the treatises state that the afflictions of the three miserable realms (the *tú*) lack the capacity for discriminative discernment and thus cannot create karma to induce collective retribution (*sǒngbào*).
By extension, this applies to the animal realm (*chùqù*). Generally speaking across all realms, one undergoes five hundred births.
II. Specifically addressing the objection regarding the *Caitika* school. Part One: The Question.
[Commentary] Question: Since the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, Maudgalyāyana has had many different mothers throughout his successive births;
why does he specifically rescue that one, Caṅkī?
△ Second, the answer.
[Commentary]: The answer is that the karmic affinity between Caitrī and Maudgalyāyana was profound; she has now been reborn as his mother.

However, this refers only to saving the mother who gave birth to his current body, not to saving that distant past Caitrī. As stated in various other treatises, these accounts are all for the sake of those who have not yet...
[The Buddha] attained [enlightenment]. Second, it is clarified that the son’s inferior virtue was not something that could be remedied by your strength alone.
[Commentary: The Master states: Your mother’s mind of stinginess was stingy toward all things; this has spanned many lifetimes and involved many people.
"How could you alone, by your own power, be able to rescue and deliver them? This third point rebukes the futility of your efforts:

though your filial piety moves heaven and earth, even the celestial deities, the spirits of the earth, the malevolent spirits and heretics, the Daoist masters, and the gods of the Four Heavenly Kings cannot do anything about it."
[Commentary] The sub-commentary (*chao*) divides the *śāstra* into two sections. First is the general explanation of the meaning of the scripture.
[The *Śāstra*] states: The Tripitaka Master said: "Even if you were to invoke celestial spirits in the upper realms and stir up terrestrial deities in the lower regions;
even if you were to subdue malevolent demons and ensnare heterodox practitioners, unifying the six directions under one house and encompassing the eight classes of beings—"
Even if they were to unite as one multitude and combine their supernatural powers, they would still be unable to prevail.
[Commentary: "The six directions" refers to the four cardinal points, above, and below. "The eight classes" refers to the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and so forth.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of each difficulty.
[Commentary]: "Non-Buddhist practitioners" refers to those who are practitioners among non-Buddhists; this distinguishes them from practitioners within the Buddhist tradition (the Inner Way).
When Buddhism was first transmitted to this land, monks were addressed as "practitioners" (*daoshi*).
As for the "Four Heavenly Kings," they are Vaiśravaṇa and the others, who protect and sustain the world.
[Commentary] As for "demonic beings" (*māra*): in the Sanskrit language it is *māra*, which here means "to destroy. This title is established because they destroy superior matters.
His name is Pāpīyas, which means "the Evil One"; the older transcription "Pāxun" is an error. As for "non-Buddhist practitioners" (*tīrthika*):
those who falsely engage in speculative inquiry outside the teachings of the Three Vehicles and establish separate paths are called non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Non-Buddhists...

They claimed for themselves the title of "men of the Way" (*daoshi*). The *Yaoshishu* states: from the Han and Wei dynasties down to the Fu and Yao houses, all referred to the various monks as "men of the Way.

It was during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Northern Wei (the second year of the Taijian era) that figures such as Kou Qianzhi began to surreptitiously appropriate the name of "man of the Way" and privately altered their titles to "Sacrificial Libationer" (*jijiu*). [The] Four Heavens...
As for the divine kings (*rājarṣi*): in the east is Dhṛtarāṣṭra; in the south, Virūḍhaka; in the west, Virūpākṣa;
and in the north, Vaiśravaṇa—here translated as "Much-Hearing" (*Bahudhāna*). They all dwell on the fourth tier of Mount Sumeru, each presiding over one side and governing the four continents.
They also reside upon the peaks of the seven golden mountains. Possessing supernatural powers and sovereign mastery, these four are all called "divine kings."
[Commentary] The fourth section clarifies that there is indeed the capacity [for liberation].
One must rely upon the majestic spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Saṃgha throughout the ten directions to attain liberation.
[Sub-commentary] The commentary divides this into two parts; first, the direct explanation of this passage.
[Commentary] The Subcommentary states: The Tripitaka Master said: "A single thread cannot restrain an elephant; one must rely on many strands.
A single person cannot eliminate karma; one must depend upon manifold virtues."
△ Second, a general explanation combining the preceding [sections].
[Commentary]: Now, examining the preceding and following scriptural passages, there are four propositions based on the relative opposition of the false and the correct, and the one and the many.
First, that which is correct but not manifold: this cannot provide salvation; therefore, it was previously stated that you alone could not do anything about it. Second, that which is manifold...

The first is neither correct nor can it provide salvation; this refers to the aforementioned deities, malevolent spirits, and heterodox teachers. The second is both numerous and correct, and only then can one be rescued and delivered;
this refers to the Sangha of the ten directions. The fourth is neither numerous nor correct, and thus it is inherently impossible;
for this reason, there is no scriptural passage concerning it. The fifth permits the method of rescue.
I shall now explain the method of deliverance, so that all who face hardships may be freed from sorrow and suffering.
[Commentary] The phrase "I shall now explain" is precisely the expression of assent; "the method of deliverance" refers to the matter being assented to.
Regarding the phrase "causing all to be equal": a crossbow capable of launching a thousand-jun weight does not set its trigger solely for a field mouse;
how could the Honored One of the Three Realms allow your mother alone to remain separated from suffering?
[Commentary] Regarding "ten *jūn*": thirty *jin* constitute one *jūn*; the weight in *jin* can thus be calculated. *Ki* refers to the trigger of a crossbow.

According to the *Shuowen*, *xi* refers to a small mouse. The Sutra’s statement, "causing all those who find it difficult to escape suffering [to do so]," serves as a heading that gives rise to two intentions:
a specific salvation from suffering and a general salvation from suffering. This is because it specifically identifies Maudgalyāyana while generally addressing the entire assembly.
△ Sixth, showing his True Dharma, in three parts. First, the analysis of the scriptural text.
[Commentary]: The sixth section shows his True Dharma. This is divided into two parts. First, the teaching on the method for a filial son to present offerings.
Next, the ritual for the assembly of monks receiving offerings consists of five initial parts: first, determining the supreme time; second, generating the supreme intention;
third, preparing the supreme offering; fourth, praising the supreme field of merit; and fifth, attaining the supreme benefit.
△ Second, the explanation of the meaning of the five sections.
[Commentary]: The day of *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence) is the supreme time, like the month of spring’s warmth. Filial piety is the supreme intention, like a fresh and excellent seed.
The hundred flavors and five fruits are the supreme offerings, like fine oxen and plows; with these, one makes the offering.
Nurturing [the field of merit] is like being able to plow and till; the noble and holy ones constitute the supreme field, just as there are fertile lands.

To ensure the survival of one's parents, six kinds of relatives, and even ancestors up to the seventh generation, enabling them to leave suffering behind and be reborn in heaven, constitutes the supreme benefit—just as a thousand chests and ten thousand bushels are harvested in autumn and stored for winter.
Is the force of the scriptural meaning not indeed so? Let the wise examine this as clearly as pointing with a finger.
"Qi zhang" (Its Baskets):
"Xiang" refers to large carts. As the *Shijing* says: "They sought ten thousand granaries; they sought ten thousand xiangs. Master Zheng’s commentary states:
"They sought ten thousand granaries to store [the grain] and ten thousand carts to transport it. Regarding the *hu*: one hundred *sheng* constitute one *hu*.
When autumn has completed the harvest, winter then stores the grain; the intended meaning is thus understandable—is it not so?
Regarding these five sections of the text, is it not the case that the principle is exactly as such? The underlying purport is not remote, like pointing at an object within one’s own palm.
△ Third, the explanation according to the topical divisions.
[Commentary] First, regarding the time when the first meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) excels:
the Buddha told Maudgalyāyana that on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, at the time of the *pravāraṇā* (the invitation for confession) of the Saṃgha in the ten directions...
[Commentary] The outline of the commentary has two parts. First, the explanation of the main text of the sutra has three parts. First, the section on the Sangha of the ten directions has two parts.
First, the specific explanation of the meaning of "Sangha" has two parts. First, the general explanation of the harmony of the assembly.

[Commentary] The author states: The Sanskrit term *saṃgha* is translated here as "the harmonious assembly. This means that if there is an assembly that lacks harmony—such as a group of merchants, a group of officials, or an army—it is not called the Saṃgha Jewel.
Conversely, if there is harmony but no assembly—as in the case of two people with a shared mind—it is likewise not the Saṃgha Jewel.
Only when there is both an assembly and harmony does it become a cause for merit; only then is it properly named [the Saṃgha Jewel].
The Sangha Jewel. [Commentary]:
There are two kinds of Sangha. Those who have realized the principle are called the Sangha of Principle-Harmony (*lihe seng*).

Those who have not yet realized the True Principle but possess the Great Precepts are called the Sangha of Ritual-Harmony (*shire seng*). Only when there are three or more individuals is it termed a "community" (*zhong*), because the meaning of "community" is narrow. If...

Regarding the sense of "harmony" (saṃgha) within the body [of the community]: even one person or two persons may be designated as a Saṃgha because they belong to that same category, just as a rhinoceros-like sage within a trichiliocosm is designated as the Jewel of the Saṃgha. As for the phrase "two people with a single mind":

The *Appended Statements* of the *I Ching* say: The Master said, "The way of the gentleman is such that he may either emerge from seclusion or remain therein; he may either maintain silence or engage in speech.
When two people share the same heart, their benefit can cut through metal. The words of those with one heart have a fragrance like that of the orchid. The commentary explains:

When the gentleman’s emerging or remaining in seclusion, his speaking or his silence, do not deviate from the Mean (*zhong*), then although his outward traces differ, his Way is necessarily the same—just as [the hardness of] metal [is uniform].
Although they are severed and divided, their nature does not differ. In Buddhism, a *saṃgha* (community) is formed through the combination of four persons;
therefore, even if two persons are in harmony, it does not constitute a *saṃgha*. △ Second, explaining the accomplishment of harmony.
[Commentary]: "Harmony" (he-ho) consists of six kinds: namely, harmony of body through collective action; harmony of speech through collective silence; harmony of mind through collective forbearance;
harmony of precepts through collective cultivation; harmony of views through collective understanding; and harmony of material benefits through collective distribution.
In the Confucian tradition, it is said that the petty man seeks harmony while the superior man seeks accord. Now, the śrāmaṇera bhikṣu achieves both harmony and accord.
[Commentary] The *Analects* states: "The superior man is harmonious but not conformist; the petty person is conformist but not harmonious. He Yan’s commentary explains:
"The heart of the superior man is harmonious, yet his views differ; therefore, it is said he is 'not conformist. The petty person shares the same preferences, yet each strives for personal gain;
therefore, it is said he is 'not harmonious. A monk, a disciple of the Buddha, possesses the virtues of the six harmonies (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*) and is thus [truly] concordant.
The supramundane path is both harmonious and identical. △ Second, the general explanation of the text.
[Commentary]: The present mention of the "ten directions" indicates that the Dharma is without limit or restriction; how could it distinguish between the near and the distant?
Regarding the term "Saṃgha," the repetition of the Chinese and Sanskrit terms reflects the translator’s lack of skill.

[Commentary]: This translator is but a clumsy one. As stated in the *Śū* (the sub-commentary), the phrasing "the assembly of monks receives offerings" was adopted to ensure the literary expression was smooth and harmonious, making it easy for others to understand;
thus, both the Chinese and Sanskrit terms were presented together. △ Second, the fifteenth day of the seventh month.

[Commentary]: Regarding the fifteenth day of the seventh month: this is because the three-month summer *varṣā* retreat has concluded, and thus the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) may be performed.
There are three days for the *pravāraṇā*: either the fourteenth, the fifteenth, or the sixteenth. Here, the middle day is cited.

[Commentary] The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: "The two periods of summer retreat (*an-gu*). Formerly translated as 'sitting through the summer' or 'sitting through the winter,' these were all regional regulations and not the orthodox intent of the Central Kingdom.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* also speaks of the two periods of summer retreat. The *Utpatti-sūtra* states: "From the sixteenth day of the fifth month" (note:
at this time in the Western Regions, the summer retreat in China has already been underway for one month), "until the fifteenth day of the eighth month, [one observes] the summer retreat."
It is also full [of days]. (The note says: "In the Western Regions, the *pravāraṇā* ceremony is held at this time; in the land of Han, it has already been one month.

However, according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, the *Saddharma-smṛty-upasthāna-sūtra*, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, the *Samantapāsādikā*, the *Vinayamātṛkā*, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-uttaragrantha*, and so forth—whether consulting the texts directly, citing them in commentaries, or questioning the masters of old—there are approximately thirty or more [such instances].
The texts of our own school all speak of the summer *varṣā* retreat (*anugata*). The discussion states: In India, the seasonal nodes (*saṃkrānti*) occur somewhat later, so two retreats are taught;

in the land of Han, the seasonal nodes occur somewhat earlier, so only the summer retreat is taught. Alternatively, there may be differences in what is taught according to the region and the capacity of the audience;

this does not contradict the general principle. Regarding the Buddha’s prescription for the retreat (*varṣā*), there are generally three intentions: first, to prevent aimless wandering, which causes hindrance...
One cultivates supramundane activities; second, one harms the lives of sentient beings, which violates the mind of compassion;

third, one incurs worldly censure. The world censures them, saying: "Even sparrows and mice have burrows and dens; why do the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, not know the proper time? For this reason, the Buddha established these rules.
Furthermore, there are three periods for the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), namely: the early, the middle, and the late. On the sixteenth day of the fourth month, the retreat begins.
The Summer Retreat (Varṣā). The members of the Saṃgha sit facing each other in pairs. Each says: "Venerable Sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], shall observe the summer retreat for the first three months within the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) of the [Name] Monastery in the [Name] Village."

The dwellings are dilapidated; they must be repaired. (Recite three times. From the seventeenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month, one continuously observes the *saṃgha* boundary for the middle *varṣā*.
On the sixteenth day of the fifth month, one observes the later *varṣā*.
The earlier *varṣā* concludes on the fifteenth day of the seventh month. The latter two periods of *varṣā* follow the *pravāraṇā* ceremony of the earlier *varṣā*.

One must wait until the full term of the months has elapsed before being permitted to leave the boundary. If there is an intercalary fourth month, the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is entered in the preceding fourth month;

if there is an intercalary seventh month, the summer retreat is concluded in the preceding seventh month. Even if there is an intercalary fifth or sixth month, the period of *anvārambhaṇa* remains one hundred and twenty days.
If the first *pūrvavārṣika* retreat is completed, one may accept the *kaṭhina* robe; however, if either of the latter two retreats is completed, one does not accept the *kaṭhina*.
Regarding robes: because they were not obtained at the proper time and no labor was performed [to acquire them], this is the case.

However, according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, when monks or nuns who maintain full ordination and reside during the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) must go out for the sake of the Three Jewels, for the illness or death of their parents, or for matters such as generating merit and extinguishing evil, if they can return on the same day, they need only inform a monk who agrees with them and may then leave the boundary.
One must protect against the appearance of dawn on the following day. If there is a reason to remain for one night or even up to seven days, one should perform the *pratimukha* (face-to-face) rite.
Once the seven days have passed and one has gone outside the boundary, one must return to this place to enter the rains retreat (*varṣā*).
If the reason extends beyond seven days, one should accept the half-month rite; if the reason extends beyond the sixteenth day, one should accept the one-month rite. These two are called...

Regarding the communal dharmas: the entire Saṃgha must be in harmony and perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* before they may leave the boundary. Once their business is concluded, they shall return to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*).
When the days of the retreat are fulfilled, the monks and nuns shall perform the *pavarana* (the end of the retreat), and the formal resolution of the summer retreat (*kṣamaṇā*) shall be held.

The procedures for assembling the community and casting voting sticks (*śalākā*) are identical to the methods of the *poṣadha*; however, the word "pavarana" replaces the word "poṣadha. Two individuals should be appointed, each [to oversee the proceedings].

One who possesses the two sets of five virtues is as follows: being without attachment, without aversion, without fear, without delusion, and knowing whether the *pravāraṇā* has been performed or not.
These five are called the virtues of *pravāraṇā*. Furthermore, one knows the proper time and not the improper time;
speaks according to reality and not falsely; acts for benefit and not for harm; is gentle and not harsh; and maintains a mind of loving-kindness and not anger.
Anger. These five are called the virtues for one who raises a charge against another.

Their intention is to remain free from strife, to cause others to repent, to manifest virtuous qualities externally, to be able to provide skillful exhortation, and to avoid faults while having compassion for sentient beings; therefore, two persons are appointed, each possessing these two sets of five virtues.

The *sthavira* deliberates and causes the formal motion (*jñapti*) and second *karma* (*dvitīya-karman*) to be performed for their appointment. He solicits consent, asks for harmony, and proceeds as is customary.
At the end, he replied: "The *karmavācanā* for appointing those who shall receive the *pravāraṇā*. The *karmavācanā* proclaims:

'The *karmavācanā* for appointing those who shall receive the *pravāraṇā*. Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If it is the time for the Saṃgha, and if the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣu [Name] as the one who shall receive the *pravāraṇā*.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). (Is the formal motion established? He replies: It is established. Venerable Saṃgha..."
Listen. The Sangha appoints the monk [Name] as the one who shall receive the invitation to self-examination (*pravāraṇā*).
Those elders who consent to the Sangha’s appointment of the monk [Name] as the one who shall receive the invitation to self-examination, let them remain silent.
Whoever does not consent, let them speak. The Sangha has consented; the appointment of the monk [Name] as the one who shall receive the invitation to self-examination is concluded. The Sangha...

Because he has accepted with patience and silence, this matter is thus upheld. (Is the *karmavācanā* accomplished? Answer: It is accomplished. Having been appointed through these five virtues, he approaches the elder, kneels on his right knee, and makes a formal request:
(Answer: This is the *jñapti* for the *pravāraṇā* *karmavācanā* to harmonize the Saṃgha. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Today the community of monks performs the *pravāraṇā*.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, being patient and listening, perform the *pravāraṇā* in harmony. This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). (Is the *jñapti* accomplished?)
The respondent replied, "It is accomplished. Having made this announcement, he had people spread the grass, with one person cutting a portion for each.
They proceeded in order, each reciting a verse: "The auspicious householder has offered soft grass; The Tathāgata, having accepted it, attained Perfect Enlightenment.

We bhikṣus, training in the Buddha’s wisdom, Sit upon the grass and purify our three karmas through the Pravāraṇā. When the spreading of the grass was finished, the five virtuous qualities were presented to the Elder.
The former kneels on the ground and announces: "All the Sangha shall sit upon the grass. With the right shoulder bared, they kneel and join their palms (the Sangha all follows this proclamation).

Next is the method for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish) directly before the Sangha. First, the one endowed with the five virtues approaches the senior monk (*sthavira*), spreads his sitting mat extensively, and kneels with joined palms.
The senior monk likewise kneels with joined palms, and the assembly of monks all follow the senior monk.
The ritual should be performed as follows: "Venerable One, please attend with one-pointed mind. Today the Saṃgha observes the Pravāraṇā. I, the bhikṣu [Name], also observe the Pravāraṇā.
If you perceive any offense—whether seen, heard, or suspected—Venerable Elder, out of compassion, please speak to me.
If I perceive an offense, I shall always confess it according to the Dharma. (Recite this three times. The second person possessing the five virtues proceeds to the second seat. The...
The one who possesses the five virtues proceeds again to the third seat, and so on until the lowest seat; this is done for all of them.

Once the assembly of monks has finished speaking, the one possessing the five virtues goes before the senior monk (*sthavira*), kneels, and says: "The Sangha has unanimously completed the invitation to confession (*pravāraṇā*). Having thus paid homage, he withdraws.

If one incurs an offense due to being censured by the five virtuous ones or by the Saṃgha, one should repent according to the Dharma. Furthermore, the Vinaya states: "On the fourteenth day, the monks perform the *pravāraṇā*;
on the fifteenth day, the nuns rely upon them to inquire about offenses. Therefore, it is only on the sixteenth day that they may leave the boundary.
△ Third, regarding the time of the Saṃgha’s *pravāraṇā*, there are two parts. First, an evaluation of the term "Saṃgha."
[Commentary: This superfluous character "seng" (monk) should be removed, as its omission would leave the sentence incomplete; this too is an error of the translator.
Why not say, "at the time of the communal *pravāraṇā*"?

△ Second, the formal explanation of *pravāraṇā* (self-invitation) has two parts. First, explaining the name to reveal its intent, which further has two sub-sections. First, the formal explanation according to its meaning. [Commentary]:
Regarding *pravāraṇā*, it means to allow others to point out one’s own transgressions. This refers to the ninety-day preparatory practice during the summer retreat (*varṣā*).
Even if one does not attain the four fruits of the path, nor the four *dhyānas*, the Buddha’s original intention in establishing this teaching was as follows. Correctly...
The same applies to the monks of the *mofa* (final dharma) age and others.
[Commentary] After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the period in which there are teaching (*śāsana*), practice (*pratipatti*), and realization (*adhigama*) is called the *saddharma* (True Dharma).

When there is only teaching and practice but no fruit of realization, it is called the *pratirūpaka-dharma* (Semblance Dharma). When there is only the teaching without practice or realization, it is called the *mofa*. Record.

The True Dharma (*saddharma*) and the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*) both last for one thousand years; the Final Dharma (*antardharma*) lasts for ten thousand years. Because of the ordination of nuns, the True Dharma is reduced by half.
Alternatively, it is said that it is not reduced and remains as before for one thousand years, because the nuns practice the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*).
△ Second, citing scriptures to resolve objections.
[Commentary: Although it is the final five hundred years, there are still those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit (merit is concentration).
△ Second, the detailed expansion of the characteristics of practice has three parts. First, the intent of the self-indulgence (pravāraṇā).

[Commentary: Now, as one prepares to transcend the sea of suffering, one must carefully guard the life-preserving bag. Yet, fearing that even the one at the helm may lose their way, one must certainly rely on those observing from the sidelines to discern gain and loss.
Even if one has severed delusions and realized the fruit, one still hopes for the extinction of transgressions and the arising of merit.

[Commentary] Regarding "carefully protecting the life-preserving bag" (*kṣapaṇaka*): The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that it is like a person in the world who wishes to cross the great ocean and obtains a single life-preserving bag, which they protect with single-minded devotion so as not to let it suffer even the slightest damage.

At that time, a *rākṣasa* says, "I beg you for this entire life-preserving bag. That person does not comply. When [the *rākṣasa*] begs for half of it, for a portion the size of a hand, and so forth...
Not even a finger’s breadth, nor even as much as a single mote of dust, shall be surrendered to it. He further reflects: "Though a single mote of dust is small, it must not be given;
gradually the bag will be damaged and one will be unable to cross the ocean.
In this way, monks, the preservation of the five-part pure precepts as a life-preserving bag is exactly like this; one must not yield to even a single affliction-demon.
If there is even a speck of dust’s worth of cause for breaking the precepts, or if there is the slightest impairment, one will be unable to cross the great ocean of birth and death.
This can be understood through the analogy of a chess game, where the player facing the board sees differently than the bystander looking on. △ Second, the words of the *Pravāraṇā* (Self-indulgence).
[Commentary: Therefore, baring one shoulder in the midst of the assembly, one says to the virtuous elders:

[Commentary: "All share the same mind" refers to the harmony of intention. That is to say, at the time of receiving offerings, all equally exercise a sense of shame and remorse, a profound and earnest mind, a mind of compassion and gratitude, and a mind of seeking to rescue and provide relief.

Regarding the phrase "all share the same single mind," the *Sūtra* explains this through five meanings: first, the mind of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*), which honors and values the worthy and good while rejecting the violent and evil;

1. The mind of compassionate protection, which uproots suffering and bestows happiness upon sentient beings; 2. The fourfold mind of repaying kindness, which keeps in mind the donors for the sake of granting them merit and benefit; 3.

"Measuring vessel. The character "he" (和) is an error. In current usage, it is simply called "bowl" (鉢), which is an abbreviation.

1. **Dhyāna**: This refers to having attained the four dhyānas and the nine meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*). 2. **Noble Fruition**: This refers to having attained the four fruits of the path, such as stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) and so forth.

The Sūtra provides the correct explanation.

[Commentary: The "six relations" (*ṣaṭ-kaula*) are father, mother, brothers, and husband and wife (some say "male and female," excluding the brothers).

At that time, the Buddha commanded the monastic community of the ten directions: "First, perform incantations and prayers for the sake of the donors' families.

In the monastery, after the monks have finished performing the incantations and prayers before the Buddha, they may then partake of the food themselves.
[Commentary] The author states: In this passage, the first half [of the verse] purifies the three types of karma, while the second half establishes the Three Jewels.
Within the first half, the recitation of the incantation (*dhāraṇī*) is vocal karma; meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is mental karma; and receiving the food is bodily karma.

Within the second half, the stupa represents the Buddha; the incantation represents the Dharma; and receiving the food represents the Saṃgha. To receive from another before eating is the rule of the Vinaya; thus, even the character "receive" (*shou*) [implies this].
This refers to the Dharma. "Stūpa" (tǎ) is a corruption of the language of the borderlands; in its correct form it is called *caitya* (zǎidǔbō), which means a "high and prominent place.
Here, the meaning extends to include both temples (*vihāra*) and stūpas. A stūpa enshrines relics (*śarīra*), while a temple enshrines images of the Buddha.
[Commentary] Regarding the ritual for the Buddha’s instruction to the assembly of monks to receive offerings: one should purify the three karmas before receiving food.
The act of reciting prayers belongs to verbal karma; the act of receiving food belongs to bodily karma; and mental karma must necessarily be present first, as it gives rise to body and speech.
Therefore, it is omitted here. As for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), its mental aspect pertains to the specific object of focus and need not be mixed with the general assembly of monks.

Regarding the three karmas: while the Tathāgata was in the world, when the Saṃgha received offerings, they were placed before the Buddha. After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, they are placed before the Buddha within the stūpa-temples.
Because this is an offering to the Buddha, the Saṃgha offers prayers of blessing; these are thus the Dharma and the Saṃgha. In this way, the Three Jewels are complete.
Although these prayers of blessing are spoken by the Saṃgha, they are originally the words of the Buddha; the Saṃgha merely transmits them. Therefore, they belong to the Dharma.
[This is] a treasure.

This section of the sutra is the introduction to the compilation; it concerns the offering made by Maudgalyāyana on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.

[Sub-commentary] Regarding the *pariṇāmanā* division: how does the World-Honored One, within this concluding section on the entrustment and dissemination of the Bequeathed Dharma, universally manifest for the great assembly the characteristics of the benefits of the *pūjā* assembly, so as to accommodate and encourage them to practice learning, serve their parents, and perform filial piety?

The Buddha’s mind is impartial; he would certainly not have revealed [the teaching] to Maudgalyāyana during the section on the True Doctrine (*saddharma-bhāṣaṇa*), only to leave it as a final instruction for the assembly during the section on Dissemination (*parīndanā*).
If one were to claim that this sutra was spoken in two separate assemblies—one before and one after—how could the latter assembly be relegated to the status of dissemination?
Examining the matter from both perspectives, it is certain that this is the section on the True Doctrine. Therefore, Maudgalyāyana said: "If, in future ages..."
"All disciples of the Buddha should likewise offer the *bōron* (alms bowl) to rescue and deliver their parents;

would you not do so? [The Buddha said: "This is for the sake of requesting the Dharma from the assembly to rescue and deliver one's parents; it is not a request concerning the receiving and upholding of the final teachings. The Buddha said: "Excellent! You have asked well. It was precisely what I intended to say, yet you have asked again.

*Zhengyi* (Correct Meaning). The commentator explains: This sūtra’s first assembly consists of two parts within its main section (*zhèngzōngfēn*). First, it specifically demonstrates Maudgalyāyana’s skillful means for rescuing his mother;

second, it universally demonstrates the essential gateway for the great assembly to provide for their parents. The first section is as previously described. The second section is divided into two parts.

First, Maudgalyāyana makes his request; subsequently, the World-Honored One expounds for him. Within this exposition, there are two parts: first, the praise and authorization to speak; second, the actual response to the request.
The response to the request is divided into three sections: first, the instruction to initiate superior practice; second, the instruction on the intention for initiating practice.
The three teachings constantly establish assemblies; these may be understood by following the textual expositions.
[Commentary] Within the *Pravartanā-vibhāga* (the section on circulation), there are three parts. First, the formal request:
Maudgalyāyana again addressed the Buddha, saying, "My late mother, through the power of the merit of the Triple Gem, has attained the assembly..."

"By the power of the Sangha's majestic spiritual authority, all disciples of the Buddhas in future ages should likewise offer the *bowl-of-liberation* (*pūrnabhadra-patra*) to rescue and deliver their present parents, as well as their parents up to the seventh generation. Would this not be appropriate?"
[Commentary] The subcommentator states: When these words were spoken, it was also after the offerings had been made; it was not the business of a single session.
It was only upon reaching the Pipphalavana Cave that they were finally compiled together as a sutra.
Maudgalyāyana cherished his own kin yet extended his concern to others, just as Ying Kaoshu admonished Duke Zhuang.
[Commentary] The words of Ying Kaoshu are recorded extensively in the *Chunqiu Zhuan* (Spring and Autumn Annals Commentary). To summarize its essentials:
Duke Wu of Zheng married a lady of the Jiang clan, who bore him Prince Zhuang and Gongshu Duan. Prince Zhuang was born while his mother was asleep;
she was startled by this, and consequently came to detest him. She loved Gongshu Duan and wished to establish him [as the heir]. She repeatedly petitioned Duke Wu to do so.
The Duke did not grant his request. When Duke Zhuang ascended the throne, he requested the city of Jing and sent [Shu] to reside there, calling him Dukes of the Capital City (Jingcheng).

[The location of the Capital City is present-day Jing County in Xingyang. Dukes completed the city walls and gathered the people; he repaired his armor and weapons and equipped his infantry and chariots (infantry are called *zu*; those in chariots are called *sheng*).
He intended to launch a surprise attack on Zheng (a "surprise" means to strike when the enemy is unprepared; "to open" means to reveal one's intent). Duke Zhuang dispatched an envoy to attack him.

The Senior Uncle fled to Gong (Gong being the name of a state; the state of Gong is the present-day Gong County in Ji Prefecture). He then placed Lady Jiang at Chengying (Chengying is a location in Zheng).
He swore an oath, saying, "As long as we do not reach the Yellow Springs, we shall never see one another again. Later, however, he regretted this.
Ying Kaoshu was the border guard of Yinggu (a border guard is one who oversees the boundaries of a territory). Having heard of this, he presented a gift to the Duke. The Duke granted him food.
He set aside some meat. The Duke asked him about it, and he replied, "I have a mother who has always tasted my food, but she has never tasted your soup.
I beg to take this to her. The Duke said, "You have a mother to whom you can give it, but I alone have none.
Ying Kaoshu asked, "What do you mean? The Duke told him the reason for his words and confessed his regret. Ying Kaoshu replied, "Why should Your Majesty worry about this?"
"If one digs into the earth or a spring until they meet face-to-face in a tunnel, who would say it is not so? The Duke followed her advice.
As the Duke entered the tunnel, his joy was *rong-rong* (the term *rong-rong* describes a state of harmonious happiness). When Lady Jiang emerged from the tunnel, her joy was *xie-xie*.

(The character "yì" [音曳] means to spread out or disperse. Thereupon, they became mother and son as before. The Gentleman said: "Ying Kaoshu was purely filial (the character "chún" [純] means profound or earnest).
His love for his mother extended even to Duke Zhuang."
[Commentary]: Second, the praise and request.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, most excellent is your question! It is precisely what I intended to explain, and you have asked it now.
[Commentary]: The exposition states: The first phrase marks the praise. "Most excellent is your question" means that it deeply accords with the Sage’s mind. The latter two phrases...

To explain the reason: just as he was about to speak, he encountered a question whose timing and resonance perfectly matched his own intention. Thus, there was a subtle and secret correspondence, leading to what is called a "prompt question.
The Buddha’s original intent was to proclaim that filial piety is the greatest virtue, that the task of uprooting suffering is of paramount importance, and that the *Ullambana* Dharma is supreme.
The World-Honored One beheld these excellent conditions and saw that the faculties of the assembly were matured and ready for transformation.
The third response to the request consists of five parts. First, the instruction on initiating practice:

"Good son, whether they be bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs, kings, crown princes, high ministers, grand secretaries, the three dukes and hundred officials, or the common people of the myriad subjects—anyone who practices loving-kindness and filial piety should first, for the sake of their current living parents, [perform the following]..."
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month— the day of the Buddha’s joy and the day of the Sangha’s *pravāraṇā*—
one should place food of a hundred flavors within an *urunda-bhājana* (alms bowl) for one's parents of the past seven generations and offer it to the self-restrained monks of the ten directions.
[Commentary] The sub-commentary divides this into two sections. First, it explains the person who is filial and obedient.

[Sub-commentary] The author states: Although there are distinctions between noble and base, and differences between the monastic and the lay, no one—unless born by transformation or from moisture—is without a father and a mother.
Even the compassionate crow and the parrot understand how to reflect upon their parents' kindness; how much more so should this be true for human beings? Not...

[The term] "rescue and deliverance" (*jibā*). [Commentary]: The *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra* states that in a past age, there was a parrot in the Snow Mountains who constantly gathered flowers, fruits, and rice to serve his blind parents.
At that time, the landowner went on an inspection tour of the crops and saw them...
At the place where birds and insects had clipped the grain ears, a net was set up and a parrot was caught.
The parrot said, "The landowner previously had a kind heart; he declared that the grain he sowed was to be shared and eaten by all living beings.
For this reason, everyone came to gather it. Why then am I being captured in a net today? It is simply because of the seeds..."
"The father is like the field; truthful speech is like the son; the field-owner is like the king, for protection depends upon him;
we are like the subjects who dwell in reliance upon him. Having heard this, the field-owner immediately released the parrot. The Buddha said, "The field-owner..."
Śāriputra, those blind parents were King Śuddhodana and Queen Māyā; the parrot that took the grain was my own self;
the compassionate crow remained as usual. △ Second, the explanation of the practice of filial piety has two parts.
The initial general explanation of filial conduct is twofold. First, the direct explanation of the meaning of the scripture. [Commentary]:
The benefits and harms regarding the filial son have already been fully discussed in the preliminary discourse. Having recognized what is right and wrong, one must rely upon the correct path;
therefore, it says, "One should first act for the sake of those who gave birth to one," and so forth.
△ Second, distinguishing the inclusion within the Piṭakas by means of their causes.
[Commentary]: According to the established regulations, whether one acts or fails to act constitutes a violation of those regulations; therefore, it must also pertain to the *vinaya* teachings.
Thus, the previous judgment also classifies it as belonging to the *Vinaya-piṭaka*.
△ Second, the explanation by way of concession and refutation.
[Commentary]: Now, although the Buddha is without joy or sorrow, his manifestation of joy on this day is in accordance with the conditions of sentient beings.
The Buddha originally appeared in the world solely to exhort people to practice cultivation. He felt sorrow when he saw people commit evil and rejoiced when he saw people cultivate goodness.
Now that the ninety-day period of intensive practice for the bhikṣus has concluded, their sincerity is redoubled;
throughout the trichiliocosm, it is the same everywhere. How could this not bring joy to the Buddha’s original intent? On this day, the offerings provided—
The merit is immense.

[Commentary] Regarding the "ninety days": the *Lunyu Liujing* (Treatise on the Six Arts) states that Huangdi’s assistant, Dainao, created the *jiayi* cycle and established ten celestial stems (*ganshen*), namely:
jia, yi, bing, ding, wu, ji, geng, xin, ren, and gui; and twelve terrestrial branches (*zhishen*), namely: zi... [and so forth].

The twelve Earthly Branches (*chī*), beginning with Chou (丑), are combined with the ten Heavenly Stems (*gān*) to form a total count. When the Heavenly Stems are exhausted, they constitute a *jun* (decade).

This refers to the sequence from Jiazi (甲子) and Yichou (乙丑) up to Guiyou (癸酉), which forms one *jun*. The remaining stems, such as Jiashu (甲戌), follow this same pattern. Because the summer retreat (*an-jū*) lasts for three months, it comprises nine *jun*.

As for the "Three Thousand Worlds," the full expression is "Three Thousand Great Thousandfold Worlds" (*sānqiān dàqiān shìjiè*). This refers to the four great continents, the sun and moon, and so forth...

In the first dhyāna, there are one thousand [worlds] each, collectively encircled by the Cakravāḍa Mountains; their measure is equal to that of the second dhyāna, and this is called a small chiliocosm.
Furthermore, ten such small chiliocosms constitute ten thousand, and one hundred small chiliocosms constitute one hundred thousand.
A thousand small chiliocosms constitute one million; encircled collectively by the Cakravāḍa Mountains, its extent is equal to the third dhyāna heaven, and is termed a medium chiliocosm.
Furthermore, ten such medium chiliocosms constitute ten million; this ten million is then collectively [summed].

One hundred million is a *koṭi*. One hundred times a *koṭi* is a *madhyama-sāhasra-lokadhātu* (middle thousandfold world system), which is one billion. One thousand times a *madhyama-sāhasra-lokadhātu* is a *mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu* (great thousandfold world system).
This great thousandfold world system is entirely encircled by the Cakravāḍa mountains, and its dimensions are equal to those of the fourth dhyāna heaven.
By combining the great with the small—uniting these small thousand, medium thousand, and great thousand worlds—it is called a "trichiliocosm" (a world system of three thousand great thousand worlds).
The Sūtra says: "Good son" refers to one who has accomplished various roots of goodness, such as faith. "Bhikṣu" is correctly transliterated as *bīcǔ*;
this term contains five meanings: first, "frightening Māra," because at the time of his initial renunciation, he terrified the palace of Māra.
1) Because they are active [in practice]. 2) They are called "mendicants" (*bhikṣu*), because they beg for food to sustain their bodies and beg for the Dharma to support the Path.

3) They are called "upholders of the precepts," because they gradually enter the ranks of the Saṃgha by maintaining pure morality. 4) They are called "those of pure livelihood," because they do not rely on greed or engage in wrong livelihoods.

5) They are called "destroyers of evil," because they gradually rely on the Noble Path to extinguish the afflictions (*kleśa*). *Nī* is a feminine suffix; it indicates that she is a woman. She possesses...

One who possesses the five virtues is called a *bhikṣuṇī*. Regarding the term "prime minister" (*zǎixiàng*): "Prime" (*zǎi*) means master; it means to assist. Because one acts as the master in making decisions and assists the sovereign, they are so named.
As for the "Three Dukes" (*sāngōng*), this originated in the Zhou period; they refer to the Grand Preceptor (*tàishī*), the Grand Tutor (*tàifù*), and the Grand Guardian (*tàibǎo*).

"Gong" (public) means "uprightness. A minister who has performed meritorious service and is loyal, upright, and selfless is called "gong. As for the "hundred officials," these are the officers of the hundred departments.
"Guan" (official) means "gong" (public); it also means "to observe. They govern according to the public good, observing the sentiments of the people and discerning right from wrong.
"The myriad people" refers to the various classes of the populace who hold official positions. "The commoners" (*shuren*): *shu* means "multitude.

These are the multitudes who hold no office; hence they are called "commoners. Altogether there are ten categories. Those who practice benevolence and filial piety may be understood from the scriptures.
[Commentary] Second, the teaching on making vows:
I vow that my current parents shall live for a hundred years, free from illness and all afflictions of suffering;
and that my parents up to the seventh generation shall be liberated from the suffering of the hungry ghosts and be reborn among humans and devas, where their merit and happiness shall be boundless.
[Commentary] The author states: What is cultivated must rely upon the gates of practice; what is attained must arise from the power of aspiration. Aspiration is the mind’s longing and desire.

One desires that there be peace and security both in life and after death. For those remaining in this world, it means preserving one's lifespan among humanity and remaining forever free from illness and affliction.

Those who have passed away shall have their spirits transferred to the heavens, forever severing the path of darkness. When practice and vows support one another, there is nothing that is not beneficial.
This is the constant teaching of the Three Teachings.
Disciples of the Buddha who cultivate filial piety and obedience should, in every thought-moment, constantly remember their parents, even back through seven generations.
Parents: on the fifteenth day of the seventh month every year, one should always, with filial piety and compassion, call to mind one's own parents who gave birth;
for their sake, one should provide the *bowl-offering* (*pātra-pūjā*) to the Buddha and the Sangha, thereby repaying the kindness of the love and nurturing bestowed by one's parents.
[Commentary] The sub-commentary states: This refers to those disciples of the Buddha who practice filial piety;

by contrast, it clarifies that for those who are not disciples of the Buddha or who are unfilial, one may simply leave things as they are and not arrange the offering of the basin. "Constantly mindful in every thought" means without end or beginning.
To nurture these matters is the function; to possess a heart of loving-kindness is the state of mind. Therefore, one first initiates practice and gives rise to vows in order to repay them.

The remaining text is easily understood. The Tripitaka Master said: "Since the love between parents is bound so tightly that it does not leave the mind for even a single thought-moment, a filial child seeking to repay their kindness must provide offerings year after year without interruption."
[Commentary] "Constantly mindful in every thought-moment" means that filial piety has neither beginning nor end. If one traces filial conduct backward, it is the natural and eternal law;
therefore, it has no beginning. If one traces filial conduct forward, it extends to the limits of the future; therefore, it has no end. This refers to the father who gave birth [to one].
"Mother" refers here to the biological parents of one's children.
[Commentary] Fourth, the exhortation to receive and uphold:
All disciples of the Buddha should reverently uphold this Dharma.
[Commentary] The author states: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says, "One accepts by the power of faith; one maintains by the power of mindfulness.
What is here termed "receiving" (*fèng*) carries the same meaning as "accepting. "Should" (*yīngdāng*) exhorts one to apply these two powers.
[Commentary] The following is the section on the dissemination (*pariṇāmanā*). It is further divided into two parts:
the first two phrases consist of the World-Honored One’s entrustment, and the latter three phrases consist of the assembly’s joyful acceptance and practice. Now, for the first part:

whether ordinary or noble, lay or monastic, all you disciples who have faith in the Buddha should practice these matters, benefiting both the living and the deceased, upholding the teachings, and receiving them with devotion.
[This concludes] the meaning of the text; thus the Sūtra says.
[Commentary]: Fifth, rejoicing and receiving the command.
At that time, the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana and the disciples of the fourfold assembly joyfully practiced and upheld [the teaching].
[Commentary] The sub-commentary divides this into two sections. First, it explains the four classes of disciples.

[Main Commentary] The author states: Regarding the "four classes," they refer to monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; alternatively, some say they are humans, devas, nāgas, and pretas. Because there is doubt, both views are preserved.
△ Second, the explanation of "Rejoicing and Practicing with Reverence.
[Commentary]: Now, all living beings rely upon and depend on their parents; thus, the kindness of parents is equal to that of Heaven and Earth.

Although one may be profoundly filial, if one does not find the proper way, it remains so. Now, having received this divine method, one knows through experience its spiritual efficacy, and will surely be able to eliminate the seven...
That which is difficult for the world: to repay the diligent labors of one's two parents. Knowing within oneself that the heart has its destination, one therefore joyfully accepts the command.

[Commentary] Regarding "knowing within oneself" and below: "zhi" (之) means "to reach. When the disciples of the four assemblies heard the Buddha’s teaching, they knew within themselves the path of filial piety.

Thus, there is that which is reached. For this reason, the countenance relaxes into joy; the heart is delighted and glad. Receiving the Buddha’s command, one receives it with faith and practices accordingly.
The Sūtra speaks of the "four classes of disciples. The *Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra* says: "Bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Indeed, "the four assemblies," "the four groups," and "the four classes" are terms commonly used in the sūtras and śāstras. (Commentary)

Regarding the two interpretations of the middle [section], the former is correct and the latter is not; there is no need to maintain both. Because he was born after his teacher, he is called a "brother" (ānuja);

because his understanding followed that of his teacher, he is called a "son" (putra). Thus, he is named a "disciple" (śiṣya). As the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu states in his commentary on the *Gayaśīrṣa-sūtra*: [text follows]
To joyfully receive and practice [the teaching] involves three meanings: first, the purity of the person who can teach; second, the purity of the Dharma being taught;
and third, the purity of the ultimate attainment of the fruit for those who rely upon and study it. Because of these three meanings, one joyfully receives and practices it.
Thus, a verse is said:
A Brief Explanation and Praise of the Profound Meaning of the *Ullambana* Sūtra:
Benefiting Oneself and Others, Delivering from Suffering, and Realizing Eternal Bliss.
Commentary on the *Buddha-spoken Ullambana Sūtra*, Compiled by Xiaoheng, Scroll Lower (End).

*Jīngshūchão Yīnshì* (Phonetic Glossary of the *Jīngshū*). By Dharma Master Chà (the character "lì" in the old edition is an error). *Jǐn* (pronounced *jù yǐn*, meaning "to press" or "to constrain"; also pronounced *jùn*). Regarding the phrase "there is an interpretation that invites difficulty": (In the old edition, it reads "Six Ci'en has an interpretation.

However, upon consulting the Zhejiang and Chuanshu editions of the ancient commentary, the word "Ci'en" is absent in all cases. Furthermore, as Ci'en was a preeminent patriarch of the Dharma-gate, it is certain that his contemporaries would not have dared to casually point him out for criticism; therefore, the term has been excised from the text. *Hónglú*.

(Lower tone for "li. A name for nine temples; "hong" means vast and great; "lu" means to set forth in order. It refers to the grand presentation of what is required to receive foreign guests with propriety. *Lüshǔ* (pronounced lù; *shǔ* means beans).

Patting (the character is pronounced *fǔ*; it means to strike). A bamboo basket and a gourd ladle (the upper character is pronounced *dān*; it is a bamboo vessel. The lower character is read as *píxiāo*; it is a horn-shaped cup, specifically a slice of a bottle-gourd used for holding water). Playing with the brain (the old edition reads *jué*, which has the same meaning).

*Ju* (pronounced *ru*; a short tunic). *Zǎo shì* (pronounced *zǎo sè*; lice and nits). *Yàn kè* (the first character pronounced *yàn*, meaning "to suffocate"; the second character, *kè*, means "to reprimand. This refers to those who, when their parents observe fasts or memorial services, do not cultivate merit with sincerity, but instead act merely to suppress the reproaches of others;

it is for this reason that they do so). *Chuǎi shí* (the first character pronounced *chū wěi*; to take privately. Furthermore, according to the *Jīng yìnyì* [Phonetic and Semantic Commentary on the Sūtras], it may also be read as a single syllable, *chuǎn*, meaning to snatch up).

*Qǐ liào* (*liào* means "to measure" or "to estimate"; *qǐ liào* means "how could one possibly fathom"?). *Jù rán* (the first character pronounced *jī*; an expletive particle; cited from the commentary to the *Lǐjì*). *Gāo yú* (pronounced *gāo yú*; fat and succulent).
*Xié* (pronounced *xī*; also called the "sweet-mouthed rat," which likes to eat ox horns). *Hé* (pronounced *hú*; radical *xià* and *gé*; a term of prohibition). *Kǎo* (cut by *kǔ* and *wài*;

according to the *Commentary on Ritual Practice of the Four-Part Vinaya*, it refers to "cleaning the husks of fruit"; the *Yìnyì Zhǐguī* says: "Husk" means coarse bran; the shell of the fruit is like bran; the note says it is the seed of pine and cypress). *Sū-rěn* (the latter pronounced *rěn*; the *Shuowén* says *suǒ* is *rěn-sū*).
*Líng* (pronounced *líng*; water chestnut). *Dìng* (pronounced *dìng*; a lamp). *Liáo* (pronounced *liǎo*; fire). *Wāng-yáng* (deep and vast). *Cái-huì* (the latter pronounced *huì*; wealth). This...

This was an analogy that people of the time avoided, yet the commentary (the *shū*) circulated widely; [I] did not dare to alter it rashly. Ying Kaoshu (the first character pronounced with the *yǒu* and *qīng* rhymes; according to the *Shuowen*, water flows from Yangcheng in Yingchuan). The *Jiaochao* cites the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, stating:

"Ying Kaoshu was the Border Guard (*fēngrén*) of Ying Valley. The commentary states: "One who oversees the boundaries. The *Spring and Autumn Annals* Sub-commentary (*Zhèngyì*) says: "According to the *Rites of Zhou*, the Border Guards (*fēngrén*) were in charge of establishing the borders and planting boundary markers.

Zheng Xuan said: 'There are boundary mounds upon the borders, like the demarcations of the present day. To speak of the 'Border Guard of Ying Valley' is to designate the office by the name of the location. It appears that the Border Guards were officials in charge of boundaries who resided in frontier towns. Ying Valley was a frontier town of the state, similar to a border city guarded today."

(The Village Head). *Xù* (pronounced with the initial *xǔ* and the rhyme *liù*; it means to exert effort and to exhort; that is, to encourage and strengthen the two powers of faith and resolve). Now he receives the divine method (concluding the previous account of Maudgalyāyana’s inquiry and instruction).
Its spiritual efficacy is verified (concluding the previous account of the benefits obtained by making offerings).

The commentary records that "zé" (the first character pronounced *zài*; "zé yě" means "it is thus," serving as a particle of emphasis identical to the word "qiě"; there is no need to interpret it as "to carry"). "Bōlà" (the second character pronounced *lǎ*; this is a Sanskrit term pronounced with the retroflex *ṛ* sound).

Sui Yang (the lower character is pronounced *yàng*; the imperial title of the Sui dynasty). *Qīng* (pronounced *qīng*; a latrine). *É* (pronounced *é*). Héhé (both are to be called with the departing tone;

it is an onomatopoeia). *Yàn kè* (for *yàn*, the departing tone; in the *Shū yìnyì*, it is pronounced *yàn*; another interpretation offers a different meaning; for a detailed analysis of the selection of meanings, refer to the commentary). *Xù* (cut by *chì* and *liù*; to accumulate). *Xiāng* (in older editions of the commentary, this is written as *xiāng*; this is a scribal error).

The commentary follows and explains [the text]. Now, relying on the ancient sub-commentaries (*shu*), I have verified and corrected it to read "box" (*xiāng*). Therefore, I cite the *Mao Shi* along with its annotations to substantiate this). Regarding the *Yi Zhuan* (the word *xi* is pronounced *xì*; it means "to link"). The old edition of the commentary cites an annotation from the *Qianziwen*:

"Two people with one heart. However, this is neither a canonical scripture nor a history; moreover, that person’s surname was Guǎn, his name Níng, and his courtesy name Yòu'ān. To take the name of a single individual and treat him as two different people is difficult to rely upon as a basis.

Therefore, I have now corrected these based on the *Commentary on the Appended Phrases* (*Zhouyi Xici*) along with its annotations. Regarding the section on "Dwelling in Peace" (*anju*): several passages in this excerpt contain errors that significantly harm the underlying principles; these have already been corrected according to the Vinaya. As for the remainder, the meaning can be somewhat reconciled, so I have retained the traditional readings.

Regarding "floatation-sack" (*fúnáng*): the second character is pronounced *núdāng* (cut). A sack with a bottom is called a *náng*, while one without a bottom is called a *tuó*. This citation from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* contains five analogies for begging, corresponding to the offenses of the five categories (*pañcāpatti*).

These will now be cited in sequence and correlated for clarification. Regarding "perfect governance" (*zhìzhì*): the second character is pronounced *zhì*. Formerly it was written as the character *lǐ* (principle), because the Tang Emperor Gaozong tabooed the word *zhì*. Thus, people used *lǐ* instead. Now, I follow the original text of the *Shangshu*.

(Also). *Qì* (upper tone; meaning "numerous"). *Wánjù* (upper tone; meaning "to settle and gather"). *Shèròu* (upper tone; meaning "to set aside and discard"). *Yízhī* (upper departing tone; meaning "to present as a gift").
The above phonetic glosses for the two fascicles have been selected and omitted in accordance with the original text.
